cards.title: One-way functions from \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\)
cards.formal:
Does \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) imply the existence of a classical one-way function secure against uniform probabilistic polynomial-time inversion? Precisely, under that premise alone, must there exist one total deterministic polynomial-time computable function
\[f:\{0,1\}^{*}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{*}\]
such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time inverter \(I\) and every real constant \(c>0\), there is an integer \(N\ge1\) for which every \(n\ge N\) satisfies
\[\Pr_{x\sim U_n,\,r}\!\left[z\in\{0,1\}^{n}\ \land\ f(z)=f(x),\quad z=I(1^n,f(x);r)\right]\le n^{-c}?\]
Here \(U_n\) is the uniform distribution on length-\(n\) binary strings, and \(r\) denotes the inverter’s independent fair random coins. Finding any length-\(n\) preimage counts as successful inversion. The function must be fixed before the inverter and security exponent are chosen.
cards.definitions:
All computation is by ordinary multitape Turing machines with fixed finite programs and finite tape alphabets, unit-cost transitions and explicitly encoded inputs/outputs. There are no oracles, nonuniform advice strings, quantum operations or external uncounted computations. Polynomial time means a bound \(a(m+1)^d\) on every input of length \(m\), for fixed positive integers \(a,d\) depending on the machine. Reading input, evaluating functions, generating random bits and writing outputs are included in the running time.

A language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) lies in \(\mathrm P\) if one deterministic polynomial-time machine decides membership on every input. It lies in \(\mathrm{NP}\) if membership is equivalent to existence of a binary certificate of polynomially bounded length accepted by one deterministic polynomial-time verifier. The verifier is total on all input/certificate pairs. The premise compares these uniform total decision classes, not circuit classes or average-case classes.

The function \(f\) is computed by one deterministic machine in polynomial time on every binary string, including the empty string; its output length is consequently polynomially bounded. No length-preserving or injectivity requirement is imposed. Its description is public and may be built into an inverter’s fixed program. Security is required at positive input lengths \(n\).

An inverter \(I\) receives the explicitly separated pair \((1^n,y)\), with the input length \(n\) in unary and \(y\) a binary string. It has one fixed program, obtains independent unbiased coin bits, and halts within one polynomial in \(n+|y|+1\) on every input and every coin sequence. It outputs a finite binary string or the failure symbol \(\bot\). Its polynomial may depend on \(I\) but not on \(n,y\). An output of the wrong length, \(\bot\), or a string whose image differs from \(y\) is a failure. The retained convention is same-length inversion: a preimage must have the sampled input length \(n\). The original sampled \(x\) need not be recovered if another such preimage exists.

The experiment first draws \(x\) uniformly from all \(2^n\) inputs, evaluates \(y=f(x)\), and runs \(I\) with fresh independent random coins. Thus outputs with more length-\(n\) preimages are encountered more frequently; \(y\) is not sampled uniformly from the range. The probability is a finite exact average, since the inverter has an all-path polynomial clock. The constants in the forward evaluation bound and the inverter bound can differ.

Negligible inversion probability means exactly the quantifier order
\[\exists f\ \forall I\ \forall c>0\ \exists N=N(f,I,c)\ \forall n\ge N.\]
Neither the inverter nor \(f\) can vary with the input length, although each may use the supplied length in its computation. Security at only infinitely many lengths is not the target. Failure of one-wayness for a fixed \(f\) means that some single polynomial-time inverter has success greater than \(n^{-c}\), for some fixed \(c>0\), at arbitrarily large lengths; the logical negation does not demand success at every sufficiently large length.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the implication in the statement or its full logical negation. An affirmative proof must establish, under \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) alone, a total function with one uniform polynomial-time evaluator and the stated eventual negligible-success guarantee against every permitted inverter. No additional circuit lower bound, average-case hardness assumption or conjectured cryptographic primitive may be left unproved. The proof may use the premise without proving it separately.

A negative proof must establish \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) and show that for every total deterministic polynomial-time function \(f\), there exist a single permitted inverter \(I\) and a constant \(c>0\) such that for every threshold \(N\), some \(n\ge N\) has inversion success greater than \(n^{-c}\). An oracle separation, a barrier to one reduction technique, or an efficient inverter for a particular candidate is insufficient. The target is an existence implication and imposes no black-box-construction requirement or prescribed proof method.

context_blocks.text: Existence of one-way functions implies \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). The converse asks for much more than a function with occasional difficult inputs: the security experiment generates inputs uniformly, and every efficient inverter must have negligible overall success at all sufficiently large lengths. Worst-case inversion difficulty by itself does not give that distributional guarantee.

Average-case decision hardness and one-wayness have distinct requirements. The former can concern a language paired with a chosen feasible instance distribution. Here instances are images of uniform inputs under the same efficiently computable function whose inversion is tested. The adversary may exploit collisions and only needs to find any permitted preimage; hard reconstruction of the original sampled input is not enough.

Håstad–Impagliazzo–Levin–Luby establish that one-way functions suffice for cryptographic pseudorandom generators, with the converse also holding. A cryptographic generator efficiently expands uniform random bits so that polynomial-time statistical tests cannot distinguish its outputs from uniform strings with nonnegligible advantage. This explains the broad consequences of the primitive without adding encryption, a trapdoor or injectivity to this question.

Known nonadaptive oracle-reduction barriers show that certain reductions from NP-complete worst-case problems to average inversion would collapse the polynomial hierarchy. Such reductions choose all their oracle questions before receiving answers and must work for every oracle satisfying the average-success promise. The barrier concerns that reduction class; it does not establish the negation of the unrestricted implication.

Liu–Pass give an unconditional equivalence between one-way functions and a particular boundary-hardness condition for randomized time-bounded description complexity. Their corresponding statement for deterministic description complexity uses an exponential circuit-hardness assumption. An equivalence with a specialized hardness condition does not by itself establish that condition from \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\); the inspected paper explicitly retains this missing connection.

The April 2026 Liu–Mazor–Pass paper derives conditional pseudorandom generators and restricted zero-knowledge consequences from hardness of specific gap-description problems. A conditional generator’s seed distribution may be inefficient to sample, whereas an ordinary cryptographic generator uses uniform seeds. The paper retains additional hardness hypotheses and says that obtaining ordinary one-way functions from plain worst-case gap hardness remains beyond its results.

The eventual security requirement matters to both sides of the question. To disprove one-wayness of a candidate, a fixed inverter with noticeable success at arbitrarily large lengths is enough. To prove one-wayness, security on a sparse infinite subsequence is insufficient. The requested implication therefore cannot be replaced by an infinitely-often variant without changing the target.

cards.title: Public-key encryption from one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of a classical cryptographic one-way function imply the existence of a classical public-key encryption scheme for one-bit messages, with negligible correctness error and security against every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time chosen-plaintext adversary, in the plain model specified below? This is an unrelativized existence implication. The construction and its security proof may inspect the program of the one-way function and need not be black-box.
cards.definitions:
The security parameter is \(\lambda\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\), supplied as the unary string \(1^{\lambda}\). All algorithms are uniform classical Turing machines on bits: one finite program works for every parameter, with no advice, oracle or quantum resource. A PPT algorithm uses independent fair random bits and halts within a fixed polynomial in its total input length on every input and every random tape. Each algorithm has its own polynomial bound. Reading, computing, random-bit generation, communication and output all have ordinary bit-machine costs. Bit-string tuples use the component encoding \(s\mapsto1^{|s|}0s\); finite lists prepend an encoded binary component count. Binary integers have no leading zeros except the representation of zero. Explicitly proved polynomial-time equivalent encodings are acceptable.

A function \(\nu:\mathbb N_{\geq1}\to[0,1]\) is negligible if \(\forall d\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\;\exists\lambda_0\;\forall\lambda\geq\lambda_0:\nu(\lambda)\leq\lambda^{-d}\). A one-way function is a total deterministic polynomial-time map \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) such that for every uniform classical PPT algorithm \(I\),
\[\Pr[\,|Y|=\lambda\ \land\ f(Y)=f(X)\,]\]
is negligible, where \(X\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\) and \(Y=I(1^{\lambda},f(X))\). The probability also includes the independent coins of \(I\). Any preimage of length \(\lambda\) counts as success; failure or a different output length does not. Injectivity and preservation of length are not required.

A candidate encryption scheme is a triple \((\mathsf{Gen},\mathsf{Enc},\mathsf{Dec})\) of uniform polynomial-time algorithms. The randomized algorithm \(\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda})\) returns two finite bit strings \((pk,sk)\), the public and secret keys. The randomized algorithm \(\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,b)\), for \(b\in\{0,1\}\), returns a finite ciphertext bit string \(c\). The deterministic algorithm \(\mathsf{Dec}(1^{\lambda},sk,c)\) returns \(0\), \(1\), or the failure symbol \(\bot\). Algorithms are total on well-formed inputs, including arbitrary key and ciphertext strings; malformed encodings return a fixed failure response in polynomial time. Their runtime bounds use the full input length, so all honestly generated keys and ciphertexts have length polynomial in \(\lambda\). Encryption uses fresh private coins on each invocation, independently of key generation.

Correctness requires, for each \(b\in\{0,1\}\), negligible
\[\Pr[\mathsf{Dec}(1^{\lambda},sk,\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,b))\ne b],\qquad (pk,sk)\leftarrow\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda}),\]
over key-generation and encryption coins; failure counts as an error. This is average correctness over honestly generated keys and coins, not a requirement that every key and every random tape decrypt correctly.

Security requires that for every uniform classical PPT algorithm \(E\) outputting a bit, its advantage
\[\left|\Pr[E(1^{\lambda},pk,c)=B]-\frac12\right|\]
be negligible, where \((pk,sk)\leftarrow\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda})\), \(B\) is an independent uniform bit, and \(c\leftarrow\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,B)\). All coins, including those of \(E\), are independent except for the displayed dependencies. The programs are public. The adversary may perform any polynomial amount of computation and generate encryptions of arbitrarily chosen bits using \(pk\) and its own fresh coins; it has no decryption oracle. This is the standard one-bit indistinguishability formulation of chosen-plaintext security for public-key encryption. Security holds for every such adversary, with its own negligible bound eventually at all sufficiently large parameters. There is no restriction to infinitely many parameters, to an average choice of the adversary, or to a particular fixed polynomial attack time.

There is no pre-existing shared secret, trusted setup, random oracle, auxiliary hardness assumption or quantum information. The quantifier order is: if some \(f\) satisfying the stated one-wayness condition exists, then some single scheme satisfying the format, cost, correctness and security requirements exists. Neither its algorithms nor its proof must use \(f\) through an oracle interface. A uniform compiler taking the code of \(f\) as input is not an additional requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this existence implication or its logical negation. A positive answer must obtain the stated uniform classical encryption scheme from the existence of one-way functions alone and prove the full correctness and chosen-plaintext guarantees. A negative answer must prove that a one-way function exists while no scheme in the stated class meets both guarantees. An oracle separation, a lower bound on a restricted class of reductions, a break of one proposed scheme, or a construction requiring some additional unproved hardness assumption does not settle the target. One-bit messages are the specified target; polynomially many independently encrypted bits yield the standard extension to longer messages with polynomial security loss. A cited or unchecked proof claim does not satisfy Lean acceptance.
cards.why: This asks whether the minimal generic assumption supporting private-key cryptography also supports encryption to a receiver whose encryption key is public. It tests whether the apparent need for additional structure in public-key constructions reflects a true difference in existence or only the known reductions. The distinction controls the foundational assumptions needed for confidential communication without a pre-existing shared secret.

context_blocks.text: Computing a one-way function is easy, while recovering a preimage of a random image is hard. Public-key encryption needs a different asymmetry: public information must enable encryption while related private information enables decryption. The question concerns the existence of that additional capability, rather than a performance improvement for a particular deployed scheme.

Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin and Luby establish that one-way functions and pseudorandom generators have equivalent existence. A pseudorandom generator deterministically expands a short uniform seed into a longer string that efficient tests cannot distinguish from uniform. Together with the standard consequences surveyed in their conclusion, this supports private-key encryption from one-wayness. Private-key encryption starts from shared secret information, which the present target does not provide.

The target retains the saved one-bit message convention. Public encryptability means an observer can generate its own chosen-plaintext examples, so concealing only a message from an observer denied that capability would be a weaker target. Indistinguishability also requires randomized encryption: a deterministic correct scheme would make the two publicly computable ciphertexts distinguishable. The card permits negligible average decryption error and does not silently impose perfect correctness.

A secure one-bit scheme extends to any prescribed polynomial message length under the same public key, with polynomial loss in correctness and distinguishing advantage. It also implies passive key agreement. General interactive key agreement permits more communication than the two-message interaction associated with public-key encryption, so the related key-agreement card has a separate conclusion. These implications concern existence and security; no additional transmission or authentication task is part of this card.

Impagliazzo and Rudich exhibit an oracle world with one-way permutations but no secure key agreement. Since public-key encryption implies key agreement, the separation also constrains public-key encryption in that world. The original result is from STOC 1989; this audit read the author manuscript dated 28 May 1994. Such a relativized separation does not assert that ordinary one-way functions exist without ordinary public-key encryption.

Barak and Mahmoody’s corrected April 2009 Theorem 1.1 quantifies the random-oracle limitation: if each party makes at most \(q\) queries and agreement probability is at least \(\rho\), then for every \(0<\delta<1\) an observer can recover Bob’s output with probability at least \(\rho-\delta\) using at most \((16q/\delta)^{2}\) oracle queries. Other computation is unbounded. The paper explicitly corrects an earlier proof and does not extend this quadratic bound unchanged to a random-permutation oracle. It is not a polynomial-time attack on all ordinary encryption schemes.

Chatterjee, Mu and Vasudevan’s EUROCRYPT 2026 construction assumes hardness of planted MinRank on random instances, equivalently a random rank-metric decoding problem. The matrices are random rather than masked members of a specially structured decodable code family. This broadens the available concrete foundations for encryption, but hardness of that specific distribution is not supplied merely by the existence of an arbitrary one-way function. The introduction and definitions were checked in the 2025 preprint; its full security proof was not independently verified.

Li, Ni and Zan’s August 2023 preprint explicitly claims a positive answer from one-way functions. Its statement was checked, but this review has not verified the proof or found a conclusive later assessment. The card therefore records an uncertain scientific status and remains active; neither an accepted resolution nor a refutation of that claim is asserted.

cards.context:
Computing a one-way function is easy, while recovering a preimage of a random image is hard. Public-key encryption needs a different asymmetry: public information must enable encryption while related private information enables decryption. The question concerns the existence of that additional capability, rather than a performance improvement for a particular deployed scheme.

Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin and Luby establish that one-way functions and pseudorandom generators have equivalent existence. A pseudorandom generator deterministically expands a short uniform seed into a longer string that efficient tests cannot distinguish from uniform. Together with the standard consequences surveyed in their conclusion, this supports private-key encryption from one-wayness. Private-key encryption starts from shared secret information, which the present target does not provide.

The target retains the saved one-bit message convention. Public encryptability means an observer can generate its own chosen-plaintext examples, so concealing only a message from an observer denied that capability would be a weaker target. Indistinguishability also requires randomized encryption: a deterministic correct scheme would make the two publicly computable ciphertexts distinguishable. The card permits negligible average decryption error and does not silently impose perfect correctness.

A secure one-bit scheme extends to any prescribed polynomial message length under the same public key, with polynomial loss in correctness and distinguishing advantage. It also implies passive key agreement. General interactive key agreement permits more communication than the two-message interaction associated with public-key encryption, so the related key-agreement card has a separate conclusion. These implications concern existence and security; no additional transmission or authentication task is part of this card.

Impagliazzo and Rudich exhibit an oracle world with one-way permutations but no secure key agreement. Since public-key encryption implies key agreement, the separation also constrains public-key encryption in that world. The original result is from STOC 1989; this audit read the author manuscript dated 28 May 1994. Such a relativized separation does not assert that ordinary one-way functions exist without ordinary public-key encryption.

Barak and Mahmoody’s corrected April 2009 Theorem 1.1 quantifies the random-oracle limitation: if each party makes at most \(q\) queries and agreement probability is at least \(\rho\), then for every \(0<\delta<1\) an observer can recover Bob’s output with probability at least \(\rho-\delta\) using at most \((16q/\delta)^{2}\) oracle queries. It is not a polynomial-time attack on all ordinary encryption schemes.

The matrices are random rather than masked members of a specially structured decodable code family. This broadens the available concrete foundations for encryption, but hardness of that specific distribution is not supplied merely by the existence of an arbitrary one-way function. cards.title: Circuit obfuscation from polynomial-hard LWE
cards.formal:
Does ordinary polynomial-hard decisional Learning With Errors imply indistinguishability obfuscation for all polynomial-size Boolean circuits, with no additional hardness, circular-security or leakage-resilience hypothesis?

Precisely, let \(H_{\mathrm{LWE}}\) be the fixed classical nonuniform decisional-LWE assumption below, with prime modulus \(q(n)\ge n^4\) and Gaussian width \(n\). Let \(I_{\mathrm{circ}}\) assert the existence of the uniform classical probabilistic obfuscator defined below, with security against all classical polynomial-size circuit families. The proposition to establish or refute is the implication
\[H_{\mathrm{LWE}}\ \Longrightarrow\ I_{\mathrm{circ}}.\]
All modulus, error, sample, correctness and security quantifiers are fixed in the definitions. Neither subexponential hardness nor additional information supplied about the LWE secret or errors is part of the premise.
cards.definitions:
LWE assumption. For each integer \(n\ge2\), let \(q(n)\) be the least prime at least \(n^4\), and let \(\mathbb Z_q\) mean integers modulo \(q=q(n)\). Define the probability distribution \(\chi_n\) on the integers by
\[\Pr_{e\leftarrow\chi_n}[e=t]=\frac{\exp(-\pi t^2/n^2)}{\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}\exp(-\pi j^2/n^2)}\quad(t\in\mathbb Z).\]
The positive normalizing sum converges. This specifies an exact mathematical distribution; it is not an input consisting of real-number samples or a unit-cost real-arithmetic oracle.

For every positive integer-valued polynomially bounded sample-count function \(m=m(n)\), compare the following distributions:
\[X_n=(A,As+e\bmod q),\qquad Y_n=(A,u),\]
where \(A\) is uniform in \(\mathbb Z_q^{m\times n}\), \(s\) is uniform in \(\mathbb Z_q^n\), the \(m\) entries of \(e\) are independent samples of \(\chi_n\), and \(u\) is uniform in \(\mathbb Z_q^m\). All these choices are mutually independent before forming \(As+e\); the same secret \(s\) is used in every row. Reduce each integer error modulo \(q\). Each residue is encoded as its canonical representative in \(\{0,\ldots,q-1\}\), using \(\lceil\log_2q\rceil\) bits, and the matrix and vector are fully listed. Public parameters \(n,m,q\) accompany the encoding. No leakage or other secret-dependent hint is given.

An ensemble pair is computationally indistinguishable if, for every family \((D_n)\) of classical Boolean circuits with description length bounded by some polynomial in \(n\),
\[\left|\Pr[D_n(X_n)=1]-\Pr[D_n(Y_n)=1]\right|\]
is negligible in \(n\). A nonnegative function \(\nu\) is negligible if for every positive integer \(c\), there is \(n_0\) such that \(\nu(n)\le n^{-c}\) whenever \(n\ge n_0\). Circuit families need not be uniformly computable and may hardwire polynomially many advice bits. Deterministic distinguishers suffice here; private random coins can equivalently be allowed. The assertion \(H_{\mathrm{LWE}}\) is indistinguishability for every such sample count and every such distinguisher family. This is asymptotic polynomial security, not a bound on the cost of attacks at a single numerical parameter.

Circuit model. A circuit has \(a\ge0\) labelled input bits, \(g\ge0\) gates in topological order, and \(b\ge1\) designated output wires. Gates are binary AND or OR, unary NOT, or constants 0 and 1. Wires may be reused. Gate predecessors must be inputs or earlier gates; each output names an existing input or gate. This defines a total deterministic function \(C:\{0,1\}^a\to\{0,1\}^b\). Constant gates are allowed as part of the conventional Boolean basis.

Use the explicit encoding \(1^a0\), then length-delimited counts \(U(g),U(b)\), followed by every gate and every output index. Here \(U(t)=1^\ell0s\), where \(s\) is the canonical binary expansion of \(t\), \(\ell=|s|\), and zero uses \(s=0\). Each gate has a fixed three-bit type tag and the appropriate zero, one or two \(U\)-encoded predecessor indices. Input nodes come first, then gate nodes; unused tags and out-of-range indices are invalid. Each output is a \(U\)-encoded index, and trailing bits are forbidden. Define \(|C|\) to be the total description length. Thus every input, gate and output is explicitly counted; exponentially many undeclared inputs or succinctly generated gate lists are not allowed. Two circuits are equivalent when their input/output arities coincide and their outputs agree on every input, exactly.

Obfuscator. There is one classical probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(O\) and positive integers \(K,d\). On \((1^\lambda,C)\), for every integer \(\lambda\ge2\), it halts within \(K(\lambda+|C|+1)^d\) bit steps on every sequence of independent fair random bits. On a valid circuit it always returns a valid circuit with the same input/output arities, of description length at most the same polynomial bound. Malformed descriptions may be rejected, within the clock. All input reading, randomness, arithmetic and output writing are charged. There is no advice, quantum state, oracle, trusted setup or free preprocessing.

Functionality requires a uniform error bound over all circuits at each size scale. For every positive integer polynomial bound \(p\), there exists a negligible function \(\mu_p\) such that for every \(\lambda\ge2\) and valid \(|C|\le p(\lambda)\),
\[\Pr_r[\forall x\in\{0,1\}^a:\ O(1^\lambda,C;r)(x)=C(x)]\ge1-\mu_p(\lambda).\]
One successful output must be correct on all inputs simultaneously; a separate high success probability for each input is insufficient.

Indistinguishability requires that for every pair of circuit sequences \((C_{0,\lambda},C_{1,\lambda})\) of polynomially bounded description length, with equal description lengths, matching arities and equivalent functions for each \(\lambda\), and every classical polynomial-size distinguisher family \((D_\lambda)\), the advantage
\[\left|\Pr_r[D_\lambda(O(1^\lambda,C_{0,\lambda};r))=1]-\Pr_r[D_\lambda(O(1^\lambda,C_{1,\lambda};r))=1]\right|\]
is negligible in \(\lambda\). The sequences themselves need not be efficiently generated. Distinguishers can hardwire the circuit pair and arbitrary polynomial-length auxiliary information. Variable-length outputs are presented with their length and zero padding to a common polynomial bound determined by the pair's size bound and the clock; actual length remains visible. Probabilities use fresh independent obfuscator coins. No efficiently verifiable certificate of circuit equivalence is supplied or required. The assertion \(I_{\mathrm{circ}}\) is existence of one machine and clock meeting both functionality and security for every polynomial size scale.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of \(H_{\mathrm{LWE}}\Rightarrow I_{\mathrm{circ}}\), or of its full logical negation. A positive construction must prove the stated uniform efficiency, simultaneous all-input functionality, and security against all nonuniform polynomial-size classical distinguishers using only the specified LWE premise and proved mathematical facts. Any parameter changes used inside a construction must be justified from that premise. The literal negation is \(H_{\mathrm{LWE}}\land\neg I_{\mathrm{circ}}\). Refuting one candidate, excluding only black-box reductions, or separating the notions in an oracle world does not establish this unrelativized negation. A construction needing stronger quantitative hardness, circular security or auxiliary-leakage resilience does not prove the specified implication unless those properties are themselves derived from the fixed premise.
cards.why: General indistinguishability obfuscation supports cryptographic capabilities well beyond ordinary encryption. Deriving it from one standard noisy-linear-equation assumption would connect that broad power to a much simpler foundation. The precise quantitative premise matters: an implication from stronger security or from secret-dependent hints does not determine the power of ordinary polynomial-hard LWE.

context_blocks.text: Indistinguishability obfuscation compares two implementations of the same function. It requires their obfuscations to be computationally indistinguishable when the original descriptions have equal size. It does not promise that a function hides information already revealed by its outputs, nor does it equate functionally different programs. These distinctions separate the mathematical notion from an informal claim that code is unreadable.

Barak and coauthors rule out general obfuscation under the stronger virtual-black-box requirement: whatever can be learned from the code should be reproducible from oracle access to the function. Their revised full paper explicitly introduces the weaker indistinguishability comparison. Its impossibility result therefore does not supply a negative answer to this card.

LWE describes noisy linear equations over a finite residue field. The same hidden vector is used in all rows, while fresh independent errors perturb the products. Regev connects suitable LWE distributions to worst-case lattice problems by a quantum reduction. That historical foundation is evidence for studying LWE, not a proof of the exact classical nonuniform hardness hypothesis selected here. In particular, its rounded-Gaussian notation should not be silently identified with this card’s integer-Gaussian convention.

Jain, Lin and Sahai construct iO using four well-studied assumptions. The February 2026 journal theorem lists LWE, sparse-noise LPN over large prime fields, a local Boolean pseudorandom generator, and DLIN in bilinear groups. It requires subexponential security guarantees and a subexponential LWE modulus-to-noise ratio. Both the extra assumptions and the quantitative regime exceed the premise here. The journal publication follows earlier work; it is not a new LWE-only construction.

Their follow-up removes LWE from the sufficient set, leaving the other three assumptions. Its introduction explicitly raises the possibility that LWE alone might suffice. Removing one assumption from a conjunction does not show that the removed assumption implies the conclusion. The distinction between subexponential security for its iO theorem and polynomial security for its functional-encryption consequence also remains substantive.

The circular-security construction eliminates factoring and pairing assumptions, but its theorem still assumes subexponential LWE hardness together with a key-randomness circular form of shielded randomness-leakage security. The latter experiment provides structured information involving encryption keys and ciphertext randomness. Its Definition 7 is an additional security premise; plain noisy LWE samples do not contain these hints. The paper also repairs a gap in an earlier efficiency transformation.

Later lattice proposals continue to separate ordinary LWE from strengthened assumptions. Hsieh, Jain and Lin explicitly introduce Circular Security with Random Opening, an LWE-with-hints assumption. Their abstract discusses attacks on earlier hint assumptions and presents the new proposal as a different target for cryptanalysis. No reduction from this card’s ordinary LWE premise is asserted in the inspected abstract.

Cini, Lai and Woo instead use NTRU and a new Equivocal LWE assumption alongside other lattice assumptions. Their abstract qualifies the post-quantum construction and identifies possible cryptanalytic targets. A construction based on lattice assumptions can be an important advance without establishing that plain LWE alone suffices.

The April 2026 authentication preprint, revised in June, likewise distinguishes several claims. Its lattice tool assumes decomposed LWE; its pseudorandom-obfuscation result additionally assumes subexponentially secure iO. A separate general-iO proposal is expressly labelled heuristic. Neither the extra-premise theorem nor that heuristic is a proof of the implication posed here.

The September 2026 trapdoor-function preprint assumes both iO and LWE for copy protection. Its separate LWE-only key-leasing result concerns another primitive. This recent application uses general iO as an input assumption rather than deriving it, so it does not close the source question.

cards.context:
Indistinguishability obfuscation compares two implementations of the same function. It requires their obfuscations to be computationally indistinguishable when the original descriptions have equal size. It does not promise that a function hides information already revealed by its outputs, nor does it equate functionally different programs. These distinctions separate the mathematical notion from an informal claim that code is unreadable.

Barak and coauthors rule out general obfuscation under the stronger virtual-black-box requirement: whatever can be learned from the code should be reproducible from oracle access to the function. Their revised full paper explicitly introduces the weaker indistinguishability comparison. Its impossibility result therefore does not supply a negative answer to this card.

LWE describes noisy linear equations over a finite residue field. The same hidden vector is used in all rows, while fresh independent errors perturb the products. Regev connects suitable LWE distributions to worst-case lattice problems by a quantum reduction. That historical foundation is evidence for studying LWE, not a proof of the exact classical nonuniform hardness hypothesis selected here. In particular, its rounded-Gaussian notation should not be silently identified with this card’s integer-Gaussian convention.

Jain, Lin and Sahai construct iO using four well-studied assumptions. The February 2026 journal theorem lists LWE, sparse-noise LPN over large prime fields, a local Boolean pseudorandom generator, and DLIN in bilinear groups. It requires subexponential security guarantees and a subexponential LWE modulus-to-noise ratio. Both the extra assumptions and the quantitative regime exceed the premise here. The journal publication follows earlier work; it is not a new LWE-only construction.

Their follow-up removes LWE from the sufficient set, leaving the other three assumptions. Its introduction explicitly raises the possibility that LWE alone might suffice. Removing one assumption from a conjunction does not show that the removed assumption implies the conclusion. The distinction between subexponential security for its iO theorem and polynomial security for its functional-encryption consequence also remains substantive.

The circular-security construction eliminates factoring and pairing assumptions, but its theorem still assumes subexponential LWE hardness together with a key-randomness circular form of shielded randomness-leakage security. The latter experiment provides structured information involving encryption keys and ciphertext randomness. Its Definition 7 is an additional security premise; plain noisy LWE samples do not contain these hints. The paper also repairs a gap in an earlier efficiency transformation.

Later lattice proposals continue to separate ordinary LWE from strengthened assumptions. Hsieh, Jain and Lin explicitly introduce Circular Security with Random Opening, an LWE-with-hints assumption. Their abstract discusses attacks on earlier hint assumptions and presents the new proposal as a different target for cryptanalysis. No reduction from this card’s ordinary LWE premise is asserted in the inspected abstract.

Cini, Lai and Woo instead use NTRU and a new Equivocal LWE assumption alongside other lattice assumptions. Their abstract qualifies the post-quantum construction and identifies possible cryptanalytic targets. A construction based on lattice assumptions can be an important advance without establishing that plain LWE alone suffices.

The April 2026 authentication preprint, revised in June, likewise distinguishes several claims. Its lattice tool assumes decomposed LWE; its pseudorandom-obfuscation result additionally assumes subexponentially secure iO. A separate general-iO proposal is expressly labelled heuristic. Neither the extra-premise theorem nor that heuristic is a proof of the implication posed here.

The September 2026 trapdoor-function preprint assumes both iO and LWE for copy protection. Its separate LWE-only key-leasing result concerns another primitive. This recent application uses general iO as an input assumption rather than deriving it, so it does not close the source question.

benchmark_focus.reason: General indistinguishability obfuscation supports cryptographic capabilities well beyond ordinary encryption. Deriving it from one standard noisy-linear-equation assumption would connect that broad power to a much simpler foundation. The precise quantitative premise matters: an implication from stronger security or from secret-dependent hints does not determine the power of ordinary polynomial-hard LWE.

cards.title: Unleveled fully homomorphic encryption from LWE alone
cards.formal:
Does the ordinary polynomial-modulus decisional Learning With Errors assumption specified below imply the existence of a classical compact fully homomorphic public-key encryption scheme whose keys are generated without a bound on the size or depth of the circuits subsequently evaluated?

The scheme must be secure against nonuniform polynomial-size classical adversaries given both its encryption and evaluation keys. Its only hardness assumption may be the stated ordinary LWE assumption; no independent circular-security or key-dependent-message assumption is allowed.
cards.definitions:
Fix the following precise LWE hypothesis. For every integer \(c\ge3\), let \(q_c(d)\) be the least prime at least \(d^c\). For every positive integer-valued polynomially bounded sample-count function \(M(d)\), sample independently
\[
 A\leftarrow\mathbb Z_{q_c(d)}^{M(d)\times d},\qquad
 s\leftarrow\mathbb Z_{q_c(d)}^d,\qquad
 u\leftarrow\mathbb Z_{q_c(d)}^{M(d)}
\]
uniformly, and let the coordinates of \(e\) be independent integers with probability proportional to \(\exp(-\pi z^2/(4d))\), reduced modulo \(q_c(d)\). Here \(\mathbb Z_q\) is the ring of integers modulo \(q\). The hypothesis is that the distributions
\[
 (A,As+e\bmod q_c(d))\quad\text{and}\quad(A,u)
\]
are computationally indistinguishable against every family of nonuniform classical randomized circuits of size polynomial in \(d\). That is, the absolute difference of their acceptance probabilities is negligible in \(d\). The integer \(c\) and the polynomial sample bound are fixed before \(d\) grows. A distinguisher may know them and \(d\). The noise is the discrete Gaussian \(D_{\mathbb Z,2\sqrt d}\); no encryptions of secrets, correlated auxiliary hints or circular-security statements are included in this assumption.

A nonnegative function \(\mu(t)\) is negligible if for every integer \(a\ge1\), there is \(t_a\) such that \(\mu(t)\le t^{-a}\) for every \(t\ge t_a\). Circuit size counts gates, input bits and private random bits, using fan-in-two Boolean gates and unary negation. Nonuniform means that each circuit may be chosen independently at each parameter value, with no efficient procedure producing the family. These are classical adversaries, not quantum ones.

The requested scheme has one fixed tuple of uniform classical algorithms
\[
 \operatorname{Gen}(1^\lambda)\to(pk,evk,sk),\quad
 \operatorname{Enc}(pk,b)\to c,\quad
 \operatorname{Eval}(evk,F,c_1,\ldots,c_t)\to c_F,\quad
 \operatorname{Dec}(sk,c)\to b.
\]
All algorithms may also receive \(1^\lambda\) implicitly. Generation, encryption and evaluation may use fresh independent fair random bits; decryption is deterministic. Generation and bit encryption have polynomial worst-case bit running time in \(\lambda\). Evaluation runs in time polynomial in \(\lambda\) and its complete input length. The model is an ordinary multitape Turing machine; no ideal cryptographic oracle is available.

Plaintexts are bits. The circuit \(F\) is explicitly given by its gate list, has \(t\) inputs and one output, and uses fan-in-two AND and OR and unary NOT. The generation algorithm receives no circuit, circuit-size bound or depth bound. There is one fixed polynomial \(P\) bounding the lengths of \(pk,evk,sk\), fresh bit ciphertexts and evaluated one-bit ciphertexts, as well as the time for decrypting these ciphertexts, by \(P(\lambda)\). This bound is independent of \(F\), its input count and its depth. All auxiliary public material is included in \(pk,evk\).

For every fixed polynomial \(p\), there must be a negligible function \(\mu_p(\lambda)\) such that, for every circuit \(F\) with size and input count at most \(p(\lambda)\) and every vector of input bits, independently encrypting those bits, evaluating \(F\), and decrypting yields \(F(b_1,\ldots,b_t)\) with probability at least \(1-\mu_p(\lambda)\). The probability includes all coins of generation, encryption and evaluation. Fresh bit decryption has negligible error as well. The algorithms and \(P\) are fixed before choosing \(p\). Thus one key-generation algorithm supports every polynomial circuit bound; choosing a large fixed polynomial depth during setup does not meet the quantifiers.

Security means that for every nonuniform polynomial-size classical circuit family \(T_\lambda\),
\[
 \left|\Pr[T_\lambda(pk,evk,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,0))=1]
       -\Pr[T_\lambda(pk,evk,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,1))=1]\right|
\]
is negligible in \(\lambda\). Each experiment generates a fresh key tuple and fresh encryption and adversary randomness. Since the public key allows arbitrary further encryptions, this is bit-message chosen-plaintext indistinguishability. The requested theorem must derive this security from the precise LWE hypothesis above. It is not a request to prove LWE hardness unconditionally.

There is no external trusted setup, subsequent secret-key assistance, random oracle or additional hardness premise. Bootstrapping and public encryptions involving secret-key bits are permitted if their security is proved from ordinary LWE. In particular, the absence of a circular-security assumption is a requirement on the proof, not a ban on a syntactic form of evaluation key. Polynomial hardness of LWE is the assumption: subexponential hardness, functional encryption and obfuscation may not simply be assumed independently.

The correctness condition is evaluation of one arbitrary polynomial-size circuit on fresh ciphertexts. A stronger guarantee for indefinitely composing new evaluations on already evaluated ciphertexts is not an extra requirement here. The related TCS-6871 instead asks for an operational reduction from worst-case polynomial-factor GapSVP, allowing quantum computation in that reduction; it has a different stated foundation.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked construction of one scheme, its uniform running-time and compactness bounds, the correctness guarantee for every polynomial circuit-size bound, and a proof of its security from exactly the specified LWE hypothesis; or give a complete Lean-checked refutation of that implication.

An additional circular-security, functional-encryption, obfuscation or stronger-hardness assumption does not meet the positive target. A construction with depth-dependent setup, a quantum evaluator or noncompact decryption also does not qualify. Breaking one proposed scheme, or separating one restricted class of black-box reductions, does not refute the general existence implication. All assumptions of a conditional obstruction must remain explicit. Numerical approximation tolerance does not weaken these asymptotic security, correctness and resource requirements.

cards.formal: Do there exist real constants \(K>0\) and \(0<c<1/2\) such that, for every \(n\ge 1\) and every monotone access structure \(\Gamma\) on \([n]\) with \(\varnothing \notin \Gamma\) and \([n]\in \Gamma\), there exists a perfect secret-sharing scheme for a uniform one-bit secret with \(\max _{i} \log _{2}|S_{i}|\le K\cdot 2^{cn}\), where \(S_{i}\) is the finite alphabet of participant i’s share?

cards.definitions: \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). An access structure \(\Gamma \subseteq 2^{[n]}\) is monotone when \(A\in \Gamma\) and \(A\subseteq B\subseteq [n]\) imply \(B\in \Gamma\). A scheme is a joint probability distribution of a secret B uniform on \(\{0,1\}\) and shares \(X_{i}\in S_{i}\), where each \(S_{i}\) is a finite nonempty set. For each \(A\in \Gamma\) there is a deterministic map \(r_{A}:\prod _{i\in A}S_{i}\to \{0,1\}\) such that \(r_{A}((X_{i})_{i\in A})=B\) with probability one. For each \(A\notin \Gamma\), the conditional distributions of \((X_{i})_{i\in A}\) given \(B=0\) and \(B=1\) are identical. This is exact reconstruction and perfect information-theoretic privacy, with arbitrary collusion within A. Share size is the base-two logarithm of its alphabet cardinality, not its Shannon entropy or the sum over participants. It is normalized by the secret size of one bit. There is no linearity, field, threshold, computation-time or uniform construction requirement. The scheme may depend on the whole finite access structure. K,c must be universal. Rounding \(\log _{2}|S_{i}|\) up to an integer encoding length changes K only by an absolute factor.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that some universal \(K>0\) and \(0<c<1/2\) satisfy the stated worst-share bound for every permitted access structure, or prove the logical negation in Lean. A negative answer must show that for every such \(K,c\) some access structure admits no perfect scheme with that bound, allowing all finite share alphabets and all joint distributions in the definition. The object quantified over is a general scheme; it need not be linear or efficiently constructed.

context_blocks.text: Status update: Nir’s August 2026 preprint states a directly matching positive result. Theorem 1.5 gives every n-party access structure a scheme for a one-bit secret with maximal share size \(2^{0.496n+o(n)}\). Taking any fixed c between 0.496 and \(1/2\) absorbs the sublinear exponent for large n; a universal K covers the finitely many smaller sizes. The proof has not been independently verified here, so the card records an uncertain claimed resolution.

An access structure describes which groups may reconstruct a secret. It need not depend only on group size: a designated participant may be essential, or several different combinations may be authorized. Monotonicity means that an authorized group stays authorized when more participants join. Perfect privacy requires even an unlimited observer holding every share of an unauthorized group to see the same distribution for either secret value.

For example, suppose participant 1 together with either participant 2 or participant 3 may reconstruct a bit B. Choose an independent uniform bit R and give shares R, B XOR R, B XOR R respectively. Either authorized pair recovers B by XOR. Participants 2 and 3 together see two copies of a uniform masked bit and learn nothing about B; participant 1 alone sees independent randomness. This simple access structure needs only one bit per share, but arbitrary patterns can be much harder.

The question concerns the largest participant’s stored alphabet, measured in bits. A share with M possible values costs \(\log _{2} M\), even if its probability distribution has smaller entropy. The total share size is between the largest share and n times that share; these measures have the same leading exponential rate. None of these conventions permits replacing perfect privacy by computational secrecy or small statistical leakage.

The classical construction treats authorized sets separately and can use exponentially large shares. Successive results reduced the exponent; Applebaum and Nir’s 2021 bound is \(1.5^{n+o(n)}\), equivalently \(2^{0.58496\ldots n+o(n)}\). This remains above the half exponent requested in the seminar question. The seminar list prints a different earlier upper exponent; the primary construction is used for the historical bound recorded here.

Linearity is a real restriction: shares are linear combinations of the secret and random field elements. Known exponential lower bounds for linear schemes do not apply to all joint distributions allowed in this card. Likewise, lower bounds for particular reconstruction degrees or graph access structures need their own hypotheses. A general upper bound must handle every monotone authorized-group pattern, with one universal exponent.

The same 2026 preprint gives a half-exponent linear construction and a strictly smaller nonlinear exponent. Its nonlinear theorem is the part relevant to this card; the linear theorem alone would not satisfy \(c<1/2\).

cards.context:
Status update: Nir’s August 2026 preprint states a directly matching positive result. Theorem 1.5 gives every n-party access structure a scheme for a one-bit secret with maximal share size \(2^{0.496n+o(n)}\). Taking any fixed c between 0.496 and \(1/2\) absorbs the sublinear exponent for large n; a universal K covers the finitely many smaller sizes. The proof has not been independently verified here, so the card records an uncertain claimed resolution.

An access structure describes which groups may reconstruct a secret. It need not depend only on group size: a designated participant may be essential, or several different combinations may be authorized. Monotonicity means that an authorized group stays authorized when more participants join. Perfect privacy requires even an unlimited observer holding every share of an unauthorized group to see the same distribution for either secret value.

For example, suppose participant 1 together with either participant 2 or participant 3 may reconstruct a bit B. Choose an independent uniform bit R and give shares R, B XOR R, B XOR R respectively. Either authorized pair recovers B by XOR. Participants 2 and 3 together see two copies of a uniform masked bit and learn nothing about B; participant 1 alone sees independent randomness. This simple access structure needs only one bit per share, but arbitrary patterns can be much harder.

The question concerns the largest participant’s stored alphabet, measured in bits. A share with M possible values costs \(\log _{2} M\), even if its probability distribution has smaller entropy. The total share size is between the largest share and n times that share; these measures have the same leading exponential rate. None of these conventions permits replacing perfect privacy by computational secrecy or small statistical leakage.

The classical construction treats authorized sets separately and can use exponentially large shares. Successive results reduced the exponent; Applebaum and Nir’s 2021 bound is \(1.5^{n+o(n)}\), equivalently \(2^{0.58496\ldots n+o(n)}\). This remains above the half exponent requested in the seminar question. The seminar list prints a different earlier upper exponent; the primary construction is used for the historical bound recorded here.

Linearity is a real restriction: shares are linear combinations of the secret and random field elements. Known exponential lower bounds for linear schemes do not apply to all joint distributions allowed in this card. Likewise, lower bounds for particular reconstruction degrees or graph access structures need their own hypotheses. A general upper bound must handle every monotone authorized-group pattern, with one universal exponent.

The same 2026 preprint gives a half-exponent linear construction and a strictly smaller nonlinear exponent. Its nonlinear theorem is the part relevant to this card; the linear theorem alone would not satisfy \(c<1/2\).

cards.definitions: The security parameter \(n\ge 1\) is given in unary as \(1^{n}\). A single deterministic Turing machine computes f on every finite binary string in time polynomial in its input length. Each inverter I is one classical randomized Turing machine with a worst-case polynomial running-time bound; its input contains \(1^{n}\), so its running time and output length are polynomial in n. It receives \(f(X)\), not X, and has no advice, oracle or secret information. An output Y succeeds exactly when \(f(Y)=f(X)\); any preimage is accepted, even one of a different length from X. An explicit failure output is unsuccessful. No injectivity, permutation property or length preservation is imposed. A probability function is negligible if it is eventually at most \(n^{- d}\) for each integer \(d\ge 1\). The threshold \(n_{0}\) can depend on I and d. Security is averaged over the uniformly sampled input and the inverter’s coins, and must hold for all sufficiently large n, not merely an infinite subsequence.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves, without an unproved computational hardness assumption, that at least one f satisfies the stated efficiency and inversion bound. A negative resolution proves that every polynomial-time f has a polynomial-time inverter whose success is non-negligible: for some \(d\ge 1\) it exceeds \(n^{- d}\) for infinitely many n. A conditional construction or a failure of one particular candidate does not decide existence.

context_blocks.title: What must be hard
context_blocks.text: Computing an output and finding an input that produces it are different tasks. The experiment first generates an ordinary random input, computes its image, and asks an efficient algorithm for any matching input. The difficulty must survive every polynomial-time inverter on this distribution. A few exceptional hard inputs, or a single unsuccessful attack, do not establish this average-case guarantee.

context_blocks.title: Forgetting information is not enough
context_blocks.text: Suppose f keeps the first \(\lceil n/2\rceil\) bits of an n-bit input and discards the rest. Recovering the exact original random string would usually be impossible because the discarded bits are missing. Inversion as defined here is easy: append enough zero bits to obtain an n-bit string with the given prefix. Its image is the required value. This example explains why the success condition accepts any preimage and why simple information loss is not cryptographic hardness.

context_blocks.title: How strong is negligible success?
context_blocks.text: An inverter that succeeds with probability \(1/n^{10}\) still violates the requirement. A probability such as \(2^{- n}\) is negligible, while \(1/n^{10}\) is not. The quantifiers allow a different eventual threshold for each algorithm and each requested exponent. They do not ask for a single finite input length at which every conceivable polynomial-time program is already defeated. The forward computation and all adversaries here are classical; a quantum primitive with different inputs or outputs is a separate model.

context_blocks.title: Relation to other open questions
What the existing theorems establish
context_blocks.text: Levin gives a concrete complete function whose one-wayness follows if any one-way function exists. Completeness identifies a universal candidate; it does not establish the premise. Liu and Pass characterize existence through an average-case hardness property of time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity, the length of a shortest program producing a string within a time bound. Their equivalence does not prove that hardness property. Hirahara and Nanashima’s June 2026 revision characterizes Pessiland, the hypothetical situation with average-case hard problems but no one-way functions. This is another structural theorem, not evidence that either hypothetical world actually occurs. The checked sources do not resolve unconditional existence.

cards.formal:
An access structure specifies which groups of participants may recover a secret; a perfect scheme gives exact recovery to those groups and no information to all other groups. Precise definitions appear in Model & notation. Is the following proposition true?
\[
\exists c>0\ \exists n_0\ge1\ \forall n\ge n_0\ \exists\Gamma_n\subseteq 2^{[n]}:
\quad\forall\text{ perfect schemes for }\Gamma_n,\qquad
\max_{i\in[n]}\log_2|\mathcal S_i|\ge 2^{cn}.
\]
Here \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), the secret is one uniform bit, \(\Gamma_n\) is a monotone access structure with \(\varnothing\notin\Gamma_n\) and \([n]\in\Gamma_n\), and \(\mathcal S_i\) is participant \(i\)'s finite share alphabet. Here \(n_0\) is an integer, and the constants are universal. Sharing and reconstruction may be nonlinear and computationally unbounded.
cards.definitions:
A monotone access structure \(\Gamma\subseteq 2^{[n]}\) is a collection of authorized subsets such that \(A\in\Gamma\) and \(A\subseteq B\subseteq[n]\) imply \(B\in\Gamma\).

A perfect scheme is a joint probability distribution of a uniform secret \(B\in\{0,1\}\) and shares \(X_i\in\mathcal S_i\), where every \(\mathcal S_i\) is finite and nonempty. For each authorized \(A\), a deterministic map from \(\prod_{i\in A}\mathcal S_i\) to \(\{0,1\}\) recovers \(B\) with probability one. For every unauthorized \(A\), the distributions of \((X_i)_{i\in A}\) conditioned on \(B=0\) and on \(B=1\) are identical. Arbitrary joint distributions are allowed; there is no field or linearity restriction.

The cost of a share is \(\log_2|\mathcal S_i|\) bits, and the scheme's cost is the largest of these costs. This measures alphabet size, not Shannon entropy. Rounding to an integer encoding length does not change the exponential-existence question. The access structures need not be efficiently recognizable, and the schemes need not be uniformly constructible. The statement concerns all sufficiently large integer participant counts, with one positive constant \(c\) chosen first.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the quantified exponential lower bound, or a complete proof of its logical negation. A lower bound restricted to linear schemes or to bounded-complexity reconstruction does not meet the universal scheme quantifier. A merely superpolynomial lower bound does not establish the stated exponential bound.
cards.why: This asks whether some access-control policies inherently require exponentially large pieces of a one-bit secret, even with unlimited computation. It would distinguish an intrinsic information cost from limitations of the constructions currently available.

context_blocks.text: For a threshold policy, any sufficiently large group can recover a secret and smaller groups learn nothing. General policies can specify much less regular combinations of participants. The conjecture asks whether that freedom forces an exponential storage cost in the worst case.

Larsen and Simkin study the exponential lower-bound conjecture attributed to Beimel. Their theorem forces either large shares or a large description of reconstruction; it does not remove the reconstruction restriction needed for an unconditional share-size lower bound.

Recent linear and multilinear lower bounds concern schemes whose algebraic structure restricts the sharing or reconstruction maps. Such restrictions are absent here. The September 2026 multislices paper proves exponential lower bounds for a broad family covering known general constructions, rather than for all perfect schemes.

The upper-bound question TCS-0465 asks whether every policy admits shares with an exponent below one half. This lower-bound question asks whether some positive exponential exponent is unavoidable. Both propositions can hold simultaneously; they express different sides of the storage gap.

cards.definitions: For security parameter \(n\ge 1, Gen(1^{n})\) samples a public key pk and a secret key sk. \(Enc(1^{n},pk,m)\) takes a bit \(m\in \{0,1\}\) and fresh independent coins and outputs a binary ciphertext; \(Dec(1^{n},sk,c)\) returns a bit or failure. All three algorithms have worst-case polynomial running time in their input length. Correctness means that max over \(m\in \{0,1\}\) of Pr[Dec(\(1^{n},sk,Enc(1^{n},pk,m)\))≠m] is negligible in n, with probability over key generation, encryption and any decryption coins. For IND-CPA, Gen runs first, and a uniform PPT adversary \(A_{1}\) receives \((1^{n},pk)\) and outputs bits \(m_{0},m_{1}\) and a state z. Independently choose a uniform bit b, generate \(c=Enc(1^{n},pk,m_{b})\), and give \((1^{n},pk,z,c)\) to its second stage \(A_{2}\), which outputs a bit \(b'\). For every pair \((A_{1},A_{2}), |\Pr [b' =b]- 1/2|\) must be negligible. A function \(\eta (n)\) is negligible if, for every integer \(d\ge 1, \eta (n)\le n^{- d}\) for all sufficiently large n. Adversaries may run the public encryption algorithm themselves polynomially many times before and after seeing c; there is no decryption oracle. The model has no trusted correlated setup, ideal oracle, secret advice or quantum algorithms. The receiver’s public key is given authentically; its replacement by an active attacker is outside this confidentiality experiment. One-bit message space fixes an equivalent existence question: independent bit encryptions and the standard hybrid argument extend IND-CPA security to every polynomial message length.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves existence of a scheme satisfying the stated correctness and computational indistinguishability bounds with no unproved computational assumption. A negative resolution proves that every efficient correct scheme fails that security requirement. An assumed-hardness construction, experimental resistance to attacks, or an impossibility theorem only for unbounded attackers does not settle this question.

context_blocks.title: Public information, private recovery
context_blocks.text: A sender receives the public key and can encrypt a message without knowing the secret key. The receiver can decrypt with that secret key. An observer has the same public encryption capability as the sender, so secrecy must come from a limitation on computation rather than from hiding the encryption algorithm. The question asks whether such a limitation can be proved to exist for some efficient scheme.

context_blocks.title: Why the challenge compares two messages
context_blocks.text: The adversary chooses two messages after seeing the public key, then receives an encryption of a fair random choice between them. Guessing always gives success \(1/2\). Security requires every efficient adversary’s additional advantage to be negligible. This is stronger than merely failing to recover a long message exactly: learning one distinguishing bit can already violate the requirement. Restricting the displayed experiment to message bits keeps the existence question concrete without requiring a particular practical ciphertext format.

context_blocks.title: A simple failure of deterministic encryption
context_blocks.text: Imagine that encryption uses no fresh randomness and the two possible messages are 0 and 1. Anyone with the public key can compute both ciphertexts and compare the challenge with them. On keys for which both messages decrypt correctly, the two ciphertexts must differ, so the comparison reveals the challenge bit. Randomized encryption avoids this immediate comparison attack, but randomness by itself is not a proof of security.

context_blocks.title: Which assumptions are still missing?
context_blocks.text: Regev’s lattice-based construction gives classical public-key encryption from learning-with-errors hardness. This is a theorem relating two computational tasks; it does not prove the assumed task hard. In March 2026, Lu, Poremba, Quek and Ramkumar gave another conditional route based on average-case hardness of quantum stabilizer decoding, with classical cryptographic algorithms. A new candidate assumption broadens the foundations available for constructions while leaving unconditional existence unresolved. The word quantum in the underlying decoding problem does not itself make the encryption algorithms quantum.

context_blocks.title: The boundary of the question
context_blocks.text: Secure public-key encryption implies one-way functions and hence \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). The converse implication from arbitrary one-way functions is a separate open question, TCS-6545; proving that implication alone would still leave their existence unproved. Computational security here permits an unbounded adversary to succeed. Consequently, the impossibility of information-theoretic secrecy from only public information does not answer the present question. Chosen-ciphertext security adds access to a decryption oracle and is also a different requirement. The requested theorem concerns precisely efficient classical attackers in the stated chosen-plaintext experiment.

cards.context:
A sender receives the public key and can encrypt a message without knowing the secret key. The receiver can decrypt with that secret key. An observer has the same public encryption capability as the sender, so secrecy must come from a limitation on computation rather than from hiding the encryption algorithm. The question asks whether such a limitation can be proved to exist for some efficient scheme.

The adversary chooses two messages after seeing the public key, then receives an encryption of a fair random choice between them. Guessing always gives success \(1/2\). Security requires every efficient adversary’s additional advantage to be negligible. This is stronger than merely failing to recover a long message exactly: learning one distinguishing bit can already violate the requirement. Restricting the displayed experiment to message bits keeps the existence question concrete without requiring a particular practical ciphertext format.

Imagine that encryption uses no fresh randomness and the two possible messages are 0 and 1. Anyone with the public key can compute both ciphertexts and compare the challenge with them. On keys for which both messages decrypt correctly, the two ciphertexts must differ, so the comparison reveals the challenge bit. Randomized encryption avoids this immediate comparison attack, but randomness by itself is not a proof of security.

Regev’s lattice-based construction gives classical public-key encryption from learning-with-errors hardness. This is a theorem relating two computational tasks; it does not prove the assumed task hard. In March 2026, Lu, Poremba, Quek and Ramkumar gave another conditional route based on average-case hardness of quantum stabilizer decoding, with classical cryptographic algorithms. A new candidate assumption broadens the foundations available for constructions while leaving unconditional existence unresolved. The word quantum in the underlying decoding problem does not itself make the encryption algorithms quantum.

Secure public-key encryption implies one-way functions and hence \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). The converse implication from arbitrary one-way functions is a separate open question, TCS-6545; proving that implication alone would still leave their existence unproved. Computational security here permits an unbounded adversary to succeed. Consequently, the impossibility of information-theoretic secrecy from only public information does not answer the present question. Chosen-ciphertext security adds access to a decryption oracle and is also a different requirement. The requested theorem concerns precisely efficient classical attackers in the stated chosen-plaintext experiment.

cards.formal:
Private information retrieval lets a user recover a selected database bit without revealing its index to either server. Do there exist a real constant \(C>0\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge2\), a classical one-round two-server protocol with perfect correctness and perfect privacy has total communication at most
\[
C(\log_2 n)^k
\]
bits for every database \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), requested index \(i\in[n]\), and outcome of the user's randomness? The two servers each hold the entire database and do not communicate or collude. Model & notation specifies the protocol and exact privacy requirement. There is no computational hardness assumption or bound on local computation.
cards.definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). For each \(n\), a protocol specifies a nonempty finite randomness set \(\mathcal R_n\), query maps \(Q_{1,n},Q_{2,n}\), deterministic answer maps \(A_{1,n},A_{2,n}\), and a deterministic recovery map \(D_n\). Queries and answers are finite binary strings. The user samples \(r\) uniformly from \(\mathcal R_n\), independently of the database, and sends \(q_j=Q_{j,n}(i,r)\) to server \(j\). The server sends back \(a_j=A_{j,n}(x,q_j)\). There is one query and one answer per server. The user starts with only \(n,i,r\), with no database-dependent advice or shared secret.

Perfect correctness means \(D_n(i,r,a_1,a_2)=x_i\) for every \(x,i,r\). Perfect privacy means that for each \(j\in\{1,2\}\) and all \(i,i'\in[n]\), the random strings \(Q_{j,n}(i,r)\) and \(Q_{j,n}(i',r)\) have identical distributions. Since answers are deterministic functions of a server's database and query, this also protects its entire view. The servers follow the protocol; robustness to false answers and confidentiality of the rest of the database from the user are not required.

The cost is the maximum of \(|q_1|+|q_2|+|a_1|+|a_2|\) over all \(x,i,r\), where \(|w|\) is the bit length of a string \(w\). Protocol descriptions may depend on \(n\) but not on \(x\) or \(i\). There is no uniformity or local-running-time restriction. The same constants \(C,k\) must work for every database size; they cannot grow with \(n\). Answers may contain more than one bit.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that such a protocol family and universal constants exist, or prove the logical negation. Privacy must be exact against each computationally unbounded individual server. The bound includes both queries and both answers in the worst case. Computational privacy, database-dependent client preprocessing, or a growing number of servers changes the target.
cards.why: Can keeping the address of a requested bit completely secret cost only a polynomial in the address length? This isolates the information cost of privacy from encryption assumptions, server computation and implementation details.

context_blocks.text: With one server, perfect private retrieval of an arbitrary bit requires sending the whole database in the standard model. Two noncommunicating copies permit much smaller communication. The user can correlate the two queries while each query separately hides the requested index.

Dvir and Gopi give a one-round protocol with communication \(\exp(O(\sqrt{\log n\,\log\log n}))\). This grows more slowly than every fixed positive power of \(n\), but faster than every fixed power of \(\log n\). Their Definition 1.1 supplies the exact correctness and privacy model used here.

Ghasemi and Kopparty explicitly identify polylogarithmic two-server communication as consistent with known lower bounds in their ITCS 2026 paper. Their lower bounds constrain a particular algebraic framework, not all protocols.

The October 2026 revision of Gupte and Ragavan improves communication for several fixed server counts. Its displayed bound at two servers still has the square-root logarithmic exponent above and does not reach the present polylogarithmic target.

TCS-7459 instead concerns computational privacy at a single server and the cost of preprocessing and answering queries. These are different models and objectives; neither card is merely a parameter change in the other.

cards.title: Sub-two-thirds exponent for random-function inversion

importance.reason: A central unresolved barrier in generic cryptanalysis with preprocessing, connecting the cost of inversion to data structures and circuit lower bounds.

category_assignment.reason: A fundamental limit on information-theoretic security or generic cryptanalysis, rather than a construction from an assumed primitive.

notes: Selects the substantive balanced two-thirds barrier from the larger time-memory tradeoff question; does not claim that this one threshold determines the full curve.
Uses exactly the deterministic, half-of-functions/half-of-inputs success convention of Chawin–Haitner–Mazor Definition 1.1.
Counts advice bits and oracle queries, permits unbounded local computation and arbitrary nonuniform rules independent of the sampled function.

cards.formal:
An inverter stores a short advice string about a function before seeing the output it will be asked to invert. Can both its stored advice and its number of later function evaluations beat the exponent \(2/3\) by a fixed positive amount?

Precisely, do there exist real constants \(0<\varepsilon<2/3\), \(C>0\), and an integer \(N_0\ge2\) such that, for every integer \(N\ge N_0\), there is a deterministic classical advice map \(P_N\) and adaptive oracle decoder \(D_N\), as defined in Model & notation, with
\[
s_N\le C N^{2/3-\varepsilon},\qquad
t_N\le C N^{2/3-\varepsilon},
\]
and
\[
\Pr_{f\sim U(\mathcal F_N)}\!\left[
\Pr_{x\sim U([N])}\!\left[
f\bigl(D_N^f(f(x),P_N(f))\bigr)=f(x)
\right]\ge\frac12\right]\ge\frac12?
\]
Here \([N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}\), \(\mathcal F_N\) is the set of all functions from \([N]\) to \([N]\), and \(U(E)\) means the uniform distribution on a finite nonempty set \(E\). The nonnegative integers \(s_N\) and \(t_N\) count advice bits and bound oracle queries, respectively. Finding any preimage counts as success.
cards.definitions:
For each \(N\), preprocessing is an arbitrary map \(P_N:\mathcal F_N\to\{0,1\}^{s_N}\), where \(\mathcal F_N\) contains all \(N^N\) functions. The map sees the complete function before the challenge is chosen. Preprocessing time is unrestricted, and only its \(s_N\)-bit output persists to the query phase.

The decoder receives a challenge \(y\in[N]\) and an advice string. It may query the oracle at an input \(z\in[N]\) and obtain \(f(z)\). Each new query can depend on the challenge, advice and all previous answers. It halts after at most \(t_N\) queries on every oracle and input, and outputs an element of \([N]\). Its computation between queries and temporary workspace are unrestricted. This is an advice-length versus query-count model, not a bound on all working memory or elapsed computation time.

The maps and decoding rules may depend on \(N\); no algorithm generating them uniformly is required. The decoder is fixed before \(f\) is sampled: it can depend on the sampled function only through the advice and the oracle replies. A uniformly random function has independent uniform values at its \(N\) inputs. For at least half of these functions, decoding must work on at least half of the independently uniform inputs \(x\) when challenged with \(f(x)\). The target does not sample \(y\) uniformly from the whole codomain, and it does not restrict \(f\) to permutations.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) permits the stated family and success probabilities, or prove the logical negation. A logarithmic saving at exponent \(2/3\) does not meet the fixed-exponent target. A negative answer must cover arbitrary advice maps and adaptive decoders in the stated model, not only a named inversion method.
cards.why: Preprocessing can make repeated inversion far cheaper than independent exhaustive searches. Determining whether the classical two-thirds barrier is intrinsic would clarify the power of generic preprocessing attacks, independently of any particular encryption or hashing assumption.

context_blocks.text: Hellman obtains advice length and query cost \(N^{2/3}\) up to factors polynomial in \(\log N\). The general lower bound only forces their product to be at least \(N\), again up to logarithmic factors, leaving the balanced exponent between \(1/2\) and \(2/3\). Corrigan-Gibbs and Kogan present this gap as a longstanding central problem.

The success convention is the one in Definition 1.1 of Chawin, Haitner and Mazor: success on at least half the inputs for at least half the random functions. Their stronger lower bounds impose restrictions on preprocessing or decoding and do not apply to every adaptive inverter.

Kuszmaul and Kuszmaul obtain an optimal tradeoff when query time is at most order \(\log N/\log\log N\), using nearly linear stored space. That small-query regime does not improve the balanced sublinear-advice exponent asked here.

A random permutation has exactly one preimage per output and admits a better tradeoff. General random functions can have many preimages or none; the present experiment always supplies an output obtained by evaluating a random input. These model distinctions matter to the claimed barrier.

cards.title: Private PAC sample complexity from VC and Littlestone dimensions
cards.formal: Do there exist universal integers \(A,k\ge1\) such that every nonempty finite Boolean concept class \(\mathcal C\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\mathcal X}\) on a nonempty finite domain \(\mathcal X\), with \(v=\operatorname{VC}(\mathcal C)\ge1\) and \(d=\operatorname{LD}(\mathcal C)\ge1\), has a positive integer sample size \[m\le A\bigl(1+v+\log^{*}d\bigr)^{k}\] and a possibly improper learner \(L\) that is \((1,1/(100m^{2}))\)-differentially private and realizes the following PAC guarantee? For every distribution \(D\) on \(\mathcal X\) and every target \(h^{*}\in\mathcal C\), when \(L\) receives \(m\) independent samples \((x_i,h^{*}(x_i))\) with \(x_i\sim D\), its output \(\widehat h\) satisfies \[\Pr\!\left[\Pr_{x\sim D}[\widehat h(x)\ne h^{*}(x)]\le1/10\right]\ge9/10.\] The same \(m,L\) must work for all \(D,h^{*}\) for the chosen class. Their choice can depend on the complete class, but \(A,k\) cannot. Computation is unrestricted. This is the previously selected concrete polynomial-overhead version of the source question; the constant accuracy, confidence and sample-dependent privacy parameters are editorial specifications, not parameter values asserted in the source.
cards.why: The theorem characterizing whether private learning is possible leaves an enormous quantitative gap. This question asks whether the extra data needed for privacy is controlled by ordinary statistical complexity and an exceptionally slowly growing function of sequential complexity. A positive answer would put a uniform bound on that privacy overhead across all finite concept classes.
