Lyu’s Theorem 2 improves the general private PAC bound to a fifth power of Littlestone dimension up to the stated logarithmic and privacy/accuracy factors; the paper appears at STOC 2026.
The COLT 2026 invited open problem explicitly proposes a polynomial VC/log-star-LD upper bound and states that the general characterization remains open.

context_blocks.text: Nonprivate PAC learning at constant accuracy and confidence has sample complexity governed by VC dimension. Approximate private learnability instead has a qualitative connection to finite Littlestone dimension. This equivalence says that a finite sample bound exists; it does not identify how large the bound must be.

For finite classes, the 2026 source summarizes a lower scale \(\Omega(v+\log^{*}d)\) and upper scales \(\min\{O(\log|\mathcal C|),\widetilde O(d^{5})\}\), suppressing privacy and learning parameters. The proposed bound depends polynomially on \(v\) and \(\log^{*}d\), so replacing \(d\) by another fixed power does not answer it. The source presents this as one concrete formulation following its broader characterization question.

Lyu’s improved PAC learner has a bound \(\widetilde O(d^{5}\log(1/\delta)/(\varepsilon\alpha))\), with the remaining confidence and logarithmic factors specified in the paper. Its dependence on \(d\) is polynomial but is still much larger than a polynomial in \(\log^{*}d\). The result was published at STOC 2026; the checked detailed theorem is in the 2025 author manuscript.

Yan proves a nearly matching iterated-logarithmic bound when \(v=1\), including an improper learner and explicit parameter dependence. The 2026 problem paper also discusses thresholds, rectangles and halfspaces where the privacy overhead is relatively small. These positive special cases do not supply a bound uniform over unbounded VC dimension.

The card retains the earlier editorial normalization \(\varepsilon=1\), error \(1/10\), failure probability \(1/10\), and \(\delta=1/(100m^{2})\). In particular, \(\delta\) is tied to the actual sample size, rather than silently treated as a fixed constant while \(m\) grows. The source suppresses these parameters, so its displayed summary bounds are context rather than claims that every hidden factor is independent of this normalization.

cards.definitions: A concept is a binary function; the learner knows \(\mathcal X\) and \(\mathcal C\). The VC dimension \(v\) is the largest cardinality of a subset \(S\subseteq\mathcal X\) on which the restrictions of \(\mathcal C\) realize every binary labeling. A complete binary tree of depth \(r\) has an instance point at each internal node and its two outgoing edges labeled 0 and 1. It is shattered by \(\mathcal C\) if every root-to-leaf edge-label sequence is produced by one fixed concept on that path's instance points. The Littlestone dimension \(d\) is the greatest shattered depth. For \(z\ge1\), \(\log^{*}z\) is the least number of successive base-two logarithms needed to obtain a value at most one; in particular \(\log^{*}1=0\). The dimension-zero case is excluded only to avoid a logarithm convention: on a fixed nonempty domain such a class contains a single distinct concept and has a data-independent exact predictor. A learner is an arbitrary probability kernel from \((\mathcal X\times\{0,1\})^m\) to the finite set \(\{0,1\}^{\mathcal X}\). It need not return a member of \(\mathcal C\). For every pair of labeled sample lists \(S,S'\) differing at one position and every subset \(E\) of output hypotheses, require \[\Pr[L(S)\in E]\le e\Pr[L(S')\in E]+1/(100m^{2}).\] Privacy holds even on samples not realizable by the class. The sample size is chosen before the target and distribution; the probability in the PAC guarantee includes both independently drawn examples and the learner's randomness. There are no runtime or representation bounds, and no uniform program across classes is required. The integer-power bound is equivalent to an unspecified universal polynomial in \(1+v\) and \(1+\log^{*}d\). A finite class on an arbitrary domain can be reduced to the finite domain of distinct label vectors \((h(x))_{h\in\mathcal C}\), of which there are at most \(2^{|\mathcal C|}\); both dimensions and these unrestricted learning/privacy requirements are preserved. Thus the finite-domain convention introduces no additional sample-complexity restriction on finite classes.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof of the universal polynomial bound or its logical negation under the exact privacy and PAC conventions above. A positive answer must supply, for every class, a sample size and private learner satisfying the guarantee simultaneously for all targets and distributions. A negative answer must show that for every proposed pair of universal integers \(A,k\), some finite class admits no such learner at any positive integer sample size within the proposed bound. Computational lower bounds, proper-learning obstructions that disappear for improper learners, or a result only for one fixed VC dimension do not refute the statement.

This question asks whether the extra data needed for privacy is controlled by ordinary statistical complexity and an exceptionally slowly growing function of sequential complexity. A positive answer would put a uniform bound on that privacy overhead across all finite concept classes. Editorial placement in this pass: a high-priority broad or central question.

Its dependence on \(d\) is polynomial but is still much larger than a polynomial in \(\log^{*}d\). The result was published at STOC 2026; the checked detailed theorem is in the 2025 author manuscript.

Yan proves a nearly matching iterated-logarithmic bound when \(v=1\), including an improper learner and explicit parameter dependence. The 2026 problem paper also discusses thresholds, rectangles and halfspaces where the privacy overhead is relatively small. These positive special cases do not supply a bound uniform over unbounded VC dimension.

The card retains the earlier editorial normalization \(\varepsilon=1\), error \(1/10\), failure probability \(1/10\), and \(\delta=1/(100m^{2})\). In particular, \(\delta\) is tied to the actual sample size, rather than silently treated as a fixed constant while \(m\) grows. The source suppresses these parameters, so its displayed summary bounds are context rather than claims that every hidden factor is independent of this normalization.

cards.title: Oblivious transfer from public-key encryption
cards.formal:
In the classical plain model, does the existence of public-key encryption secure against chosen-plaintext attacks imply the existence of 1-out-of-2 bit oblivious transfer secure against static semi-honest corruption of either party?

Let \(E\) assert the existence of the bit-encryption scheme defined below, and let \(T\) assert the existence of the two-party protocol and simulators defined below. The target is the unrelativized implication
\[E\ \Longrightarrow\ T.\]
All honest algorithms and simulators are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time classical machines; security is against arbitrary nonuniform polynomial-size classical circuit families. The implication may use the full code of the encryption algorithms, non-black-box reasoning and polynomially many messages. It must not assume an additional property of encryption unless that property is proved to follow from the stated premise.
cards.definitions:
Common conventions. The security parameter \(\lambda\ge1\) is provided as the unary string \(1^\lambda\). A nonnegative function \(\mu\) is negligible if for every positive integer \(c\), some \(\lambda_0\) satisfies \(\mu(\lambda)\le\lambda^{-c}\) for all \(\lambda\ge\lambda_0\). An algorithm is uniform probabilistic polynomial time if it has one fixed finite multitape Turing-machine program and a bound \(K(L+1)^d\) on its bit steps for every input of total length \(L\) and every sequence of independent fair random bits, for some fixed positive integers \(K,d\). Reading, arithmetic, coin generation and all output bits are charged. Malformed inputs may be rejected but must satisfy the clock. There is no advice, ideal oracle, quantum resource or uncharged preprocessing.

For polynomial-length random bit strings \(X_\lambda,Y_\lambda\), write \(X_\lambda\approx_c Y_\lambda\) when for every Boolean circuit family \((D_\lambda)\) of polynomially bounded description length,
\[\left|\Pr[D_\lambda(X_\lambda)=1]-\Pr[D_\lambda(Y_\lambda)=1]\right|\]
is negligible in \(\lambda\). Such a family need not be uniformly generated. It may hardwire polynomial-length auxiliary information, including the input sequence under consideration. Deterministic circuits with binary AND/OR gates, unary NOT gates and constants suffice; private random coins could equivalently be allowed. Encodings expose actual string lengths, with zero padding to a common polynomial bound for the distinguisher. Tuples and messages are encoded by their number of components and each component's length followed by its bits. Nonnegative lengths use \(U(t)=1^\ell0s\), where \(s\) is the canonical binary expansion of \(t\), \(\ell=|s|\), and zero uses \(s=0\).

Public-key encryption. A scheme consists of three uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithms, with public code:
\[(pk,sk)\leftarrow\mathrm{KeyGen}(1^\lambda),\quad z\leftarrow\mathrm{Enc}(1^\lambda,pk,m),\quad \widehat m\leftarrow\mathrm{Dec}(1^\lambda,sk,z).\]
Keys and ciphertexts are ordinary finite bit strings; \(m\in\{0,1\}\), and decryption returns a bit or a failure symbol \(\bot\). All invocations use fresh independent coins. Keys generated at parameter \(\lambda\), honest ciphertexts and their encodings have polynomial length in \(\lambda\). Correctness requires one negligible function \(\mu_E\) such that for every \(\lambda\) and both message bits,
\[\Pr[\mathrm{Dec}(1^\lambda,sk,\mathrm{Enc}(1^\lambda,pk,m))\ne m]\le\mu_E(\lambda),\]
where the probability includes fresh key-generation, encryption and any decryption randomness.

IND-CPA security for bits means
\[(pk,\mathrm{Enc}(1^\lambda,pk,0))\ \approx_c\ (pk,\mathrm{Enc}(1^\lambda,pk,1)),\]
with fresh keys and encryption coins in each experiment. The secret key is not given to the distinguisher. The encryption algorithm is public, so polynomially many encryptions chosen by an attacker can be computed locally. No decryption oracle is available. For this bit-message case the two displayed challenge distributions specify the chosen-plaintext confidentiality requirement. The assertion \(E\) is existence of any scheme satisfying this correctness and security, without algebraic, rerandomization, key-sampling or ciphertext-sampling promises.

Oblivious transfer. The sender \(S\) receives private bits \((m_0,m_1)\), and the receiver \(R\) receives a private choice bit \(c\). Both receive \(1^\lambda\), have independent private fair coins, and exchange a finite ordered sequence of classical messages directly. There is one fixed protocol, with polynomially many bit steps per party, messages and communicated bits on every honest execution and every random-tape choice. Equivalently, all these quantities are bounded by some \(B(\lambda)=K(\lambda+1)^d\) independent of the inputs. The receiver outputs \(y\in\{0,1,\bot\}\); the sender has no output. Correctness requires a negligible \(\mu_T\) such that
\[\forall\lambda\ \forall(m_0,m_1,c)\in\{0,1\}^3:\quad\Pr[y=m_c]\ge1-\mu_T(\lambda).\]
The failure symbol counts as an error. There is no requirement of two rounds or constant rounds.

Static semi-honest corruption means that at most one party is designated corrupted before execution, then follows the prescribed algorithm with the prescribed coin distribution while retaining all information it sees. It may afterwards apply any polynomial-size computation to this information. It does not modify messages, bias its randomness, change its input during the protocol or erase data to satisfy a security condition. The real view \(\operatorname{View}_S\) includes the sender's input, its complete random tape and all sent/received messages. The real view \(\operatorname{View}_R\) includes the receiver's input, its complete random tape, all messages and its final output. A fixed polynomial number of fair bits may be sampled at the start and unused bits retained. Internal computation is determined by the input, coins and messages and is thus recoverable from the view.

Privacy requires two fixed uniform probabilistic polynomial-time simulators \(\operatorname{Sim}_S,\operatorname{Sim}_R\). For every sequence of input triples \((m_{0,\lambda},m_{1,\lambda},c_\lambda)\), the following ensemble pairs must be computationally indistinguishable:
\[\operatorname{View}_S(1^\lambda,m_{0,\lambda},m_{1,\lambda},c_\lambda)\ \approx_c\ \operatorname{Sim}_S(1^\lambda,m_{0,\lambda},m_{1,\lambda}),\]
\[\operatorname{View}_R(1^\lambda,m_{0,\lambda},m_{1,\lambda},c_\lambda)\ \approx_c\ \operatorname{Sim}_R(1^\lambda,c_\lambda,m_{c_\lambda,\lambda}).\]
The source of randomness on the left is an honest interaction of both parties; each right-hand experiment uses the simulator's own fresh coins. Input sequences need not be efficiently computable. The sender simulator receives no choice bit; the receiver simulator receives no unchosen message. The simulators precede the quantifiers over sequences and distinguishers, and have worst-case polynomial clocks rather than merely expected polynomial time. The assertion \(T\) is existence of a protocol and simulators satisfying these requirements.

The plain model supplies no common reference string, random oracle, trusted third party or hardware, and no pre-shared correlated randomness or secret. It permits only the independent randomness and communication just described. The security task is one standalone execution with static passive corruption; malicious deviation, adaptive corruption, fairness, guaranteed delivery against abort and universal composability are not additional requirements.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of \(E\Rightarrow T\) or its full logical negation. A positive proof must obtain the specified uniform protocol and simulators, establish all polynomial clocks and communication bounds, and prove correctness and both privacy ensembles from the encryption premise alone. Non-black-box use of encryption code and non-black-box security arguments are permitted. The literal negative answer is \(E\land\neg T\) in the ordinary, unrelativized model. An oracle world with encryption but no OT, a lower bound on black-box reductions, an attack on one protocol or a failure at a prescribed round count does not prove that negation. Any extra sampling or rerandomization property used by a proposed construction must also be derived from the premise.
cards.why: Public-key encryption protects a message from someone without its decryption key. Oblivious transfer must also protect a sender from a receiver who is entitled to learn one selected message, while hiding that selection from the sender. Determining whether the first capability already implies the second would clarify a basic boundary between secure communication and general private computation.

cards.status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. context_blocks.text: The two privacy obligations are different. The sender must not learn the receiver’s choice, and the receiver must not learn anything about the unselected message beyond what its allowed input and output already imply. Simulation expresses both requirements without assuming the messages themselves are random or secret from all prior information. Correctness is separate: a protocol that exchanges nothing may reveal nothing, but it does not deliver the selected bit.

Gertner and coauthors ask directly whether public-key encryption implies OT. Their positive results require additional oblivious-sampling properties of public keys or ciphertexts. Their negative result constructs an oracle relative to which encryption exists but even semi-honest OT does not. That theorem is a substantial restriction on relativizing construction methods; it is not an ordinary-world separation of the two existence statements.

The historical oracle theorem also has an explicit uniformity qualification. Its authors prove security and separation for probabilistic polynomial-time adversaries and state that extension to nonuniform circuit adversaries would require further work. The present card fixes nonuniform distinguishers, so the original theorem should not be presented as an exact separation for every quantifier in its definitions.

Allowing non-black-box techniques means a proof may use the actual finite descriptions of encryption algorithms. Replacing those algorithms by a freely chosen oracle can remove information that such a proof uses. An oracle barrier therefore cannot simply be reinterpreted as the negation of the unrestricted implication. The target also allows polynomially many rounds, so a barrier at a fixed small round count is insufficient.

Even passive-security OT is a powerful goal. Haitner and coauthors give a fully black-box transformation from semi-honest OT to maliciously secure OT and then to general secure computation. Their formulation uses static corruption, standalone security and, for the stronger malicious task, simulators that may run in expected polynomial time. It does not promise fairness or delivery despite malicious abort. These are consequences in a specified model, not extra requirements silently added to this card.

Li, Zhang and Lin replace earlier oblivious-sampling conditions by public rerandomizability: given a public key, an algorithm can turn a ciphertext into a fresh one with the same plaintext. Their abstract gives OT constructions under this property. IND-CPA confidentiality by itself does not include such an algorithm, so the result covers an enriched encryption primitive.

The March 2026 updatable-encryption article likewise retains precise extra properties. Its two-round OT implication uses oblivious samplability of original ciphertexts and update tokens; its three-round implication uses oblivious samplability of updated ciphertexts. Updatable encryption is a structured symmetric encryption primitive with tokens for transforming ciphertexts across keys. The inspected theorem summaries do not start from an arbitrary IND-CPA public-key scheme.

The January 2026 Minicrypt preprint gives a particularly relevant distinction between a non-black-box implication and an oracle construction. Its abstract claims OT from a standard-model oblivious interactive hash function, and separately constructs that hash primitive in a random-oracle model. It explicitly says that these two statements cannot be composed into OT from a random oracle: the non-black-box step applies only to an ordinary finite implementation. No generic construction of that implementation from arbitrary PKE is claimed in the checked abstract.

The March 2026 stabilizer-decoding preprint gives another kind of progress: a new average-case hardness premise supports both PKE and OT. Having a common sufficient assumption does not show that either primitive follows from every implementation of the other. The additional algebraic structure of that decoding problem remains part of its construction’s foundation.

Fair coin tossing provides a related comparison. Maji and Wang prove limits on protocols that use PKE or key agreement as black boxes, whereas an OT resource supports the optimal fairness scale considered there. That result concerns a different functionality and a restricted construction model. It adds evidence about the hierarchy without resolving the unrestricted semi-honest OT implication.

cards.title: Key agreement from one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of a classical one-way function imply the existence of a classical two-party key-agreement protocol in the plain public-channel model below? The parties must output \(\lambda\)-bit keys with negligible disagreement, and either honest key must be computationally indistinguishable from an independent uniform key given the entire public transcript. This is the unrelativized existence implication, allowing arbitrary constructions and security proofs, including those that inspect the program implementing the one-way function.
cards.definitions:
The security parameter is an integer \(\lambda\geq1\), given as the unary string \(1^{\lambda}\). Every algorithm has one finite program for all parameters and is a classical Turing machine operating on bits; no nonuniform advice or oracle is available. A probabilistic polynomial-time (PPT) algorithm uses independent fair random bits and has a polynomial worst-case running-time bound on every input and every random tape. For standalone algorithms, the bound is in the total input length. Machine steps, reading and writing bits, and producing outputs all count. Each algorithm may have its own fixed polynomial bound. Tuples of bit strings use the prefix-free component encoding \(s\mapsto1^{|s|}0s\); a finite list is encoded by its number of components in the same encoding, followed by its encoded components, with integers represented in binary without leading zeros except for zero itself. Any explicitly proved polynomial-time equivalent encoding is acceptable.

A function \(\mu:\mathbb N_{\geq1}\to[0,1]\) is negligible if \(\forall d\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\;\exists\lambda_0\;\forall\lambda\geq\lambda_0:\mu(\lambda)\leq\lambda^{-d}\). A one-way function is a total deterministic polynomial-time function \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) such that, for every uniform classical PPT inverter \(I\), the function \(\Pr[\,|Y|=\lambda\ \land\ f(Y)=f(X)\,]\) is negligible, where \(X\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\) and \(Y=I(1^{\lambda},f(X))\). The probability includes the independent coins of \(I\). A failure output or a string of the wrong length is an unsuccessful inversion; recovering any preimage of the stipulated length suffices. The function need not be injective or length preserving. Its program is public.

A candidate protocol consists of two uniform interactive machines \(A,B\). On the common input \(1^{\lambda}\), they start with independent private coins and no other secret or correlated input. They exchange finite classical bit strings through a noiseless public channel. Fix the conventional alternating-message execution, with \(A\) first and empty messages permitted; public termination flags indicate when each machine has finished. A polynomial in \(\lambda\), fixed for the protocol, bounds the combined computation, messages, message lengths, and execution length on every pair of honest random tapes. Both parties always terminate with strings \(K_A,K_B\in\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\). The public transcript \(T\) is the finite ordered list of messages with sender labels, message boundaries and termination flags, encoded as above. Private working tapes and private coins are not part of \(T\). Communication occurs only through these messages; there is no additional timing channel. No trusted setup, preshared secret, correlated randomness, random oracle, quantum computation or quantum communication is permitted.

Correctness means that \(\Pr[K_A\ne K_B]\) is negligible in \(\lambda\), over independent honest coins. Passive secrecy means that for every uniform classical PPT algorithm \(D\) outputting a bit, the advantage
\[\left|\Pr[D(1^{\lambda},T,K_A)=1]-\Pr[D(1^{\lambda},T,U_{\lambda})=1]\right|\]
is negligible, where each experiment runs the honest protocol and \(U_{\lambda}\) is an independent uniform element of \(\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\). The coins of \(D\) are independent of all other randomness. Correctness makes the same requirement with \(K_B\) equivalent. The eavesdropper sees the whole transcript and the public programs but does not modify messages. Its polynomial running time allows it to store the entire polynomial-length transcript: there is no extra storage bound. Negligibility is required eventually at all sufficiently large parameters, not just along a subsequence; its thresholds may depend on the adversary. The quantifier order is: if some \(f\) satisfying one-wayness exists, then some single pair \((A,B)\) satisfying the resource bound, correctness and secrecy against every such \(D\) exists. No uniform compiler from descriptions of functions to protocols, black-box interface, fixed number of rounds or perfect correctness is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated existence implication or its logical negation. A positive answer must establish an unrelativized protocol satisfying all of the specified correctness, secrecy, uniformity and cost requirements from the one-way-function premise alone. A negative answer must establish that a one-way function exists and that no protocol in the stated class satisfies both correctness and secrecy. Failure of a particular protocol, an oracle separation, a restriction to black-box reductions, a result assuming perfect correctness, or an attack with polynomially many oracle queries but unbounded computation does not establish that negation. Additional unproved cryptographic assumptions and security only at infinitely many parameters do not settle the full target.
cards.why: This asks whether generic computational one-wayness suffices for two strangers to establish a shared classical secret through publicly visible interaction. It separates the minimal hardness underlying symmetric cryptography from the additional structure used for secret establishment, while allowing more interaction than public-key encryption. A resolution would determine whether that foundational gap concerns existence itself or the known forms of cryptographic reductions.

context_blocks.text: A one-way function concerns the difficulty of reversing a computation on a randomly generated input. Key agreement concerns a joint distribution generated by two initially independent parties: they must learn the same string while a public observer cannot distinguish it from a fresh uniform string. Hardness of inversion by itself does not directly assert this joint secrecy property.

The secrecy experiment includes the candidate key as well as the transcript. A key can be difficult to recover in full while still revealing predictable bits, so mere resistance to complete key recovery is not the chosen definition. The saved card already required indistinguishability from uniform; this review preserves that stronger standard formulation and makes the probability spaces and adversary-dependent negligible bounds explicit.

Impagliazzo and Rudich established an oracle world in which one-way permutations exist but secure key agreement does not. A one-way permutation is a length-preserving bijective special case of a one-way function. This separates the relativized primitives and obstructs reductions that continue to work in that world. It is not a proof that ordinary one-way functions exist without ordinary key agreement. The author manuscript checked here is dated 28 May 1994; the original conference publication was STOC 1989.

Black-box uselessness asks a further composition question: can adding a one-way-function primitive help obtain key agreement from some auxiliary primitive that did not suffice alone? Couteau, Farshim and Mahmoody prove restricted forms, rather than the general statement. Their ITCS 2021 Theorem 17 uses infinitely-often security, perfect correctness and a constant bound on one party’s queries to the one-way-function oracle; the other auxiliary oracle is still available. These restrictions and the paper’s specified reduction notions are part of that theorem. They are not assumptions of this card.

Public-key encryption implies passive key agreement, whereas the target here permits a general polynomial amount of interaction. The two existence questions are therefore closely related but have different conclusions. The agreed key must remain secret only against an observer; this does not assert authentication or security against a party that replaces the messages. The absence of pre-existing shared information is an essential part of the question.

Brzuska, Couteau, Egger and Quach obtain key agreement from one-way functions in a bounded-storage model. Their publisher abstract describes a large public stream and an a priori storage restriction on the observer, and reports polynomial storage gaps. That additional physical resource restriction is absent here: a PPT observer may retain the entire honest transcript. The abstract and publication metadata were checked; this review does not claim to have verified the full bounded-storage construction.

Li, Li, Li and Liu’s August 2026 preprint states a many-round quantum random-oracle impossibility result. With independent initial private states, classical messages, a Boolean-output random oracle and perfect agreement, it claims a classical eavesdropper making \(O((q_A+q_B)^{5})\) oracle queries when the parties make \(q_A,q_B\) quantum queries. The observer is allowed unbounded other computation. The statement was checked in the paper, but its proof was not independently verified. Its oracle, perfect-correctness and query-cost conditions differ from this card’s classical, negligible-error, polynomial-time target.

Li, Ni and Zan’s 2023 preprint explicitly claims public-key encryption from one-way functions. If valid, this would also settle the key-agreement implication. This audit checked the claim but did not verify its proof or find a conclusive later assessment. Its presence therefore changes the recorded scientific status to uncertain; it does not justify archival.

cards.title: One-way permutations from one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of a classical one-way function secure against every nonuniform polynomial-size classical adversary imply the existence of an efficiently generated public-key family of one-way permutations on full Boolean cubes, with the same adversary convention? Require a bijection on the entire cube for every key the generator can output, and negligible inversion probability averaged over an honestly generated public key and a uniform input. No trapdoor is required.
cards.definitions:
All inputs and outputs are finite binary strings. Uniform polynomial time means one finite classical Turing program with a polynomial worst-case bit-operation bound in its input length. Randomized programs use independent fair random bits within that bound. A nonuniform polynomial-size adversary is a family of polynomial-size Boolean circuits, with polynomially many random input bits allowed. Its description and any auxiliary advice have polynomial length in the security parameter and may depend on that parameter, but not on independently sampled secret experiment coins.

A function \(\mu:\mathbb N\to[0,1]\) is negligible if, for every integer \(a\ge1\), there exists \(N_a\) such that \(\mu(n)\le n^{-a}\) for all \(n\ge N_a\).

The premise is that a single deterministic polynomial-time program computes a family
\[
 f_n:\{0,1\}^n\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{\ell(n)},
\]
where \(\ell(n)\) is a nonnegative integer, polynomially bounded and computable in polynomial time from \(1^n\), such that every nonuniform polynomial-size randomized family \(I_n\) has negligible success probability in the following experiment. Sample \(X\) uniformly from \(\{0,1\}^n\), give \((1^n,f_n(X))\) to \(I_n\), and declare its output \(Z\) successful exactly when \(Z\in\{0,1\}^n\) and \(f_n(Z)=f_n(X)\). Any preimage counts. The function's description is public, and no injectivity or subexponential hardness is assumed.

The desired permutation family consists of a fixed polynomially bounded integer function \(m(n)\ge n\), computable in polynomial time from \(1^n\), a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm \(\operatorname{Gen}(1^n)\to pk\), and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time evaluation algorithm \(\operatorname{Eval}(1^n,pk,x)\). Let \(K_n\) be the support of Gen: the finite set of keys that occur with positive probability. For every \(n\ge1\) and every \(pk\in K_n\), evaluation on the whole input cube defines a map
\[
 \pi_{n,pk}:\{0,1\}^{m(n)}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{m(n)},
 \qquad \pi_{n,pk}(x)=\operatorname{Eval}(1^n,pk,x),
\]
and this map must be a bijection. Equivalently, for each output in that cube there is exactly one input in the cube with that output. This is an exact structural property for every generated key, not a property permitted to fail on a negligible fraction of keys or inputs.

One-wayness requires that, for every nonuniform polynomial-size randomized adversary \(A_n\), the probability of the event
\[
 Z=A_n(1^n,pk,\pi_{n,pk}(X))\in\{0,1\}^{m(n)}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \pi_{n,pk}(Z)=\pi_{n,pk}(X)
\]
is negligible in \(n\), where \(pk\leftarrow\operatorname{Gen}(1^n)\), \(X\) is independently uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{m(n)}\), and adversary coins are independent. An incorrectly sized or malformed output fails. Each adversary may have its own polynomial resource bound and negligible success bound. The public key and all algorithm descriptions are available to the adversary; the generator's private coins are not supplied.

Full domain refers to each permutation's input and output sets, both the complete Boolean cube. It does not require \(K_n\) to contain all strings of some length, to have efficiently recognizable membership, or to be independent of the construction's building blocks. No requirement is imposed on bijectivity for keys outside \(K_n\), although the evaluation program must still terminate within its polynomial bound on all inputs. No inverse algorithm, secret trapdoor, key recovery or hardness for every individual key is demanded. A trapdoor construction would qualify if its public family has the required properties and satisfies the stated security.

All algorithms and security guarantees are classical. The implication is about existence in the ordinary model with no ideal oracles. It may use the full description of an underlying one-way function, and its polynomial bounds may depend on that function. It is not restricted to a black-box compiler or reduction and assumes no obfuscator, additional cryptographic primitive or stronger security level.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated existence implication, supplying uniform generation and evaluation, the length function, every-key bijectivity and the negligible inversion bound against all stated adversaries; or give a complete Lean-checked proof of its negation in the ordinary computational model.

A restricted-domain permutation or merely injective length-expanding function does not satisfy the target. Additional assumptions must themselves be derived from ordinary one-way functions. An oracle separation or exclusion of a class of black-box constructions is a barrier, not a refutation of this unrestricted implication. Proving that ordinary one-way functions do not exist would establish the implication vacuously, not refute it. No numerical approximation tolerance applies.

cards.title: Collision-resistant hashing from one-way functions
cards.formal:
In the ordinary classical computational model, is the following existence implication true?
\[\bigl(\exists f\;\operatorname{OWF}(f)\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \bigl(\exists\operatorname{Gen},H\;\operatorname{CRH}(\operatorname{Gen},H)\bigr).\]
The predicates are defined below. The honest functions and algorithms are uniform and polynomial-time, and security is against every nonuniform family of polynomial-size classical Boolean circuits. The hash family has a freshly sampled public key \(k\) and maps \(H_k:\{0,1\}^{2\lambda}\to\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\) for every positive integer security parameter \(\lambda\). Both members of a proposed collision may be chosen after the key is known. The implication permits unrestricted constructions and proof techniques, including use of a one-way function's implementation.
cards.definitions:
Parameters and computation. All strings are finite binary strings. The security parameters \(n,\lambda\) range over the positive integers, and \(1^n\) denotes the unary string of \(n\) ones. Honest algorithms are ordinary Turing machines with one fixed finite program, no advice and no oracles. Deterministic algorithms have polynomial bit running time in the total input length. A probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm additionally uses independent fair random bits and has a polynomial running-time bound on every random tape; it therefore uses at most polynomially many random bits. The polynomial and its degree are fixed for each program, independent of the parameter and sampled inputs.

Adversaries. A nonuniform polynomial-size circuit family \((A_n)_{n\ge1}\) consists of finite acyclic Boolean circuits over AND, OR, NOT and constant gates, with fan-in at most two and unrestricted fan-out. Size counts all gates and input and output wires, including random input wires. There are constants \(C,d\in\mathbb N_{>0}\) such that each size is at most \(C(n+1)^d\). A randomized circuit receives independent uniform bits on its random wires. Circuit descriptions may be arbitrary functions of the parameter and the fixed public honest programs; no algorithm generating the family is required. They are fixed before the fresh challenge or hash key is sampled. Each family has its own polynomial bound.

Finite-string encoding. To supply a string \(z\) of length at most an integer bound \(P\) to a fixed-width circuit, use \(\operatorname{enc}_P(z)\): the binary representation of \(|z|\), padded to exactly \(\lceil\log_2(P+1)\rceil\) bits, followed by \(z\) and enough zero bits to fill a \(P\)-bit data field. Bounds used below are positive integer-valued polynomials. This encoding reveals the string and its length and adds only polynomial overhead. In particular, variable-length function outputs and public keys are not supplied as a length-regularity promise.

Negligibility. A function \(\mu:\mathbb N_{>0}\to[0,1]\) is negligible if
\[\forall c\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \exists N_c\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall n\ge N_c:\quad\mu(n)\le n^{-c}.\]
The threshold may depend on the exponent and the adversary, as well as on the fixed primitive. Security must hold eventually for every parameter, not merely on an infinite subsequence. No fixed inverse-polynomial or constant error is allowed.

One-way function. A candidate \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) is total and uniformly deterministic polynomial-time computable. Fix a positive integer-valued polynomial \(p\) bounding \(|f(x)|\) whenever \(|x|=n\). In its inversion experiment, sample \(X\) uniformly from \(\{0,1\}^n\), independently sample the circuit's random wires \(R\), and compute exactly once
\[Y=A_n(1^n,\operatorname{enc}_{p(n)}(f(X));R)\in\{0,1\}^n.\]
Define \(\operatorname{Inv}_{f,A}(n)=\Pr[f(Y)=f(X)]\). Then \(\operatorname{OWF}(f)\) means this probability is negligible for every permitted family \(A\). Any preimage of the challenge of length \(n\) is accepted; recovery of the original \(X\) is not required. Restricting the circuit output to \(n\) bits only removes invalid answers, which could always be replaced by a fixed \(n\)-bit candidate. The choice of the polynomial padding bound does not change security because valid encodings with different bounds can be converted in polynomial time.

Publicly keyed hash family. A candidate consists of a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time generator \(\operatorname{Gen}(1^\lambda)\) and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time evaluator \(H(1^\lambda,k,x)\). There is a fixed positive integer-valued polynomial \(q\) such that every generated key has length at most \(q(\lambda)\). For every key in the support of the generator and every \(x\in\{0,1\}^{2\lambda}\), the evaluator outputs exactly \(\lambda\) bits. Write \(H_k(x)=H(1^\lambda,k,x)\) when the parameter is understood. No evaluator property is required for keys outside that support. The key need not be uniform over all strings; its actual distribution is the output of the generator. It is fully public, and evaluation needs no secret.

Collision experiment. Independently sample the generator's random tape \(S\) and the adversary's random wires \(R\), set \(k=\operatorname{Gen}(1^\lambda;S)\), and compute exactly once
\[(x,x')=B_\lambda(1^\lambda,\operatorname{enc}_{q(\lambda)}(k);R)\in\{0,1\}^{2\lambda}\times\{0,1\}^{2\lambda}.\]
Define
\[\operatorname{Coll}_{\operatorname{Gen},H,B}(\lambda)=\Pr[x\ne x'\ \land\ H(1^\lambda,k,x)=H(1^\lambda,k,x')].\]
The predicate \(\operatorname{CRH}(\operatorname{Gen},H)\) means this probability is negligible for every permitted circuit family \(B\). The adversary can compute the public evaluator within its circuit budget and select both inputs as functions of the key. It does not receive the generator's private random tape. Fixed-width candidate outputs again lose no successful attacks.

Scope of the implication. Existence of any one-way function in this model is the only cryptographic hypothesis. The conclusion is existence of some secure hash family; it need not be a particular proposed transformation applied to every one-way function. There is no requirement that a single algorithm transform arbitrary program descriptions into hash-family descriptions. No random oracle, trusted setup, quantum computation, extra hardness assumption or stronger exponential-security requirement is supplied. The all-parameter, nonuniform security and exact factor-two compression conventions are retained from the inherited card.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated implication or its logical negation. A positive proof must establish the existence of the specified public-key generator and evaluator from the one-way-function hypothesis alone, including uniform polynomial-time computability, exact compression for every generated key, and negligible collision success against every nonuniform polynomial-size circuit family. All transformations of parameters and security guarantees used in that proof must be justified. A proof may use function implementations and need not be black-box.

The logical negation requires proving both that a one-way function exists and that no hash family satisfying this model exists. For the latter assertion, every pair of uniform polynomial-time programs meeting the hash syntax must admit a permitted circuit family with nonnegligible collision probability. Equivalently, for each such pair there must be an adversary and a fixed \(c\in\mathbb N_{>0}\) whose success exceeds \(\lambda^{-c}\) for infinitely many \(\lambda\). Merely proving that a chosen construction fails, even for one secure one-way function, is insufficient.

An oracle world separating these primitives or an impossibility theorem restricted to black-box reductions establishes a barrier, not this ordinary-model negation. Target-collision resistance, resistance only to finding three or more colliding inputs, injective noncompressing functions, security only for uniform adversaries or only infinitely often, and constructions assuming quantitative product hardness do not meet the full conclusion. This is an exact yes-or-no implication, with no additive numerical tolerance on the security requirement.

progress.text: Rompel obtains universal one-way hashing and secure signatures from arbitrary one-way functions; this uses the weaker target-before-key collision game.
Simon proves an oracle separation from one-way permutations, establishing the classical black-box obstacle.
Holmgren–Lombardi construct collision-resistant hashing from quantitatively strong one-way product functions, an additional assumption.
Folwarczný and coauthors extend total-search barriers to specified single-query semi-black-box reductions; the preprint appears at ITCS 2024.

Mao–Zhang report a fully black-box separation between successive constant-multiplicity collision-resistance notions, including pair resistance from triple resistance. The unrestricted one-way-function implication remains open.
Rothblum constructs bounded-space interactive arguments from one-way functions, without resolving the hashing implication.

cards.status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. The March/April 2026 primary multicollision paper explicitly leaves construction from general one-way functions open. It adds a fully black-box hierarchy, while the July interactive-argument result bypasses full collision resistance in a specific application. context_blocks.text: A collision-resistant hash compresses its input while making it computationally difficult to find two distinct messages with the same digest. Collisions must exist by the pigeonhole principle: there are \(2^{2\lambda}\) possible inputs and only \(2^{\lambda}\) outputs. Security is therefore not a claim that collisions never occur, or that a digest uniquely identifies a message. It is a claim about what an efficient adversary can construct after learning the hash key.

A one-way function poses a different challenge. The attacker receives the image of a random input and must find any preimage. An injective one-way function can have no collisions at all, yet it is not a compressing hash. Conversely, a compressing map may have easily found collisions even if some inversion tasks look difficult. The question asks whether the minimal assumption of computationally hard inversion can always supply the more structured difficulty of finding collisions.

The public key matters to the asymptotic definition. If a single compressing function were fixed at each security parameter and security were required against nonuniform circuits, an attacker could hard-code one collision for each parameter. A fresh polynomial-length key prevents that pair from being selected in advance for the actual function used. The key is not secret: the adversary sees it before choosing either colliding message.

Target-collision resistance changes the order of moves. An attacker first commits to one message, then sees a random key and seeks a second message colliding with its committed target. Rompel constructs universal one-way hash functions of this kind from arbitrary one-way functions, as part of the route to secure signatures. That theorem does not give the present game, where both messages are chosen after the key is known. The order difference is small syntactically but central to the unresolved assumption gap.

Simon constructs an oracle setting with one-way permutations but no collision-resistant hash functions in the relevant relativized sense. It rules out building and proving the desired primitive by treating the assumed function purely as an oracle in the separated framework. The theorem does not rule out exploiting a function’s implementation or a proof that fails to relativize. The ordinary mathematical implication in this card therefore remains stronger than the black-box construction question already answered negatively.

Holmgren and Lombardi construct collision-resistant hashing under stronger assumptions on simultaneously inverting independently sampled challenges. Their Theorem I.5 uses symmetric injective two-product functions whose batch inversion probability is at most \(2^{-n-\omega(\log n)}\) for polynomial-time attackers; a separate theorem treats noninjective functions under stronger quantitative hardness. Ordinary one-wayness only requires a negligible single-challenge inversion probability. The product assumption is therefore additional structure and security, not an established consequence of the hypothesis on this card.

Collision finding is also a total search problem: an explicitly represented shrinking circuit always has two distinct inputs with the same output, and a proposed pair can be checked efficiently. The published ITCS 2024 paper of Folwarczný and coauthors extends separation results to a restricted class of reductions for total NP search. Its main condition permits a single call to a total-search solver and no query to the one-way function before that call. The result includes semi-black-box reductions, but is still a limitation on a specified reduction model.

Mao and Zhang's March 2026 manuscript, published on ECCC in April, reports a further black-box hierarchy: for every fixed \(K\ge2\), \(K\)-collision resistance cannot be constructed fully black-box from \((K+1)\)-collision resistance in their model. Here an attacker seeks \(K\) distinct inputs with one common hash value. In particular, hardness of finding a triple does not give a black-box construction of hardness of finding a pair. The paper also separates distributional collision resistance from three-collision resistance. These are barriers among weaker primitives; the ordinary unrestricted implication from one-way functions remains open in the introduction.

Rothblum's July 2026 manuscript reports interactive arguments for deterministic computations taking time \(T\) and space \(S\), assuming one-way functions. The communication is \(S\operatorname{poly}(\log T,\kappa)\), the verifier time is \((S+n)\operatorname{poly}(\log T,\kappa)\), and the number of rounds is polylogarithmic in \(T\). Soundness loses a factor polynomial in \(T\) in the adversary-size bound. This weakens assumptions for an interactive application; its use of target-collision-resistant hashing does not supply full public-key collision resistance.

A resolution would clarify the foundations of many protocols that use short commitments to large data. It would either place full collision resistance on the same assumption level as ordinary one-wayness, or demonstrate a separation that survives beyond black-box barriers. The card asks for polynomial security only; requiring near-optimal exponential security or resistance to quantum attacks would introduce additional questions.

Honest algorithms are uniform and polynomial-time, while security must hold against every polynomial-size nonuniform classical circuit family.

Known oracle separations, stronger product-hardness constructions and the 2026 multicollision and interactive-argument results leave this ordinary-model implication unresolved.

cards.title: Noninteractive zero knowledge from one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of a classical one-way function imply the existence of a reusable, adaptively secure noninteractive zero-knowledge argument for Boolean circuit satisfiability in the honestly generated common-reference-string model? Require computational soundness and computational zero knowledge against every nonuniform polynomial-size classical adversary, with negligible errors and one public proof message per statement. The implication may use the code of the one-way function and has no black-box restriction.
cards.definitions:
All strings are finite binary strings. A uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm is one finite classical Turing program with independent fair random bits and a polynomial worst-case bit-operation bound. A nonuniform polynomial-size adversary is a family of Boolean circuits, possibly with polynomially many independent fair random input bits, whose description, advice, input and output lengths are bounded by a polynomial in the security parameter. Its advice may depend on that parameter, but not on independently sampled secret coins of an experiment. Adaptive algorithms are represented by such polynomially bounded computations with the oracle access specified below. A function \(\mu:\mathbb N\to[0,1]\) is negligible if, for every integer \(a\ge1\), there is \(N_a\) such that \(\mu(\lambda)\le\lambda^{-a}\) for every \(\lambda\ge N_a\).

The premise is that some single deterministic polynomial-time program computes maps \(f_n:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^{\ell(n)}\), where \(\ell\) is polynomially bounded, and for every nonuniform polynomial-size randomized circuit family \(I_n\),
\[
 \Pr_{X\leftarrow\{0,1\}^n,I_n}
 [\,Z=I_n(1^n,f_n(X))\in\{0,1\}^n\ \text{and}\ f_n(Z)=f_n(X)\,]
\]
is negligible in \(n\). Any preimage counts as successful inversion; the original sampled preimage need not be recovered. The function's description is public. No injectivity, trapdoor, subexponential hardness or algebraic structure is assumed.

Encode a Boolean circuit by a finite explicit gate list over fan-in-two AND and OR gates and NOT gates, with a specified output and input wires. A statement \(x\) is such an encoding. A witness \(w\) assigns its input wires, and \(R(x,w)=1\) exactly when the encoding and assignment are valid and the circuit evaluates to one. The language \(L\) consists of the statements having such a witness. Malformed circuit encodings are outside \(L\).

The desired argument has uniform polynomial-time algorithms
\[
 \operatorname{Setup}(1^\lambda,1^B)\to\mathsf{crs},\qquad
 \operatorname{Prove}(\mathsf{crs},x,w)\to\pi,\qquad
 \operatorname{Verify}(\mathsf{crs},x,\pi)\to\{0,1\}.
\]
The parameter \(B\ge1\) bounds each statement and witness length separately. Both parameters are included in the public string. Setup and Prove are randomized; Verify is deterministic. There is one fixed polynomial \(P\) bounding their time, the setup length and the proof length by \(P(\lambda+B)\) on inputs within the prescribed bounds. The verifier rejects statements longer than \(B\) and proofs longer than the prescribed bound, and rejects malformed inputs; bounded-prefix scanning suffices for rejecting excessively long inputs. Honest setup depends only on \(\lambda,B\), not on later statements. Its private random coins are not published or given to the adversary. Once the string is generated, proving a statement consists of sending only \(\pi\); verification is public.

The following requirements hold for every integer-valued polynomially bounded choice \(B=B(\lambda)\), using the same algorithms. Completeness means that one negligible function \(\mu_B\) bounds
\[
 \Pr[\operatorname{Verify}(\mathsf{crs},x,
        \operatorname{Prove}(\mathsf{crs},x,w))=0]
 \le\mu_B(\lambda)
\]
uniformly over all \(|x|,|w|\le B\) with \(R(x,w)=1\), where the probability uses independent honest setup and prover coins.

Adaptive computational soundness means that, for every nonuniform polynomial-size adversary given \(1^\lambda,1^B,\mathsf{crs}\), the probability of outputting a pair \((x,\pi)\) with \(|x|\le B\), \(x\notin L\), and \(\operatorname{Verify}(\mathsf{crs},x,\pi)=1\) is negligible. The statement may be selected after seeing the setup string. The negligible bound may depend on the adversary and on \(B\).

Reusable adaptive computational zero knowledge means there are fixed uniform polynomial-time algorithms \(\operatorname{SimSetup}\) and \(\operatorname{SimProve}\) satisfying the following experiments. A nonuniform polynomial-size distinguisher, with arbitrary polynomial-size auxiliary information fixed before setup, receives \(1^\lambda,1^B\) and the experiment's public string. It adaptively makes polynomially many queries \((x,w)\), possibly choosing each after seeing earlier answers, and then outputs a bit. In the real experiment the string is sampled by Setup, and each valid query is answered by a fresh honest Prove execution. In the simulated experiment \(\operatorname{SimSetup}(1^\lambda,1^B)\) produces a public string and private simulation state. A valid query is answered by \(\operatorname{SimProve}\) from the public string, current state and \(x\); the simulator may update its state but is not given \(w\). In both experiments the query-handling wrapper checks \(|x|,|w|\le B\) and \(R(x,w)=1\), returning the same distinguished rejection symbol for invalid queries without invoking the prover or simulator. These checks do not reveal witnesses to the simulator. For every such distinguisher and auxiliary-information family, the absolute difference between its two output-one probabilities is negligible in \(\lambda\). The simulated setup distribution need not equal the honest distribution; indistinguishability of the complete experiments is required. Simulation takes polynomial time in the security parameters and total query length.

There is no bound fixed at setup on the number of future proofs beyond each attacker's polynomial total computation. No random oracle, extra cryptographic assumption, online challenge, extraction requirement or succinctness requirement is supplied. The actual system publishes only its honestly generated string and subsequent proofs; simulation state belongs solely to the security definition.

cards.title: Fully homomorphic encryption from public-key encryption
cards.formal: Does the existence of IND-CPA-secure public-key bit encryption imply the existence of an IND-CPA-secure, compact, unleveled fully homomorphic bit-encryption scheme for every polynomial-size Boolean circuit, with the algorithms and security convention below?
cards.definitions:
All algorithms are uniform probabilistic Turing machines with worst-case polynomial bit running time in their explicit input lengths; decryption is deterministic. The security parameter \(\lambda\) is supplied in unary. An adversary is a nonuniform family of randomized Boolean circuits of size polynomial in \(\lambda\), including its advice and random-input nodes. All random bits are independent and fair. A function \(
u:\mathbb{N}	o [0,1]\) is negligible when for every positive integer a there exists \(\lambda _{0}\) such that \(
u (\lambda )\le \lambda ^{- a}\) for all \(\lambda \ge \lambda _{0}\). Security is quantified separately over every such adversary family, with a negligible bound allowed to depend on the family. A public-key bit-encryption scheme consists of \(Gen(1^{\lambda})=(pk,sk), Enc(pk,b)=c\) for \(b\in \{0,1\}\), and \(Dec(sk,c)\in \{0,1,\perp\}\). There is one negligible \(
u\) such that for every \(\lambda\) and b, \(\Pr[\operatorname{Dec}(sk,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,b))
e b]\le
u(\lambda)\), over key generation and encryption. In the IND-CPA experiment Gen is run, the adversary receives pk and selects bits \(b_{0},b_{1}\) and a state, an independent uniform \( eta \in \{0,1\}\) is chosen, \(c=Enc(pk,b_{ eta})\) is returned, and the adversary outputs \( eta '\). Require \(|\Pr[ eta\prime= eta]-1/2|\) to be negligible. The adversary may perform any polynomial number of public encryptions on its own before and after the challenge. There is no decryption oracle. Bit encryption suffices; longer messages are represented by bit lists. For FHE, Gen outputs (pk,evk,sk); the evaluation key evk is public and is included with pk in the IND-CPA experiment. Gen receives no circuit size or depth bound. Eval(evk,\(C,c_{1},\ldots ,c_{t}\)) outputs one ciphertext for a circuit \(C:\{0,1\}^{t}	o \{0,1\}\), encoded as an acyclic \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}/\mathrm{NOT}\) circuit with listed wires. For every polynomial s there is a negligible \(
u _{s}\) such that for every \(\lambda\), every such C of description length and input count at most \(s(\lambda )\), and every \(m\in \{0,1\}^{t}\), independently of the generated keys, \(\Pr[\operatorname{Dec}(sk,\operatorname{Eval}(evk,C,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,m_1),\ldots,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,m_t)))
e C(m)]\le
u_s(\lambda)\). The probability includes key generation, fresh encryption coins for each bit, and evaluation coins. Eval’s time is polynomial in the entire supplied circuit and ciphertext encoding, with one algorithm for all C. There is one polynomial q, independent of C,t and s, bounding every evaluated ciphertext length and its decryption time by \(q(\lambda )\); keys also have polynomial length. The scheme must also correctly decrypt fresh encryptions. Multiple output bits mean separate output ciphertexts, so compactness scales linearly with output length. Only the usual one-evaluation correctness contract is required; no circuit privacy or additional guarantee for arbitrary malformed or previously evaluated ciphertexts is imposed. The assertion is an existence implication between these two primitives in the classical standard model; it permits non-black-box constructions and supplies no extra setup, ideal oracle, circular-security or number-theoretic assumption.

It therefore supplies a barrier and motivation, not a negative answer to an arbitrary non-black-box implication. The existing LWE-to-FHE card starts from a specific stronger assumption.

cards.title: Succinct noninteractive arguments for NP from LWE alone
cards.formal: Does the specified ordinary LWE assumption imply a noninteractive succinct argument for every NP relation in the common-reference-string model, with adaptive soundness and proof length polynomial in lambda and log T for T-step witness verification?
cards.definitions:
The security parameter is lambda, supplied in unary. Efficient algorithms are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time Turing machines; security is against nonuniform probabilistic polynomial-size circuit families with polynomially many oracle queries. A function is negligible if it is eventually smaller than lambda^{-c} for every constant c>0. All message, instance and witness lengths in a security experiment are polynomial in lambda. No random oracle, trusted hardware or additional computational assumption is available.

The selected plain-LWE assumption is decisional LWE in dimension lambda, with q the least prime at least lambda^3 and integer error distribution assigning probability proportional to exp(-pi e^2/lambda^2) to each e in Z, reduced modulo q. For every polynomial m(lambda), a uniform matrix A in Z_q^{m by lambda}, a uniform secret s in Z_q^lambda and independent errors e give (A,As+e) computationally indistinguishable from (A,u) with uniform independent u in Z_q^m. Hardness is against the circuit adversaries above with negligible distinguishing advantage. This explicitly fixes polynomial modulus and inverse-polynomial relative noise; it does not assume evasive LWE, subexponential security or leakage resilience. It is an editorial parameter choice, not a claim that every formulation called LWE is equivalent.

Fix a deterministic polynomial-time relation verifier R. A bound T≥2 limits its running time on (x,w), including reading its inputs, and witnesses have length at most T. Setup(1^lambda,R,T) produces a public CRS independent of x and w. It may run in polynomial time in lambda+T+|R|, but CRS length must be polynomial in lambda+log T+|R|. Prove(crs,x,w) runs in polynomial time in lambda+T+|R| and outputs one proof pi. Verify(crs,x,pi) is deterministic and runs in polynomial time in lambda+|x|+log T+|R|. Proof length is polynomial in lambda+log T+|R|, with exponents independent of T and |x|. No interaction follows setup.

Completeness holds with probability one minus negligible for each valid R(x,w)=1 verified within T steps. Adaptive soundness means an adversary given an honestly generated CRS cannot choose (x,pi) accepted by Verify when no length-at-most-T witness makes R accept within T steps, except with negligible probability. This holds for every polynomially bounded choice of T(lambda) and polynomial-size adversary, with the algorithms and efficiency exponents fixed independently of those polynomials. The prover knows the witness; the verifier does not. No witness extraction, zero knowledge or security under a malicious CRS is required. Setup randomness is not given to the adversary beyond the CRS.

cards.title: Polynomial-time private release of all marginals
cards.formal: Do there exist an integer \(C\ge1\), a function \(\alpha:\mathbb N_{\ge2}\to[0,1]\) with \(\lim_{d\to\infty}\alpha(d)=0\), a uniform randomized mechanism \(M\), and a uniform deterministic evaluator \(E\) satisfying the following statement? For every integer \(d\ge2\), put \(n=d^{C}\). For every explicitly given database \(D\in(\{0,1\}^{d})^{n}\), \(M(d,D)\) runs in worst-case time polynomial in \(n+d\), satisfies \((1,1/(100n^{2}))\)-differential privacy under replacement of one row, and outputs a finite binary synopsis \(S\). With probability at least \(2/3\) over \(M\)'s random bits, this one synopsis satisfies \[\left|E(d,S,J,a)-q_{J,a}(D)\right|\le\alpha(d)\] simultaneously for every \(J\subseteq[d]\) and \(a\in\{0,1\}^{J}\). The evaluator runs in worst-case time polynomial in \(d+|S|\), outputs a binary-encoded rational, and has no further access to the database. The synopsis may be arbitrary: it need not be synthetic data or describe a consistent probability distribution.
cards.definitions: \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\). A marginal query \((J,a)\) asks for the fraction of rows agreeing with the assignment \(a\) on the coordinates in \(J\): \[q_{J,a}(D)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf 1\{\forall j\in J,\ D_{ij}=a_j\}.\] All orders \(0\le|J|\le d\) are included; the empty query equals one. Each query can be encoded as a length-\(d\) word over \(\{*,0,1\}\), indicating omitted coordinates or required bits; fix any constant-length binary encoding of these symbols. Thus there are \(3^{d}\) queries with descriptions of length \(O(d)\). The database is an ordered \(n\)-by-\(d\) bit matrix. For every ordered pair of equal-size databases \(D,D'\) differing at one row and every set \(O\) of binary output strings, privacy requires \[\Pr[M(d,D)\in O]\le e\Pr[M(d,D')\in O]+1/(100n^{2}).\] It is a guarantee on the whole synopsis distribution. \(M\) and \(E\) are ordinary classical multitape Turing machines with no advice, oracle or shared private database state; \(M\) uses independent fair bits. One fixed polynomial bounds its time, output length and number of random bits on every execution. One fixed polynomial bounds the evaluator's time on every valid query and synopsis. The probability of simultaneous accuracy is required separately for every database, with no input-distribution promise. All of \(C,\alpha,M,E\) and their polynomial bounds are chosen before \(d,D\). The convergence condition means that for every real \(\eta>0\), there is \(d_0\) such that \(\alpha(d)\le\eta\) for all \(d\ge d_0\); no computable convergence rate or procedure for evaluating \(\alpha\) is required. Error is an absolute error in a row fraction in \([0,1]\), not in the unnormalized count. Vadhan’s 2017 open question asks for vanishing error with polynomially many records and polynomial computation. The survey’s alternative question about some growing but restricted order is not substituted for the all-orders requirement.

Chandrasekaran, Thaler, Ullman and Wan give a subexponential per-query algorithm on small databases. Theorem 1.1 handles a sequence of adaptively chosen marginal queries at fixed absolute error and its database-size guarantee depends on the length of that sequence. This is meaningful progress, but is not a polynomial-time construction of one synopsis answering all orders with vanishing error.

The survey’s synthetic-data hardness theorem assumes one-way functions and restricts the output to a new database, even for two-way marginals. It does not rule out an arbitrary synopsis: the survey explicitly contrasts that obstruction with efficient nonsynthetic answers to low-order marginals. The benchmark deliberately retains this broader output interface.

The checked December 2025 weighted-Fourier paper provides exact optimality for weighted or maximum noise variance within Gaussian factorization mechanisms. Its runtime is polynomial in the dataset and the explicit output/workload size. For the entire \(3^{d}\)-query family that size is exponential, and variance optimality within that mechanism class is not a general polynomial-synopsis theorem or impossibility result.

cards.title: Chosen-ciphertext security from ordinary public-key encryption
cards.formal: Does the existence of an IND-CPA-secure public-key encryption scheme imply the existence of an IND-CCA2-secure public-key encryption scheme in the plain model, with correctness and classical security as defined below, against all nonuniform polynomial-size adversaries? The sole premise is ordinary chosen-plaintext-secure public-key encryption, and the conclusion is full adaptive chosen-ciphertext security with no fixed bound on an attacker's polynomial number of decryption queries.
cards.definitions:
A public-key encryption scheme consists of one fixed triple of uniform classical algorithms
\[
 \operatorname{Gen}(1^n)\to(pk,sk),\qquad
 \operatorname{Enc}(pk,m)\to c,\qquad
 \operatorname{Dec}(sk,c)\to m\text{ or }\bot .
\]
Here \(n\ge1\) is a security parameter, and keys, messages and ciphertexts are finite binary strings. The symbol \(\bot\) is distinct from every message. Gen and Enc use independent fair random bits; Dec is deterministic. Each algorithm is a finite Turing program with worst-case time polynomial in its full input length, including \(n\), which may be included in the keys. In particular, Gen has polynomially bounded output length. Encryption supports arbitrary binary messages; decryption is defined and halts on every ciphertext string, with malformed encodings rejected. The algorithms use no external oracle or advice.

A function \(\mu:\mathbb N\to[0,1]\) is negligible if, for every integer \(a\ge1\), there is \(N_a\) such that \(\mu(n)\le n^{-a}\) for all \(n\ge N_a\). Correctness requires that, for every polynomial length bound \(p\), some negligible function \(\mu_p\) satisfies
\[
 \max_{|m|\le p(n)}
 \Pr_{(pk,sk)\leftarrow\operatorname{Gen}(1^n),\ \operatorname{Enc}}
 [\operatorname{Dec}(sk,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,m))\ne m]
 \le\mu_p(n).
\]
The maximum includes the empty message. Neither perfect correctness nor recovery of the encryption randomness is required.

An adversary is a nonuniform family of classical polynomial-size computations with polynomially many fair random bits and polynomial-size advice. Advice can depend on \(n\), but not on the independently sampled keys, challenge bit or honest encryption coins. Total running time, state, message lengths, oracle-query lengths and number of queries are bounded by some polynomial in \(n\) that may depend on the adversary. Equivalently, these are polynomial-size Boolean circuits with the specified adaptive oracle interfaces. Arbitrary polynomial-size auxiliary information independent of the fresh experiment is included in the advice.

In the IND-CPA experiment, generate \((pk,sk)\), give \((1^n,pk)\) to the first stage \(A_1\), and let it output two equal-length messages \(m_0,m_1\) and a state \(\sigma\). Choose an independent uniform bit \(b\), form \(c^*=\operatorname{Enc}(pk,m_b)\) with fresh coins, and give \((1^n,pk,\sigma,c^*)\) to \(A_2\), which outputs a bit \(\widehat b\). Its advantage is
\[
 \left|\Pr[\widehat b=b]-\frac12\right|.
\]
The probability includes all key-generation, challenge-encryption, challenge-bit and adversary randomness. The quantification is over adversaries obeying the equal-length challenge rule and producing a bit; failures to follow this syntax may instead be defined to yield an independent fair guess. Both stages can compute arbitrary encryptions themselves using the public algorithm, so a separate encryption oracle is unnecessary. The scheme is IND-CPA secure if this advantage is negligible for every adversary just defined.

The IND-CCA2 experiment is the same except for adaptive decryption access. Before the challenge, \(A_1\) may query any ciphertext \(c\), receiving \(\operatorname{Dec}(sk,c)\). After it chooses the messages and receives \(c^*\), \(A_2\) has the oracle
\[
 \mathcal D_{sk,c^*}(c)=
 \begin{cases}
 \bot,&c=c^*\text{ as binary strings},\\
 \operatorname{Dec}(sk,c),&c\ne c^*.
 \end{cases}
\]
Every later query may depend on the challenge and all earlier answers. The exclusion applies only after the challenge is issued; it does not retroactively invalidate a pre-challenge query. Any different string is permitted, even if it encodes related data or decrypts to the challenge plaintext. The scheme is IND-CCA2 secure if the same advantage is negligible for every such two-stage adversary.

For each security notion, one fixed scheme must satisfy the definition for every polynomially bounded adversary. The scheme cannot be chosen after fixing a maximum number of decryption queries. Its negligible bound may depend on the adversary. All security is classical; no quantum adversary is requested.

The plain model provides no ideal random oracle, externally supplied common reference string, trusted hardware or separate setup. The recipient's own random key generation is allowed. The question is an implication between existence statements. A resulting scheme may use the descriptions of the starting algorithms, change all formats and incur any fixed polynomial overhead. No particular compiler, black-box access discipline or preservation of the starting efficiency is required.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof that an IND-CPA scheme implies an IND-CCA2 scheme satisfying the precise definitions, with proofs of uniform implementation, polynomial running time, correctness and security; or give a complete Lean-checked proof of the negation of this existence implication in the ordinary computational model.

Breaking a particular CPA scheme under chosen-ciphertext attack does not disprove the existence of a different secure scheme. A separation restricted to black-box constructions, or relative to an oracle, is not a negative resolution here. Additional trapdoor, proof-system, pseudorandomness or setup assumptions must themselves follow from the sole premise. Security only before the challenge, only against an a priori bounded number of decryption queries, or only against ciphertext modification without the stated decryption access is insufficient. No numerical approximation tolerance applies.

cards.title: One-way functions from errorless average-case NP hardness
cards.formal: Is the following implication true? \[(\mathrm{NP},\mathrm{PSamp})\not\subseteq\mathrm{AvgP}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{there exists a classical one-way function}.\] Here the antecedent means that some fixed NP language, under some fixed polynomial-time samplable distribution ensemble, has no deterministic exact decider with average polynomial running time in the moment sense below. The conclusion asks for a total polynomial-time computable function \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time inverter \(I\) and every integer \(c\ge1\), there exists \(n_0\) for which, for every \(n\ge n_0\), \[\Pr_{x\sim U_n,\ I}\bigl[|z|=n\ \land\ f(z)=f(x)\bigr]\le n^{-c},\qquad z\leftarrow I(1^n,f(x)).\] The statement is unrelativized and has no additional hardness, derandomization or cryptographic assumption.
cards.why: A problem can be difficult to decide on typical efficiently generated inputs without obviously providing an efficiently computed map that is hard to invert. Connecting these two kinds of difficulty would clarify the minimum computational assumptions needed for classical cryptography. The precise decision-error and security-length conventions are essential to that comparison.

sentences: This card selects the average-case-to-one-way-function branch of a broader question in Wigderson’s book.
The hardness assumption concerns exact deterministic decision under an efficiently samplable distribution, with average polynomial time defined by a runtime moment.
The conclusion requires a polynomial-time function that every uniform probabilistic inverter fails to invert with more than negligible probability at all sufficiently large lengths.
Recent heuristic-hardness characterizations, infinitely-often security results and oracle separations use different guarantees.
A resolution would clarify whether broad distributional hardness already forces the computational structure underlying classical one-wayness.

cards.definitions: A language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) is in NP if there are a fixed deterministic polynomial-time predicate \(R\) and a polynomial \(p\) such that \(x\in L\) exactly when some \(u\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}\) satisfies \(R(x,u)=1\). A sampler is one probabilistic Turing machine \(S\) that, on the unary size parameter \(1^n\), uses independent unbiased random bits and halts within \(q(n)\) bit steps on every random tape, for a fixed polynomial \(q\). Its exact output distribution is \(D_n\), over finite strings of length at most \(q(n)\). The ensemble parameter \(n\) need not equal the output length. PSamp is the class of these ensembles. A deterministic exact decider \(A\), given \((1^n,x)\), must halt and return the membership bit of \(L\) correctly for every \(n\ge1\) and every finite \(x\), including inputs outside the support of \(D_n\). Let \(T_A(1^n,x)\) be its number of bit steps. The pair \((L,D)\) belongs to AvgP if there exist \(A\), constants \(\alpha>0,C>0\), and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that \(\mathbb E_{x\sim D_n}[T_A(1^n,x)^\alpha]\le C(n+1)^k\) for every \(n\ge1\). These choices may depend on \(L,S\), but not on \(n\). This is an exact, deterministic moment-based notion, not merely a polynomial first moment or a heuristic allowed to misclassify a small fraction of inputs. The antecedent asserts the existence of one pair \((L,D)\) in the stated class failing this condition. In the conclusion, \(U_n\) is uniform on all \(n\)-bit strings, and the probability also includes the inverter’s independent unbiased coin flips. An inverter is a fixed finite probabilistic Turing program whose running time is polynomial in its input length on every random tape; all reading, writing and arithmetic are charged. It receives both \(1^n\) and \(f(x)\). It may output any preimage of \(f(x)\) of length exactly \(n\), not necessarily the original \(x\); malformed or wrong-length outputs fail. The function \(f\) is computed by one fixed finite deterministic polynomial-time program on all input strings, so output length is automatically polynomially bounded. All programs are uniform and have no advice or oracle. Security is required for all sufficiently large \(n\) for each inverter and exponent; security on only infinitely many lengths is a different guarantee.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the implication or its logical negation. A positive answer must derive the existence of a function with the full uniform, all-sufficiently-large-length inversion guarantee from the stated distributional hardness alone. The implication does not require an efficient black-box transformation from a description of the hard pair. A negative answer must establish the antecedent together with nonexistence of every such function in the unrelativized model; an oracle world, a barrier to one type of reduction or failure of one candidate construction is insufficient. A result assuming randomized heuristic hardness instead of the specified deterministic exact hardness, or yielding only infinitely-often security or a fixed polynomial security gap, does not alone settle this formulation.

The paper explicitly requires hardness on all sufficiently large instance sizes to upgrade its conclusion to standard security. Its corrected revision changes the approximation regime and does not settle the exact deterministic AvgP implication on this card.

Such a separation is relevant evidence about proof limitations, not an unconditional answer to this card.
