cards.title: Average-case RSA inversion versus factoring for exponent 65537
cards.formal: For the fixed exponent \(e=65537\) and the balanced-prime ensemble below, does the existence of a uniform randomized polynomial-time RSA inverter with inverse-polynomial average success imply the existence of a uniform randomized polynomial-time factoring algorithm with inverse-polynomial average success?
cards.definitions: For each integer \(n\ge 3\) let \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) be the finite set of primes p with \(2^{n- 1}\le p<2^{n}\) and \(\gcd (e,p- 1)=1\). Choose an ordered pair \((p,q)\) uniformly from \(\{(p,q)\in \mathrm{P}_{n}^{2}:p\ne q\}\), and set \(N=pq\). All assertions are for sufficiently large n with at least two such primes. Conditional on N, choose x uniformly from \(\mathbb{Z}_{N}^{*}=\{a\in \{0,\ldots ,N- 1\}:\gcd (a,N)=1\}\), independently of algorithm coins, and set \(y=x^{e}\) mod N. The inverter I receives \((1^{n},N,y)\), in binary except for \(1^{n}\), and must output the unique \(x\in\mathbb{Z}_{N}^{*}\) with that image. Nonnegligible success here means that some integer \(a\ge 1\) and \(n_{0}\) exist such that \(\Pr [I(1^{n},N,y)=x]\ge n^{- a}\) for every \(n\ge n_{0}\). The factoring algorithm F receives \((1^{n},N)\) and succeeds by outputting p or q; require some \(b\ge 1\) and \(n_{1}\) such that \(\Pr [F(1^{n},N)\in \{p,q\}]\ge n^{- b}\) for every \(n\ge n_{1}\). Both machines use independent fair random bits and have worst-case running time bounded by their own fixed polynomials in their input lengths on every random tape. The probabilities average over the stated modulus ensemble as well as x and the coins, with no promise of success separately on each modulus. The assertion is the ordinary existence implication \((\exists I,a,n_{0})\Rightarrow (\exists F,b,n_{1})\). It does not restrict a proof to black-box reductions: a construction of F may use the fixed code of I and count all calls to it in F’s polynomial running time. No independent oracle or advice is supplied.

context_blocks.text: Factoring an RSA modulus gives the private exponent and hence breaks encryption, but the reverse reduction is a longstanding cryptographic question. It would identify whether RSA inversion rests on precisely the factoring assumption or on a potentially weaker computational task.

Boneh’s survey asks about factoring with an RSA inversion oracle. This card retains the imported fixed-exponent average-case specialization and explicitly compares inverse-polynomial average success on its balanced-prime ensemble. The implication permits arbitrary constructions; restricted-model separation results do not refute it.

cards.title: Public-key quantum money from LWE alone
cards.formal: Does quantum hardness of the fixed decisional Learning with Errors distributions below imply the existence of a reusable, unforgeable public-key quantum money scheme in the plain computational model? The scheme must have a static classical public key, polynomial-time quantum minting and verification, and security against every nonuniform polynomial-size quantum adversary with classical advice.
cards.definitions:
The security parameter is an integer \(\lambda\ge2\), supplied in unary. Let \(q_\lambda\) be the least prime at least \(\lambda^4\), let \(\mathbb Z_{q_\lambda}\) denote integers modulo this prime, and define an integer error distribution by
\[
 \chi_\lambda(z)=\frac{\exp(-\pi z^2/\lambda^2)}{\sum_{a\in\mathbb Z}\exp(-\pi a^2/\lambda^2)},\qquad z\in\mathbb Z.
\]
For every polynomially bounded function \(m:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\), sample independently a uniform matrix \(A\in\mathbb Z_{q_\lambda}^{m(\lambda)\times\lambda}\), a uniform vector \(s\in\mathbb Z_{q_\lambda}^{\lambda}\), errors \(e_i\) independently from \(\chi_\lambda\), and a uniform vector \(u\in\mathbb Z_{q_\lambda}^{m(\lambda)}\). All field elements have their ordinary binary encodings. The LWE premise says that the two classical ensembles
\[
 (1^\lambda,A,As+e\bmod q_\lambda)
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 (1^\lambda,A,u)
\]
are computationally indistinguishable against the quantum adversaries defined below. That is, every such distinguishing circuit has negligible absolute difference between its two acceptance probabilities, for every such sample-count function. The discrete Gaussian specifies a probability law, rather than granting an exact sampling oracle to any algorithm.

A nonnegative function \(\mu(\lambda)\) is negligible if for every integer \(a\ge1\) it is at most \(\lambda^{-a}\) for all sufficiently large \(\lambda\). The threshold may depend on \(a\). A different negligible function may be used for each fixed adversary, sample-count function or repetition bound.

Quantum computations use qubits, the fixed Clifford-plus-T gate set, zero-state ancillas and computational-basis measurements, with polynomial-time classical control. A quantum state is a positive semidefinite trace-one operator on the finite qubit register concerned; mixed states are allowed. A uniform polynomial-time algorithm has one finite classical program generating and controlling these operations, with a fixed polynomial bound on the number of gates, qubits and classical bit operations on every measurement branch. Classical random bits may be generated by fair quantum measurements. A nonuniform polynomial-size adversary is a family of such circuits with polynomial-size classical descriptions and classical advice depending only on \(\lambda\). Its size and advice polynomial may depend on the adversary. There is no quantum advice or advice correlated with the fresh samples or keys. Uniform honest algorithms and nonuniform adversaries have no external oracle.

A money scheme is one fixed triple of uniform quantum polynomial-time algorithms
\[
 \operatorname{Gen}(1^\lambda)\to(pk,sk),\qquad
 \operatorname{Mint}(sk)\to(\sigma,\rho),\qquad
 \operatorname{Verify}(pk,\sigma,\rho)\to(b,\rho').
\]
Both keys and the serial number \(\sigma\) are classical binary strings; the keys may encode \(\lambda\). The note \(\rho\) occupies a register whose size is bounded by a fixed polynomial in \(\lambda\), as are all honest classical lengths. A scheme specifies its admissible serial and register formats and rejects malformed inputs. The bit \(b=1\) means acceptance. Verification returns the residual note register in its prescribed format, so it can be verified again with the same serial number. Its public inputs are only \((pk,\sigma,\rho)\): it has no secret key, persistent verifier state, external time input or interaction with the bank. Each call uses fresh ancillas and randomness. Mint calls are independent conditional on the classical secret key; the bank retains no correlated quantum minting state. All banknotes have one unit of value.

Reusable correctness requires that for every polynomially bounded integer function \(t(\lambda)\ge1\) there is a negligible \(\mu_t\) such that the following experiment succeeds with probability at least \(1-\mu_t(\lambda)\): generate the keys, mint one honest note, and invoke Verify on that note \(t(\lambda)\) times in succession, feeding each residual register into the next invocation with the unchanged public key and serial. Success means all invocations accept. The probability includes key generation, minting and all verification measurements. The scheme and the original minted note's size are not chosen as a function of \(t\); there is no prescribed expiration time or replacement by the bank.

For security, fix any polynomially bounded integer function \(k(\lambda)\ge0\) and any nonuniform polynomial-size quantum adversary \(\mathcal A\). Generate \((pk,sk)\), mint \(k(\lambda)\) independent notes under this secret key, and give \(1^\lambda\), \(pk\), all serials and all note registers to \(\mathcal A\). It outputs \(k(\lambda)+1\) serial/register pairs. Measure its classical serial outputs and run fresh local copies of Verify on the respective registers. The output registers may be jointly entangled; the acceptance event is the joint outcome of these local tests, not a product of their marginal probabilities. Security requires
\[
 \Pr[\text{all }k(\lambda)+1\text{ output notes are accepted}]
 \le\mu_{\mathcal A,k}(\lambda)
\]
for a negligible function \(\mu_{\mathcal A,k}\). The probability includes all honest randomness and all quantum measurements. Wrong output syntax is a loss. The serials may repeat or differ from those received; no condition of distinct serials weakens the game. The case \(k=0\) forbids creating an accepted note from the public key alone. Since Verify is a public algorithm, the adversary can run it as often as its polynomial circuit size permits. One fixed scheme must satisfy correctness and security for every polynomial repetition count, note count and adversary.

The question is an unrestricted implication between this LWE hardness statement and existence of such a money scheme. No black-box restriction, security-tightness requirement or preservation of the LWE parameter's numerical size is imposed on the reduction; polynomial overhead and polynomial reparameterization are permitted. No ideal random oracle, generic group oracle, trusted hardware, externally supplied setup or additional unproved hardness, obfuscation or leakage assumption is available. The bank's own randomized generation of its public and secret keys is allowed. Anonymity, tracing, public minting and quantum-lightning security are not additional requirements.

context_blocks.text: Public verification and unclonability must coexist: anyone can execute the verifier, while a holder of several valid notes cannot produce one additional accepted note. The definition counts notes even when they share a serial number.

The anonymous-money construction supplies additional privacy and tracing features under stronger assumptions. Its LWE-based auxiliary encryption primitive does not by itself give money from LWE alone.

The evasive-obfuscation obstruction limits the oracle access used by the mint and verifier. The current target allows arbitrary constructions and reductions, so that restricted barrier is not its negation.
The group-representation approach supplies money and lightning under group-action or specially structured homomorphism assumptions. These remain different premises from decisional LWE.
A reduction to group-action discrete logarithm can still retain an idealized group-action interface. The generic-model theorem does so, whereas this card requires ordinary finite quantum algorithms.

The 2026 time-dependent construction from post-quantum one-way functions uses public key announcements and banknotes that expire after their authentication layers are exhausted. Its transfer lifetime is chosen at minting and exhausted notes must return to the bank. The card instead requires a fixed note format reusable for every polynomial number of local verifications.

cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated implication, including the uniform polynomial-time algorithms, reusable correctness and security reduction to the fixed LWE premise; or give a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation in the ordinary computational model. The latter means the LWE premise holds while no scheme satisfying the full definition exists.

A broken candidate, a black-box barrier or an oracle separation alone does not refute this unrestricted existence implication. Schemes with private verification keys, changing public verification keys, expiring notes, a preselected polynomial transfer limit, generic oracles or additional unproved assumptions do not establish it. No numerical approximation tolerance applies to this yes/no target.

cards.title: Witness encryption from plain LWE
cards.formal: Assuming the specified polynomial-modulus decisional LWE hardness, does every polynomial-time NP witness relation admit standard-model witness encryption with correctness for valid witnesses and message indistinguishability on false instances?
cards.definitions:
The security parameter is lambda, supplied in unary. Efficient algorithms are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time Turing machines; security is against nonuniform probabilistic polynomial-size circuit families with polynomially many oracle queries. A function is negligible if it is eventually smaller than lambda^{-c} for every constant c>0. All message, instance and witness lengths in a security experiment are polynomial in lambda. No random oracle, trusted hardware or additional computational assumption is available.

The selected plain-LWE assumption is decisional LWE in dimension lambda, with q the least prime at least lambda^3 and integer error distribution assigning probability proportional to exp(-pi e^2/lambda^2) to each e in Z, reduced modulo q. For every polynomial m(lambda), a uniform matrix A in Z_q^{m by lambda}, a uniform secret s in Z_q^lambda and independent errors e give (A,As+e) computationally indistinguishable from (A,u) with uniform independent u in Z_q^m. Hardness is against the circuit adversaries above with negligible distinguishing advantage. This explicitly fixes polynomial modulus and inverse-polynomial relative noise; it does not assume evasive LWE, subexponential security or leakage resilience. It is an editorial parameter choice, not a claim that every formulation called LWE is equivalent.

For a fixed polynomial-time relation R(x,w) with a polynomial witness-length bound, let L_R={x: some w satisfies R(x,w)}. A scheme consists of Enc_R(1^lambda,x,m;r) and Dec_R(1^lambda,x,c,w). Runtime and ciphertext length are polynomial in the explicit inputs and security parameter. There is no key-generation or setup secret: x is the public encryption instance. Correctness requires that whenever R(x,w)=1, decrypting an honestly generated ciphertext returns m except with negligible probability, uniformly over valid polynomial-size x,w,m.

False-instance security means that for every polynomial-size sequence x_lambda outside L_R, any two equal-length polynomial-size messages m0_lambda,m1_lambda, and any adversarial auxiliary strings of polynomial length, the encryptions of the two messages at x_lambda are computationally indistinguishable to the adversary given x_lambda and those strings. No confidentiality is required on true instances lacking a known witness. The implication allows non-black-box constructions and reductions; a separation limited to a particular use of LWE is not a refutation of the unrestricted implication.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked construction and a reduction from every violation of correctness or false-instance security to the stated assumptions, or prove a genuine impossibility of the implication. A candidate supported only by evasive LWE or obfuscation assumptions is insufficient. Black-box-only barriers must be described as restricted barriers.

cards.title: General functional encryption from plain LWE
cards.formal: Does the specified ordinary decisional LWE assumption imply public-key functional encryption for all polynomial-size Boolean circuits, with adaptive indistinguishability security against arbitrarily polynomially many colluding functional-key queries?
cards.definitions:
The security parameter is lambda, supplied in unary. Efficient algorithms are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time Turing machines; security is against nonuniform probabilistic polynomial-size circuit families with polynomially many oracle queries. A function is negligible if it is eventually smaller than lambda^{-c} for every constant c>0. All message, instance and witness lengths in a security experiment are polynomial in lambda. No random oracle, trusted hardware or additional computational assumption is available.

The selected plain-LWE assumption is decisional LWE in dimension lambda, with q the least prime at least lambda^3 and integer error distribution assigning probability proportional to exp(-pi e^2/lambda^2) to each e in Z, reduced modulo q. For every polynomial m(lambda), a uniform matrix A in Z_q^{m by lambda}, a uniform secret s in Z_q^lambda and independent errors e give (A,As+e) computationally indistinguishable from (A,u) with uniform independent u in Z_q^m. Hardness is against the circuit adversaries above with negligible distinguishing advantage. This explicitly fixes polynomial modulus and inverse-polynomial relative noise; it does not assume evasive LWE, subexponential security or leakage resilience. It is an editorial parameter choice, not a claim that every formulation called LWE is equivalent.

Setup(1^lambda,1^n,1^s) generates a public encryption key pk and master secret msk for n-bit messages and circuits of at most s gates, with n,s polynomially bounded in lambda but otherwise arbitrary. KeyGen(msk,C) produces a functional secret key for any such Boolean circuit C with n input bits and a polynomial-length output. Enc(pk,m) encrypts m; Dec(sk_C,c) outputs C(m) for an honest ciphertext except with negligible error. All algorithms have polynomial cost in their explicit parameters and inputs. The circuit-size bound is allowed at setup; no collusion-count bound is supplied.

In the adaptive security game an adversary receives pk and requests keys for circuits of its choice. It then submits equal-length messages m0,m1 such that C(m0)=C(m1) for every circuit queried so far. It receives Enc(pk,m_b) for uniform b and may continue requesting keys subject to the same equality condition. Its advantage in guessing b must be negligible. The adversary can make any polynomial number of requests, with no fixed exponent built into the scheme; setup and ciphertext sizes do not grow with a declared number of users or queries. Only admissible adversaries satisfying all equality restrictions are considered. Public encryption already lets them generate other ciphertexts. No decryption oracle or function-hiding guarantee is required. This selects adaptive indistinguishability, not simulation-based security.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked construction, correctness proof and adaptive-security reduction using only the stated LWE assumption, or refute this precise implication. Security for a bounded declared number of keys, for only inner products, or under stronger combined assumptions does not meet the target.

cards.definitions: For an integer \(T\ge 2, a\) mechanism is a family of Borel probability distributions \(M_{x}\) on \(\mathbb{R} ^{T}\), one for each binary stream \(x\in \{0,1\}^{T}\). Its output \(Y_{t}\) is released immediately after observing \(x_{t}\). Causality means that whenever x and \(x'\) have the same first t bits, the marginal distributions of \((Y_{1},\ldots ,Y_{t})\) under \(M_{x}\) and \(M_{x}'\) are equal. The horizon T is known before the first output. Streams are fixed inputs, not adaptively chosen in response to outputs. Neighbors differ in exactly one bit, and pure privacy requires \(M_{x}(S)\le \exp (1/2)M_{x}' (S)\) for every pair of neighbors and every Borel \(S\subseteq \mathbb{R} ^{T}\). This protects the entire joint transcript, with no additive failure allowance. There is no restriction on computation, memory, real precision, output integrality or monotonicity; internal randomness may be correlated across times. A different family of probability distributions may be chosen for each T. The maximum over streams is outside the expectation; the maximum over time is inside it. The infimum is used without assuming attainment. \(E(T)\) is finite, for example because a data-independent all-zero transcript has error at most T. All logarithms in asymptotic comparisons may use any fixed base greater than one.

context_blocks.text: Continual counting publishes a running total as events arrive. For the stream \((1,0,1,1)\), the exact outputs are \((1,1,2,3)\). Changing its second bit gives \((1,1,1,1)\) and exact outputs \((1,2,3,4)\): one protected event changes several releases. Privacy must therefore hold for the whole visible transcript. Separate guarantees for isolated timestamps do not establish the stated joint guarantee.

The causal requirement forbids using future events to improve earlier releases. It also concerns their joint distribution, not merely the marginal law of each single output; otherwise correlations among old outputs could reveal future data. The offline query-release problem may inspect the complete database before producing any answer and consequently asks for a different capability.

The order of maximum and expectation is central. Imagine an error vector that equals one at a single uniformly random timestamp and zero elsewhere. Its expected maximum is one, but the largest expected absolute error at any predetermined timestamp is only \(1/T\). This example concerns error criteria, not a proposed private mechanism. Squared-error bounds and average-over-time bounds also cannot be substituted without checking the conversion.

For the fixed privacy budget here, the July 2026 Bairaktari–Larsen result gives the lower benchmark \(\Omega (\log ^{3/2}T)\), while the best upper bound summarized in their Table 1 is \(O(\log ^{2}T)\). The binary-tree mechanism aggregates intervals and reuses their noisy counts across prefixes. The paper closes the dependence on T for approximate privacy at fixed parameters, but its pure-privacy row retains the square-root-of-logarithm gap.

Arkhipov and Kalinin improve constants for mean and maximum per-coordinate squared error using matrix mechanisms. Those criteria take expectations before choosing the worst coordinate, or average squared errors. Improving them is useful, but does not by itself determine the expected largest absolute error of the entire transcript.

Bhowmik and Hasan’s August revision claims tight squared-error order for arbitrary real factorizations within Laplace matrix mechanisms. It explicitly excludes expected maxima and unrestricted non-matrix mechanisms. Thus even accepting its claimed theorem would not settle this card’s minimax quantity.

Lin, Mirrokni and Woodruff independently give a near-optimal lower bound for a prefix-matrix factorization cost. Its quantification is over factorizations, while this card allows every causal private output distribution. The distinction remains essential when reading a result advertised as optimal for a class of mechanisms.

A matching order for \(E(T)\) would identify the unavoidable worst-time accuracy cost of a basic continually released statistic under pure privacy. The target is a minimax information bound: it does not additionally ask for an efficient implementation or restrict the form of a candidate mechanism.

cards.answer_criterion: Determine an asymptotic rate \(g(T)\) and prove constants \(c,C>0\) and \(T_{0}\) such that \(c g(T)\le E(T)\le C g(T)\) for every \(T\ge T_{0}\). The upper guarantee must be achievable by permitted causal pure-private mechanisms, and the lower guarantee must cover all such mechanisms. Constants may not depend on T. The expected maximum absolute-error criterion must be the same on both sides.

cards.title: Additive privacy cost for adversarial bandits
cards.formal: Does there exist a pure centrally \(\varepsilon\)-differentially private adversarial-bandit algorithm, absolute constants \(C,p\ge0\), and a finite nonnegative function \(F(K,\varepsilon)\), independent of the horizon, such that for every \(K\ge2\), \(T\ge1\), \(0<\varepsilon\le1\) and oblivious loss array, its expected regret is at most \[C\sqrt{KT}\,(\log(2+KT))^p+F(K,\varepsilon)(\log(2+T))^p?\] This is the broad additive-separation question; no particular polynomial dependence of \(F\) is required.
cards.definitions:
Before play, the adversary fixes \(\ell=(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_T)\), where \(\ell_t\in[0,1]^K\). At round \(t\), the learner chooses an action \(I_t\in[K]\) using its own randomness and only the past actions and observed losses \((I_s,\ell_s(I_s))\), \(s<t\). It then observes the single loss \(\ell_t(I_t)\), not the other entries. Its expected regret is \[R_T(\ell)=\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^T\ell_t(I_t)\right]-\min_{i\in[K]}\sum_{t=1}^T\ell_t(i).\] The comparator is one fixed best action in hindsight; the loss array is not sampled from a stochastic model.

Two input loss arrays are neighbors when all rows but one agree; the differing row may change all K entries. Only the action transcript \((I_1,\ldots,I_T)\) is public. Pure central privacy requires, for every neighboring pair \(\ell,\ell'\) and every \(E\subseteq[K]^T\), \(\Pr[A(\ell)\in E]\le e^\varepsilon\Pr[A(\ell')\in E]\). There is no additive privacy failure parameter. Raw observed losses and internal state are not public outputs. The learner is trusted to access the observed losses centrally; local privatization of each observation is a stronger restriction absent here.

The same finite algorithm accepts K, T and the privacy parameter; knowing the horizon is permitted. No running-time bound is imposed. The exponent p and leading constant C must be independent of K, T and privacy. F may depend arbitrarily, but finitely, on K and privacy and must be specified in a positive solution. In particular, privacy cannot enter a coefficient multiplying the square-root-in-T term. Only a fixed power of the logarithm of the horizon is allowed in the additive term. This explicit broad convention retains the imported question without choosing an unsupported preferred dependence such as K divided by privacy.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked algorithm and proof of pure privacy and the uniform regret bound, including the function F and absolute constants, or a Lean-checked refutation of this broad additive-separation statement. Bounds for stochastic losses, full-information feedback, approximate privacy or only restricted algorithm families do not settle it. A multiplicative privacy factor in the leading square-root term does not meet the stated separation.

import_provenance.original_statement: For K-armed bandits with an oblivious adversary and central ε-differential privacy, can expected regret match the nonprivate O(√(KT)) term plus a privacy penalty independent of T up to logarithms? cards.title: Pseudorandom functions from worst-case hardness of learning
cards.formal:
For every circuit class
\[
\mathcal C\in\{\mathrm{AC}^0,\ \mathrm{AC}^0[p]\ (p\text{ any fixed prime}),\
\mathrm{ACC}^0,\ \mathrm{TC}^0,\ \mathrm{NC}^1,\
\mathrm{Formula},\ \mathrm{Circuit}\},
\]
does the following implication hold?
\[
\neg\operatorname{Learn}_{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathcal C)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{PRF}_{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathcal C).
\]
Here learning means uniform randomized polynomial-time improper learning under the uniform input distribution, with adaptive membership queries. The conclusion is a uniformly polynomial-time samplable family of functions computed by polynomial-size \(\mathcal C\)-circuits, secure against every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time oracle distinguisher. Both notions are defined below.

The hypothesis is only worst-case failure of learning: each candidate learner may fail on its own target function. No efficiently samplable common distribution of hard targets is assumed.

source_formulation.text: The source asks whether ordinary failure of efficient learning already forces pseudorandom functions within the same circuit class, and distinguishes this from earlier results assuming a hard distribution over targets.
source_formulation.caption: Paraphrase of p. 18:7, with the uniform polynomial-time target made explicit and the paper’s nonuniform exponential-regime theorem kept separate.

cards.why: A function class may resist every efficient learner without coming with a usable way to sample difficult targets. Cryptographic pseudorandomness requires a single efficient sampling procedure whose outputs defeat every efficient observer. The question asks whether the first obstruction alone supplies the second object within the same class.
cards.status_note: The source proves a related dichotomy for nonuniform learning and a different security/time regime, not the uniform polynomial-time implication specified here. The checked 2021 uniformization adds a constructive distinguisher premise, the 2025 work still asks a related bounded-query dichotomy, and the 2026 characterization concerns average-case learning. No resolution of the selected implication was found in the bounded review.

sentences: A learning algorithm receives query access to an unknown function and must output a circuit that predicts it accurately on uniformly random inputs.
The question asks whether failure of efficient learning forces an efficiently sampled pseudorandom function family in the same circuit class.
The premise permits a different hard target for each learner and does not assume a common samplable distribution of hard targets.
Both the learner and the sampler are uniform polynomial-time algorithms, and security permits adaptive chosen queries.
The source’s nonuniform exponential-regime theorem and the checked later qualified results do not establish this implication.

cards.definitions:
All targets are Boolean functions on \(\{0,1\}^n\), with \(n\ge2\). Circuits are finite directed acyclic graphs with input bits, optional constants, and a single Boolean output. Size counts wires; depth is the longest input-to-output gate path. Negation gates have one input. General \(\mathrm{Circuit}\) uses AND and OR gates of fan-in at most two and NOT gates, with unrestricted depth. \(\mathrm{Formula}\) uses the same basis but has a tree of gates, with no reuse of a gate output. \(\mathrm{NC}^1\) uses that bounded-fan-in circuit basis with depth at most \(d\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) for a fixed integer \(d\).

For \(\mathrm{AC}^0\), AND/OR gates may have unbounded fan-in and depth is at most a fixed integer \(d\). The class \(\mathrm{AC}^0[p]\) additionally permits a gate testing whether the number of ones among its inputs is divisible by the fixed prime \(p\). For \(\mathrm{ACC}^0\) the same definition permits any fixed integer modulus \(m\ge2\); the modulus does not grow with \(n\). The class \(\mathrm{TC}^0\) instead additionally permits unweighted majority gates, which output one when at least half their inputs are one. Negations and constants are allowed in all classes. These conventions specify classes of target functions; targets need not themselves be uniformly generated.

A fixed polynomial subfamily is specified by an integer \(k\ge1\), the wire bound \(n^k\), and, where relevant, fixed \(d\) and \(m\). Write \(\mathcal C_{\theta,n}\) for the resulting set of \(n\)-input functions, where \(\theta\) collects these fixed constants. For \(\mathrm{AC}^0[p]\), \(p\) is fixed as part of the choice of class.

The assertion \(\operatorname{Learn}_{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathcal C)\) means that for every fixed \(\theta\) there is one probabilistic oracle Turing machine \(L_\theta\) and a polynomial \(P_\theta\) with the following property. For every \(n\ge2\), integer \(q\ge2\), and \(f\in\mathcal C_{\theta,n}\), the machine \(L_\theta^f(1^n,1^q)\) halts within \(P_\theta(n,q)\) steps on every execution and, with probability at least \(2/3\), outputs a finite ordinary Boolean circuit \(h\) satisfying
\[
\Pr_{x\leftarrow\{0,1\}^n}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le 1/q.
\]
It may adaptively query any \(n\)-bit input and receive its exact value under \(f\); writing queries and the hypothesis counts toward its time. The hypothesis need not belong to \(\mathcal C\), and the target circuit description is not supplied. The polynomial running-time bound also holds for every other Boolean oracle. There is no advice depending on \(n\). Negating this definition gives the hardness premise with its quantifiers, including the possibility that the hard target depends on the learner and on \(n\).

The assertion \(\operatorname{PRF}_{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathcal C)\) means that for some fixed \(\theta\), some polynomial-time computable seed length \(a(n)\le n^r\), and a single deterministic polynomial-time sampler \(S\), every \(S(1^n,s)\), \(s\in\{0,1\}^{a(n)}\), describes a circuit for a function \(f_{n,s}\in\mathcal C_{\theta,n}\). The sampler runs in polynomial time in \(n\), including writing its entire output. It may be a general polynomial-time algorithm; only the sampled functions are required to have the stated \(\mathcal C\)-circuits.

For every uniform probabilistic oracle Turing machine \(D\) running in polynomial time in \(n\), the advantage
\[
\left|
\Pr_{s\leftarrow\{0,1\}^{a(n)}}[D^{f_{n,s}}(1^n)=1]
-
\Pr_{g\leftarrow\mathcal F_n}[D^g(1^n)=1]
\right|
\]
is negligible in \(n\), where \(\mathcal F_n\) is the set of all Boolean functions on \(n\) bits with its uniform distribution. Both probabilities include \(D\)'s random bits. The same sampled function answers all queries consistently. The distinguisher may choose polynomially many queries adaptively but does not receive the seed or circuit description. A nonnegative function \(\eta(n)\) is negligible when for every integer \(j\ge1\), \(\eta(n)\le n^{-j}\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). Security is eventual at all lengths, not merely on an unspecified infinite subsequence.

The implication is asked in the ordinary, unrelativized model. It does not require a black-box construction or an algorithm that extracts a sampler from a description of a hardness proof. This card fixes the uniform polynomial-time meaning of the source’s broader question; its exponential and nonuniform theorem is recorded separately as context.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed implication for the specified classes and quantifiers. A proof must obtain the efficiently sampled same-class family from the stated learning-hardness premise alone. Assuming a samplable hard target distribution, proving only a nonuniform or exponential-time dichotomy, or supplying a conditional PRF candidate does not suffice. A refutation must establish a failure of this implication in the stated unrelativized model; a relativizing or black-box barrier alone is not a refutation. This is a binary implication question, with exact security and learning quantifiers; numerical \(1/100\) slack does not alter them.

cards.title: Low-noise LPN hardness from Nearest Codeword hardness
cards.formal:
Does the following implication hold?
\[
\operatorname{NCP}_2\notin\mathrm{BPP}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\forall D\in\mathrm{PPT}\ \forall c>0\ \exists n_0\ge9\ \forall n\ge n_0:
\quad n\text{ a square}\ \Longrightarrow\ \operatorname{Adv}_D(n)<n^{-c}.
\]
Here \(\operatorname{NCP}_2\) is the unrestricted binary Nearest Codeword decision problem defined below. The distinguisher receives either \((A,As+e)\) or \((A,u)\), with a uniform \(n^2\times n\) binary matrix, independent uniform secret and comparison vector, and independent noise bits of probability \(1/\sqrt n\). The conclusion requires negligible advantage at all sufficiently large square dimensions for every uniform classical probabilistic polynomial-time distinguisher.
cards.why: A basic security assumption would obtain an explanation through independently studied hardness. The extra assumption in the new reduction makes the remaining target concrete.

progress.text: The primary work obtains low-noise LPN hardness from a simultaneous decoding/dual-code distinguishing assumption and identifies removing that extra foundation as a future direction.
Revision 1 retains that distinction. Its decoder also handles random noise in the stated reduction, rather than supplying a decider for arbitrary Nearest Codeword inputs.

The new reduction offers a choice: decode the code from random noise or distinguish noisy dual-code structure. Removing the second branch is a substantive additional demand.

cards.definitions:
The field \(\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}\) uses addition and multiplication modulo two. For a binary vector \(v\), its Hamming weight \(\operatorname{wt}(v)\) is the number of its one coordinates. An instance of \(\operatorname{NCP}_2\) is an explicitly given binary matrix \(G\in\mathbb F_2^{a\times b}\), a binary vector \(y\in\mathbb F_2^a\) and an integer \(t\) with \(0\le t\le a\), where \(a,b\ge1\). It is a YES instance exactly when some \(z\in\mathbb F_2^b\) has \(\operatorname{wt}(Gz-y)\le t\). The input lists the dimensions, entries and threshold with delimiters, using binary integers and row-major matrix entries. Invalid encodings are NO instances. There is no rank, balance, noise-distribution or closeness promise, and the task asks for one decision bit, not a codeword.

A language is in BPP if a single probabilistic Turing machine halts within a polynomial in the total binary input length on every input and every random tape, and answers correctly with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input. Its fair random bits are private; no advice or oracle is supplied. The premise means that no such machine decides this entire Nearest Codeword language.

For the average-case experiments let \(n=q^2\) with an integer \(q\ge3\). Independently draw all entries of \(A\), all bits of \(s\), and all bits of \(u\) uniformly. In the noisy experiment draw \(e_1,\ldots,e_{n^2}\) independently with \(\Pr[e_i=1]=1/q\), also independently of \(A,s,u\). The noisy vector is \(As+e\), computed over \(\mathbb F_2\); the other experiment uses \(u\). The distinguisher receives \(1^n\), the row-major entries of \(A\), and the corresponding vector with fixed delimiters. The sample count is exactly \(n^2\). It receives neither \(s\) nor \(e\), and cannot request extra samples. Square dimensions make the noise probability exactly rational.

A distinguisher \(D\in\mathrm{PPT}\) is one classical probabilistic Turing machine outputting a bit in worst-case polynomial time in the encoded input length, on every random tape. On these inputs that is equivalent to a polynomial in \(n\). Its description is independent of \(n\), and it has no advice, oracle or preprocessing depending on the particular random matrix. The advantage is
\[
\operatorname{Adv}_D(n)=\left|\Pr[D(1^n,A,As+e)=1]-\Pr[D(1^n,A,u)=1]\right|,
\]
where both probabilities include all experiment randomness and the independent internal randomness of \(D\).

The conclusion is eventual negligible advantage along the square dimensions: for each fixed distinguisher and positive exponent there is a threshold beyond which every square dimension satisfies the displayed upper bound. Its failure means that some fixed distinguisher and exponent have inverse-polynomial advantage at arbitrarily large square dimensions. The user explicitly selected this stronger length convention on 18 September 2026. The unrestricted decision premise, exact sample count and exact noise rate remain editorial specifications of the broader source direction, rather than a theorem stated verbatim there.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed implication. An affirmative proof must obtain eventual negligible advantage, including exclusion of a distinguisher that succeeds only on an unbounded subsequence of square dimensions. A sufficient route converts any such nonnegligible distinguisher into a BPP decider for the entire unrestricted Nearest Codeword language. A refutation must establish both the Nearest Codeword premise and a distinguisher violating the conclusion; an oracle separation or failure of a particular reduction is insufficient. An additional dual-code hardness assumption, a different sample/noise regime or only the exclusion of distinguishers successful at every sufficiently large length does not settle this target.

cards.title: Unbounded fully homomorphic encryption from polynomial-factor GapSVP
cards.formal: Does there exist a classical compact fully homomorphic public-key encryption scheme, with keys generated without any circuit-depth bound, and an integer \(a\ge1\), such that there is a quantum polynomial-time reduction from solving worst-case Euclidean \(\mathrm{GapSVP}_{n^a}\) to breaking its chosen-plaintext security, in the precise sense below? The scheme must support every polynomial-size Boolean circuit using the same key-generation algorithm. No independent circular-security or other cryptographic assumption may be used. A quantum reduction is permitted, while key generation, encryption, homomorphic evaluation and decryption are classical.
cards.why: Leveled encryption chooses its keys for a known computation depth. This asks for one reusable key setup supporting arbitrary polynomial-depth computation, with a security proof grounded entirely in a standard worst-case lattice problem.
cards.status_note: The checked 2016 question remains distinct from later constructions using functional encryption, a different lattice problem, depth-dependent keys or quantum evaluation. September 2026 cryptanalysis rejects a specific claimed worst-case construction. Bounded checks through 17 September 2026 found no scheme with the selected sole polynomial-factor GapSVP reduction; cited proofs and attacks were not independently Lean-verified.

sentences: The target is classical compact fully homomorphic encryption with keys generated before any computation-depth limit is chosen.
One scheme must correctly evaluate every polynomial-size Boolean circuit while keeping ciphertexts and decryption bounded by one fixed polynomial in the security parameter.
Its only security foundation is the worst-case difficulty of Euclidean GapSVP with a fixed polynomial approximation factor.
A quantum security reduction may inspect a classical attacker and must turn its distinguishing advantage into a solver for arbitrary promised lattice instances.
A complete Lean-checked construction or refutation is required; additional circular-security assumptions and depth-dependent constructions do not settle the target.

cards.definitions:
For a full-rank rational matrix \(B\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\), let
\[
 \mathcal L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\},\qquad
 \lambda_1(\mathcal L)=\min_{v\in\mathcal L\setminus\{0\}}\|v\|_2.
\]
An instance of \(\mathrm{GapSVP}_{n^a}\) is \((B,r)\), where \(r>0\) is rational and either \(\lambda_1(\mathcal L(B))\le r\) (YES) or \(\lambda_1(\mathcal L(B))>n^a r\) (NO). There is no requirement in the gap between these cases. Matrix entries and \(r\) are encoded by signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators; \(L\) denotes their total bit length. The basis is arbitrary and is not sampled from the key-generation distribution or restricted to ideal lattices. The integer \(a\) is chosen once with the construction, independently of the attacker and input size.

A scheme consists of uniform classical algorithms
\[
 \operatorname{Gen}(1^n)\to(pk,evk,sk),\quad
 \operatorname{Enc}(pk,b)\to c,\quad
 \operatorname{Eval}(evk,F,c_1,\ldots,c_t)\to c_F,\quad
 \operatorname{Dec}(sk,c)\to b\in\{0,1\}.
\]
Generation and encryption may use fresh independent fair random bits; evaluation may also be randomized, and decryption is deterministic. Their time is measured in ordinary bit operations. Generation and encryption run in time polynomial in \(n\); evaluation runs in time polynomial in \(n\) and its full input length. The security parameter \(n\) is indexed by the lattice rank in the reduction below. The public encryption key \(pk\), public evaluation key \(evk\) and private key \(sk\) have length bounded by one fixed polynomial \(P(n)\).

The plaintexts are bits, and \(F\) is an explicitly encoded finite Boolean circuit with \(t\) inputs, one output, and fan-in-two AND and OR gates and unary NOT gates. Neither \(F\), its size, its depth nor an upper bound on these is an input to \(\operatorname{Gen}\). Both fresh ciphertexts and evaluated one-bit ciphertexts have length at most \(P(n)\); decryption of these ciphertexts takes at most \(P(n)\) bit operations, independently of \(F\). Thus returning a circuit and its original ciphertext inputs for the holder of the secret key to evaluate is not compact evaluation.

For every polynomial \(p\), there must be a negligible function \(\mu_p(n)\) such that, uniformly over all circuits of size and input count at most \(p(n)\), and all input bit vectors, independently encrypting those bits, applying \(\operatorname{Eval}\), and decrypting produces \(F(b_1,\ldots,b_t)\) with probability at least \(1-\mu_p(n)\). Probability includes all generation, encryption and evaluation coins. Ordinary fresh encryption has the same negligible-error correctness guarantee. A function \(\mu\) is negligible if for every integer \(u\ge1\), eventually \(\mu(n)\le n^{-u}\). The scheme and polynomial \(P\) are fixed before \(p\) is chosen. Unbounded therefore means arbitrary polynomial circuit size and depth without selecting a depth limit during key generation, rather than literal infinite computation.

To state the security reduction without leaving its quantifiers implicit, let \(A\) be a classical randomized Boolean circuit receiving \((pk,evk,c)\) and outputting a bit. Define its distinguishing advantage at parameter \(n\) by
\[
 \operatorname{Adv}_A(n)=
 \left|\Pr[A(pk,evk,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,0))=1]
       -\Pr[A(pk,evk,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,1))=1]\right|.
\]
Each experiment includes a fresh generation of the key tuple, encryption coins and the attacker’s private coins. The size of \(A\) counts its gates, input bits and random bits. The family of attacker circuits may be nonuniform; it need not be produced by one efficient algorithm. The public key allows further encryptions, so this is the usual bit-message chosen-plaintext indistinguishability requirement.

The requested reduction guarantee is the following. For every fixed integer \(u\ge1\), there exist a uniform quantum algorithm \(R_u\), a polynomial \(Q_u\), and an integer \(N_u\), such that whenever \(n\ge N_u\), \(|A|\le n^u\) and \(\operatorname{Adv}_A(n)\ge n^{-u}\), the algorithm
\[
 R_u(1^n,\langle A\rangle,B,r)
\]
correctly decides every promised rank-\(n\) instance \((B,r)\) of \(\mathrm{GapSVP}_{n^a}\) with probability at least \(2/3\), in time at most \(Q_u(n+L+|A|)\). The clock holds on every execution. Here \(\langle A\rangle\) is the full attacker circuit description, which the reduction may inspect; black-box access is not required. Quantum time uses a uniform finite gate model, for example Hadamard, T, CNOT and computational-basis measurements, together with charged classical bit operations. No ideal cryptographic oracle is supplied.

This states a polynomial-loss worst-case security foundation rather than assuming the scheme’s security outright. In particular, a nonnegligible polynomial-size attack yields a quantum polynomial-time solver on all promised lattice inputs at the corresponding infinitely many insecure ranks. Under worst-case GapSVP hardness against such nonuniform quantum solvers on infinitely many ranks, the scheme has negligible advantage against every polynomial-size classical attacker. The task does not ask for an unconditional proof that GapSVP is hard. Quantum algorithms in the security proof do not mean that the scheme itself uses quantum messages or that security against quantum attackers is additionally required.

All public auxiliary material must be generated by \(\operatorname{Gen}\) and included in the attacker’s view. Bootstrapping and encryptions involving secret-key bits may be used, but their security must follow from the stated reduction. There is no separate circular-security, key-dependent-message, obfuscation or functional-encryption assumption, no random oracle, and no external trusted setup. The evaluator receives no subsequent assistance from the secret-key holder.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked construction of the scheme and its correctness, compactness and quantum worst-case reduction, with all the displayed quantifiers and bounds, or a complete Lean-checked refutation of this existence statement. A positive result must specify an actual fixed polynomial approximation factor; hardness of a superpolynomial-factor problem or an unspecified lattice problem does not establish this specialization.

A construction whose keys depend on a preselected depth, one that adds a circular-security or other independent assumption, or a scheme with a quantum evaluator does not meet the target. An attack on one candidate or a separation for one restricted type of security reduction does not rule out all the constructions allowed here. A conditional obstruction must retain its hypothesis unless that hypothesis is also proved. No numerical tolerance weakens the resource, security or correctness requirements.

source_formulation.text: Peikert asks whether unbounded fully homomorphic encryption can be based solely on a worst-case complexity assumption. The user selected Euclidean GapSVP with a polynomial approximation factor and allowed a quantum security reduction, while retaining classical compact encryption and keys generated without a depth bound. The neighboring question about avoiding bootstrapping is separate.
source_formulation.caption: Paraphrase of A Decade of Lattice Cryptography, §7.2 Question 11, printed p. 76 / PDF p. 78; specialization selected on 17 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: The survey separates two questions: reducing the cost or use of bootstrapping, and proving unbounded security solely from a worst-case assumption. This card selects the latter; a construction may bootstrap if its entire security proof meets the stated foundation.

The 2023 construction avoids a circular-security assumption by using functional encryption under additional assumptions. Its nonuniform-security statement also needs a further complexity assumption. It therefore does not supply the selected sole GapSVP foundation.

The revised 2026 lattice-isomorphism construction is explicitly leveled and uses a different underlying assumption. The presence of fully homomorphic encryption in its title is not by itself a depth-independent-key guarantee.

September 2026 cryptanalysis breaks a proposed unbounded CRT-based scheme and explains why expressing its encryption equation as a structured lattice task is not a worst-case security reduction. This rejects that candidate, not the possibility of the target construction.

cards.title: Noninteractive SZK versus SZK
cards.formal: Does NISZK equal SZK? Equivalently, does there exist a uniform deterministic polynomial-time reduction that maps every promised pair of sampling circuits X,Y to a sampling circuit Z, preserving the near/far promises specified below?
cards.definitions: A sampling circuit is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit with AND and OR gates of fan-in two, NOT gates, constants, a specified list of random input bits and an ordered list of output bits. Its description explicitly lists gates and wires in binary. Fresh independent uniform bits are supplied to all random inputs; the output distribution is the resulting distribution on bit strings. X and Y may have different numbers of random inputs but have the same output length. For finite distributions P,Q on the same set, \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=\tfrac12\sum_z|P(z)-Q(z)|\). The source convention for Statistical Difference has YES instances with \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(X,Y)<1/3\) and NO instances with \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(X,Y)>2/3\). Inputs between these promises impose no correctness obligation. The reduction outputs one circuit Z with \(m\ge 3\) output bits. On every YES input require \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(Z,U_{m})<1/m\); on every NO input require \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(Z,U_{m})>1- 1/m\), where \(U_{m}\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{m}\). The reduction runs in a fixed polynomial of the combined encoded input length on every syntactically valid input, including inputs outside the promise; writing Z and all its input/output nodes counts in that time. It receives no advice or sampling oracle. These are the source’s Statistical Difference and Statistical Difference from Uniform promise problems. Their completeness under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions makes existence of this reduction equivalent to the original class equality. Thus the complete-problem formulation fixes the question without having to choose a new auxiliary-input or setup convention for protocols.

context_blocks.text: Statistical zero knowledge asks whether a verifier can be convinced while learning only information that a simulator could reproduce. The unresolved equality asks whether interaction adds power when a noninteractive protocol has an honestly sampled public random string.

The same question can be stated entirely in terms of finite sampling circuits. Statistical Difference is complete for SZK, while Statistical Difference from Uniform is complete for NISZK. The requested reduction therefore tests the original class equality with a fully discrete input and output contract.

cards.why: Determine the intrinsic role of interaction in information-theoretic zero-knowledge proofs.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of a deterministic uniform polynomial-time many-one reduction satisfying both stated promises, or a Lean proof that such a reduction does not exist. The source’s complete-problem equivalence identifies these alternatives with equality or inequality of NISZK and SZK. Randomized reductions or computational zero knowledge concern different targets.

cards.title: One-way functions in \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\) from one-way functions
cards.formal:
Does the existence of a classical one-way function imply the existence of a classical one-way function computed by a polynomial-time uniform \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\) circuit family? With the definitions below, the proposition is
\[
\bigl[\exists f\;\mathrm{OWF}(f)\bigr]
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\bigl[\exists g\;\mathrm{OWF}(g)\land\mathrm{PUniformNC}^{0}(g)\bigr].
\]
Both sides require security against every nonuniform polynomial-size classical circuit family. The conclusion asks for the existence of some such \(g\), with some constant depth and some polynomial bounds. These constants may depend on \(g\), but not on its input length or on an adversary. There is no additional assumption on the starting function's circuit depth, no requirement that \(f\) and \(g\) have the same input or output lengths, and no requirement of a black-box construction or an efficient compiler from descriptions of \(f\).
cards.definitions:
A candidate function is a family \(f=(f_n)_{n\ge1}\), with a length function \(m_f:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb N\) and total maps
\[
f_n:\{0,1\}^{n}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{m_f(n)}.
\]
The output length depends only on \(n\), and zero is an allowed length. Let \(\mathrm{PolyEval}(f)\) mean that there are a single deterministic machine \(M\) and integers \(B,k\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\) and every \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\), the machine outputs exactly \(f_n(x)\) and halts within \(B(n+1)^k\) steps, with \(m_f(n)\le B(n+1)^k\). The machine is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with finitely many tapes, a fixed finite alphabet containing binary symbols, a separator and a blank, and one-cell head moves; each transition counts as one step. The input is the binary string on a read-only input tape with end markers, work tapes are initially blank, and output bits are written sequentially on an output tape. This fixes ordinary bit computation; the number of tapes, alphabet and program are fixed independently of \(n\). No advice, oracle or random coins are supplied to the evaluator.

A Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph whose input nodes carry the input bits, whose constant nodes carry \(0\) or \(1\), and whose internal gates are binary AND, binary OR or unary NOT. Fan-out is unrestricted, and the same predecessor may occupy both input positions. Outputs are an ordered list of references to nodes, with repetitions allowed. Size is the number of nodes plus the number of output positions. Depth is the largest number of internal gates on a path from an input or constant node to an output. Circuit descriptions list the nodes in a topological order, with gate tags and predecessor indices, followed by the output indices; indices and list lengths are in binary with separators from a fixed finite alphabet. No gates for arbitrary functions or oracle evaluation are present.

For a candidate \(f\), an allowed inverter is any family \(A=(A_n)_{n\ge1}\) of Boolean circuits of this basis, together with integers \(r(n)\ge0\), such that
\[
A_n:\{0,1\}^{n+m_f(n)+r(n)}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{n},
\qquad
\exists C,c\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge1,
\quad\max\{\operatorname{size}(A_n),r(n)\}\le C(n+1)^c.
\]
No uniform procedure for producing \(A_n\) is required, and its depth is unrestricted. The input blocks are \(1^n\), a proposed function value, and \(r(n)\) independent fair random bits. Thus the security parameter is given in unary, the adversary may depend on the input length nonuniformly, and it is not restricted to shallow circuits. For independent uniform strings \(X\in\{0,1\}^{n}\) and \(R\in\{0,1\}^{r(n)}\), put
\[
s_{f,A}(n)=\Pr\!\left[
f_n\bigl(A_n(1^n,f_n(X),R)\bigr)=f_n(X)
\right].
\]
Success means finding any preimage of the specified length \(n\), not necessarily the sampled \(X\). The function itself is deterministic; the probability is only over \(X\) and the adversary's coins \(R\). The negligible-success requirement is
\[
\forall A\text{ allowed}\ \forall a\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists N\ge2\ \forall n\ge N,
\qquad s_{f,A}(n)\le n^{-a}.
\]
The threshold \(N\) may depend on \(f,A,a\). Define \(\mathrm{OWF}(f)\) to mean \(\mathrm{PolyEval}(f)\) together with this requirement. Security holds at every sufficiently large length for each adversary and exponent, rather than merely on infinitely many lengths. There is no requirement of injectivity, length preservation, expansion, or any fixed ratio of output to input length.

The predicate \(\mathrm{PUniformNC}^{0}(g)\) means that there are a single deterministic circuit-generating Turing machine \(G\), integers \(B,k\ge1\), and an integer \(D\ge0\), such that for every \(n\ge1\), on input \(1^n\), the machine \(G\) outputs the full description of a circuit \(C_n\) in at most \(B(n+1)^k\) steps. That circuit has exactly \(n\) input bits, exactly \(m_g(n)\) outputs, size at most \(B(n+1)^k\), and depth at most \(D\), and satisfies \(C_n(x)=g_n(x)\) for every \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\). Generation uses the same deterministic bit-computation convention as above. The depth bound is a single constant for the entire family; in particular, every output depends on at most \(2^D\) input bits. The question places no bound on how many outputs a given input bit may influence. Circuit generation has no random setup, randomly chosen graph, public key or advice. The two existentially quantified functions may have different length functions and polynomial bounds.

context_blocks.text: Applebaum, Ishai and Kushilevitz explicitly ask whether an arbitrary one-way function implies a one-way function in \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\). A local function can expose many output bits, each depending on only a constant number of inputs, while inversion must remain difficult for general polynomial-size circuits.

Their theorems establish the implication when the starting one-way function has a polynomial-time uniform nondeterministic branching-program representation of polynomial size, which in particular covers logspace and uniform \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\).

This card retains its existing editorial choices of deterministic polynomial-time uniform evaluation, length-dependent output size, same-length preimages, and nonuniform circuit security; the source uses polynomial-time uniformity by default and explicitly extends its security results to nonuniform adversaries.

The Ren–Santhanam revision of August 2025 still explicitly describes the general implication as open and gives a characterization through average-case Kolmogorov complexity in its stated uniform-adversary setting.

cards.why: The question tests whether the minimal computational assumption underlying much of cryptography already guarantees functions with constant-depth local evaluation. A positive answer would make this extreme parallelism available under the general one-way-function assumption; a negative answer would separate local cryptographic hardness from unrestricted polynomial-time cryptographic hardness.
cards.answer_criterion:
An accepted answer is a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed implication or of its logical negation, using exactly the evaluation, uniformity and nonuniform-security conventions above. A positive proof must establish the existence of a secure family with one constant depth bound from the sole assumption that a one-way function exists. A negative proof must establish both
\[
\exists f\;\mathrm{OWF}(f)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall g,\quad\mathrm{PUniformNC}^{0}(g)\Longrightarrow\neg\mathrm{OWF}(g).
\]
Equivalently, for every candidate \(g\) with such a uniform constant-depth implementation, it must establish an allowed polynomial-size inverter family \(A\) and an integer \(a\ge1\) with
\[
\forall N\ge2\ \exists n\ge N,\qquad s_{g,A}(n)>n^{-a},
\]
as well as the existence of an unrestricted one-way function. The inverter and exponent may depend on \(g\). A separation only relative to an oracle, an obstruction only to a selected kind of reduction, or failure of a particular local candidate does not prove this negation. A theorem under an additional computational assumption establishes only that conditional result.

progress.text: Applebaum, Ishai and Kushilevitz show that a one-way function computed by a polynomial-time uniform family of polynomial-size nondeterministic branching programs implies a one-way function with output locality four. Their general open question allows any constant output locality and starts from an arbitrary polynomial-time one-way function.

The Mao–Mazor–Zhang revision gives non-adaptive constructions of universal one-way hash functions from arbitrary one-way functions. Its constant-depth corollary still assumes that a one-way function exists in \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\); treating oracle calls as gates does not remove that hypothesis.

Ren and Santhanam retain the general question in their revised introduction, alongside their characterization of local one-way functions by average-case hardness of \(\mathrm{KT}\) complexity. Their separate characterization of unrestricted one-way functions uses a different time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity measure, so these results do not establish the displayed implication.

Applebaum, Ishai and Kushilevitz explicitly ask whether an arbitrary one-way function implies a one-way function in \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\). A local function can expose many output bits, each depending on only a constant number of inputs, while inversion must remain difficult for general polynomial-size circuits.

Their theorems establish the implication when the starting one-way function has a polynomial-time uniform nondeterministic branching-program representation of polynomial size, which in particular covers logspace and uniform \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\).

This card retains its existing editorial choices of deterministic polynomial-time uniform evaluation, length-dependent output size, same-length preimages, and nonuniform circuit security; the source uses polynomial-time uniformity by default and explicitly extends its security results to nonuniform adversaries.

The Ren–Santhanam revision of August 2025 still explicitly describes the general implication as open and gives a characterization through average-case Kolmogorov complexity in its stated uniform-adversary setting.

cards.title: Verifiable random functions from one-way functions alone
cards.formal: Does the existence of arbitrary one-way functions imply a standard-model verifiable random function on all lambda-bit inputs with adaptive pseudorandomness and perfect uniqueness even for malformed public keys?
cards.definitions:
The security parameter is lambda, supplied in unary. Efficient algorithms are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time Turing machines; security is against nonuniform probabilistic polynomial-size circuit families with polynomially many oracle queries. A function is negligible if it is eventually smaller than lambda^{-c} for every constant c>0. All message, instance and witness lengths in a security experiment are polynomial in lambda. No random oracle, trusted hardware or additional computational assumption is available.

One-way functions means that a uniformly polynomial-time computable family f_lambda:{0,1}^lambda to {0,1}^{ell(lambda)}, for some polynomially bounded output length ell, exists such that every adversary given f_lambda(U_lambda) finds any x-prime with f_lambda(x-prime)=f_lambda(U_lambda) with only negligible probability. Inverters know lambda and must output a lambda-bit preimage. The function need not be injective or a permutation.

KeyGen(1^lambda) returns a public key pk and secret key sk. Deterministic Eval(sk,x) returns a lambda-bit value for each x in {0,1}^lambda, and Prove(sk,x) returns a proof. Deterministic Verify(pk,x,y,pi) accepts or rejects. Honest evaluations and proofs must be accepted except with negligible probability over key generation and proof randomness. All sizes and runtimes are polynomial in lambda.

Perfect uniqueness requires that for every public-key string of the permitted polynomial length, every x, and any two pairs (y,pi),(y-prime,pi-prime) accepted by Verify, y=y-prime. A malformed key may reject everything. There is no requirement that the proof string itself be unique.

For pseudorandomness, an adversary receives an honest pk and adaptively queries an oracle returning (Eval(sk,x),Prove(sk,x)). It chooses a fresh challenge x-star not previously queried, receives either Eval(sk,x-star) or an independent uniform lambda-bit string, and continues oracle queries excluding x-star. No proof for the challenge is supplied. Its distinguishing advantage must be negligible. The domain has 2^lambda inputs; weak security on randomly selected inputs is insufficient. Non-black-box techniques are allowed, and there is no setup beyond the individual generated key pair.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked construction with correctness, uniqueness and adaptive-security proofs from arbitrary one-way functions, or refute the unrestricted implication. A black-box separation alone does not rule out constructions using the one-way-function description.
cards.why: The question tests whether public verifiability requires stronger assumptions than ordinary private pseudorandomness.

cards.title: Blind signatures from one-way functions alone
cards.formal: Does the existence of arbitrary one-way functions imply a classical plain-model blind-signature scheme with concurrent blindness and one-more unforgeability, allowing polynomially many interaction rounds and non-black-box constructions?
cards.definitions:
The security parameter is lambda, supplied in unary. Efficient algorithms are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time Turing machines; security is against nonuniform probabilistic polynomial-size circuit families with polynomially many oracle queries. A function is negligible if it is eventually smaller than lambda^{-c} for every constant c>0. All message, instance and witness lengths in a security experiment are polynomial in lambda. No random oracle, trusted hardware or additional computational assumption is available.

One-way functions means that a uniformly polynomial-time computable family f_lambda:{0,1}^lambda to {0,1}^{ell(lambda)}, for some polynomially bounded output length ell, exists such that every adversary given f_lambda(U_lambda) finds any x-prime with f_lambda(x-prime)=f_lambda(U_lambda) with only negligible probability. Inverters know lambda and must output a lambda-bit preimage. The function need not be injective or a permutation.

KeyGen generates a signer key pair (pk,sk). A polynomial-round interactive protocol between Signer(sk) and User(pk,m) gives the user a signature sigma or an abort symbol. Deterministic Verify(pk,m,sigma) checks signatures. Messages have polynomial length. Honest executions yield accepted signatures except with negligible probability. The scheme has no CRS or globally accessible oracle.

Blindness is tested against a malicious signer that chooses a public key and two equal-length messages m0,m1. A hidden uniform bit b assigns mb to one honest-user session and m(1-b) to another. The signer interleaves both sessions arbitrarily with any further polynomially many sessions on messages of its own choice. If both challenge users finish, it receives their final signatures ordered by message (m0 first, m1 second), without session labels; if either aborts it receives only the common failure notification instead of either signature. Together with its entire interaction view, this must give only negligible advantage in guessing b. Honest users verify signatures before reporting success; malformed public keys may lead to abort.

For one-more unforgeability a malicious user interacts with an honest signer under an honest public key in any polynomial number q of sessions, scheduled concurrently. It wins by outputting q+1 accepted message-signature pairs with pairwise distinct messages. Here q counts all sessions initiated, including aborted sessions; no stronger completed-session accounting is required. The win probability must be negligible for every polynomial-size adversary. Signer sessions use fresh random coins. This fixes the session-count convention explicitly. Signatures need not be unique, and no ideal-world universally composable security or extraction is demanded.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked construction and correctness, blindness and one-more-unforgeability reductions from arbitrary one-way functions, or refute the unrestricted implication. Black-box-only separations and constructions in a global random-oracle model do not settle the plain-model target.

cards.title: Optimal regret for private stochastic online learning
cards.formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors, the optimal expected pseudo-regret \(R^{*}(K,T,\varepsilon,\Delta)\) for pure differentially private stochastic full-information online learning. The domain is integers \(K\ge2\), \(T\ge1\), and real parameters \(\varepsilon>0\), \(0<\Delta\le1\). For independent loss distributions \(P_1,\ldots,P_K\) on \([0,1]\), let \(\mu_j=\mathbb E_{P_j}[L]\); require a unique minimizer \(j^{*}\) and \(\mu_j-\mu_{j^{*}}\ge\Delta\) for every \(j\ne j^{*}\). At round \(t\), select \(I_t\in[K]\) using only earlier observations and private randomness, incur loss \(L_{I_t,t}\), and then observe the entire vector \(L_t\), where all \(L_{j,t}\sim P_j\) are independent across actions and rounds. Put \[R^{*}(K,T,\varepsilon,\Delta)=\inf_A\sup_{(P_1,\ldots,P_K)}\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}(\mu_{I_t}-\mu_{j^{*}})\right],\] where the supremum ranges over the promised product distributions and the infimum over the causal \(\varepsilon\)-private strategies defined below. The requested rate retains every dependence on \(K,T,\varepsilon,\Delta\), including logarithmic factors and the small-horizon regime.
cards.why: This asks how protecting one round of observations changes the achievable accuracy of sequential decisions even when the environment is stationary and all actions are observed. A sharp rate would identify the statistical price of pure privacy and whether the remaining dependence on the number of actions is necessary.

sentences: A learner repeatedly chooses an action and then observes the losses of every action.
The losses are independent draws from fixed unknown distributions, and one action has strictly smallest mean loss.
The card asks for matching-order expected pseudo-regret under pure privacy protecting one entire round of observations.
A published 2026 upper bound removes the time-horizon factor but leaves a logarithmic gap in the number of actions.
A solution must identify the rate throughout the stated parameter domain and certify both achievable guarantees and unavoidable loss in Lean.

cards.definitions: \([K]=\{1,\ldots,K\}\). The public parameters are \(K,T,\varepsilon,\Delta\); the gap bound \(\Delta\) is a promise supplied to the strategy, while the distributions, their means, and the best-action index are unknown. This is the minimax interpretation of the source's gap-dependent optimal-rate question: the worst case is over all instances whose minimum gap is at least the supplied threshold, rather than one specified vector of means. A strategy is a family of Borel-measurable probability kernels for \(I_t\), given the public parameters, earlier actions, and earlier full loss vectors. It may retain arbitrary private state and use correlated internal randomness; equivalently use the conditional kernels of its observable history. No running-time, memory, or properness restriction is imposed. The output available to a privacy observer is the complete action sequence, not the privately observed losses. For every pair of deterministic sequences \(s,s'\in([0,1]^K)^T\) differing in at most one entire loss vector, and every event \(E\subseteq[K]^T\), require \[\Pr[A(s)\in E]\le e^{\varepsilon}\Pr[A(s')\in E].\] This requirement applies to all loss sequences, including nonstochastic ones, and has no additive privacy slack. Its prefix versions follow by projection. The utility expectation includes both the stochastic losses and the strategy's independent initial randomness. Pseudo-regret compares against the smallest expected loss, not the smallest realized cumulative loss. The first action is selected before any losses are revealed. There is no adversarial dependence of later losses on released actions. Infima need not be attained; approaching strategies qualify.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a nonnegative rate function \(B(K,T,\varepsilon,\Delta)\), an explicit family of admissible private strategies, and universal constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\), with a Lean-checked proof that \(cB\le R^{*}\le CB\) throughout the stated domain. The upper bound must hold for every promised product distribution; the lower bound must apply to every causal private strategy and allow a worst-case promised distribution. If an infimum is not attained, certify arbitrarily close upper bounds instead of requiring an optimal strategy. Constants cannot depend on any of the four parameters. A bound only for deterministic losses, bandit feedback, approximate privacy, or only one side of the rate does not meet this criterion. This is asymptotic precision in unnormalized cumulative pseudo-regret, not an additive \(1/100\) approximation.

source_formulation.text: Determine matching-order bounds for gap-dependent pseudo-regret under pure differential privacy in stochastic full-information decision-theoretic online learning.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase

context_blocks.text: After each decision, the learner sees how every action performed. This makes the problem different from a bandit problem, where it sees only the chosen action. In a stationary environment, the mean-loss gaps measure how much evidence separates the best action from its competitors. The total error from exploring those competitors can remain bounded as the number of rounds grows.

Privacy treats one complete observed loss vector as one record and protects the joint distribution of all released actions. Protecting each action separately would not suffice: an observer can combine decisions across many rounds. Pure privacy also excludes a small additive exceptional-event term, which is explicitly outside the source question.

The 2024 paper compares an upper bound \(O(\log K/\Delta_{\min}+\log K\log T/\varepsilon)\) with a long-horizon lower scale \(\Omega(\log K/\Delta_{\min}+\log K/\varepsilon)\). Its authors expressly do not conjecture that this lower scale is optimal. Those displayed rates describe the nontrivial parameter regime; a lower bound independent of \(T\) cannot hold for arbitrarily short horizons because regret is at most \(T\).

Wu and Wang prove the improved stochastic upper bound \(O(\log K/\Delta_{\min}+\log^{2}K/\varepsilon)\). It removes dependence on \(T\) from the gap-dependent upper bound. A logarithmic factor in \(K\) remains between the stated upper and lower privacy terms. Their matching \(\Theta(\log K/\varepsilon)\) result applies to the separate model with deterministic loss vectors and does not settle the stochastic question.

The card makes the minimax quantifier convention explicit by supplying a lower gap promise \(\Delta\) and retaining finite \(T\). An upper bound using only the actual minimum gap also applies to this promise class. Sharp finite-horizon transitions and boundary gaps are part of the stated rate; the displayed long-horizon literature bounds are not claimed uniformly tight there.
