cards.title: PZK versus SZK
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{PZK}=\mathrm{SZK}\) for classical single-prover interactive proofs of promise problems in the precise input-only simulation model below? Both classes use uniform polynomial-time verifiers and simulators, negligible completeness and soundness errors, and zero knowledge against every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time verifier. Perfect simulation may output a failure symbol with probability at most \(1/2\); conditioned on success its distribution must be exactly correct. Statistical simulation permits negligible total variation distance.
cards.definitions:
A promise problem is a pair \(L=(Y,N)\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^*\). An interactive proof has a single computationally unbounded honest prover \(P\) and a uniform probabilistic Turing verifier \(V\), both receiving the common input \(x\). They exchange binary messages over an ordinary interactive channel. The verifier uses at most polynomially many random bits, computational steps and communicated bits, with a fixed polynomial in \(|x|\); its bound holds on every random tape and against every prover. A message or interaction exceeding the verifier's prescribed length or turn limit can be rejected. The prover has arbitrary computation and private randomness, but sees only the input and communicated history, not the verifier's private random tape.

A function \(\varepsilon:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) is negligible if for every real \(d>0\), some integer \(n_d\) has \(\varepsilon(n)\le n^{-d}\) for all \(n\ge n_d\). There must be one negligible error bound with honest acceptance probability at least \(1-\varepsilon(|x|)\) for every \(x\in Y\), and acceptance probability at most \(\varepsilon(|x|)\) for every \(x\in N\) and every possibly unbounded cheating prover strategy. Soundness thus concerns proofs, not arguments secure only against computationally bounded provers. No correctness or simulation condition is imposed outside the promise. Completeness is not required to be perfect.

A malicious verifier \(V^*\) is any fixed uniform probabilistic polynomial-time interactive Turing machine, with polynomial worst-case bounds on its computation, random bits and communication on every interaction. The honest prover has a specified behavior on every received history, including malformed messages or early halting. The view \(\operatorname{View}_{P,V^*}(x)\) is the resulting finite record of \(x\), the verifier's random bits and all exchanged messages with their order and delimiters. Its output and final state are determined by this record and its program. Random tapes can be padded to the verifier's fixed polynomial bound. This fixes one finite binary encoding of views; the special simulator failure symbol \(\bot\) is not a view.

The promise problem belongs to SZK if it has such a proof \((P,V)\) and, for every \(V^*\), a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time simulator \(S^*\) and a negligible function \(\mu_{V^*}\) such that for every \(x\in Y\),
\[
\operatorname{TV}\bigl(S^*(x),\operatorname{View}_{P,V^*}(x)\bigr)\le\mu_{V^*}(|x|).
\]
For distributions on finite binary records, \(\operatorname{TV}(D,E)=\tfrac12\sum_z|\Pr[D=z]-\Pr[E=z]|\); the sum may include records given zero probability by one distribution. Any simulator output not encoding a real view counts in that distance.

PZK uses the same requirements on the proof but replaces the last simulation condition by
\[
\Pr[S^*(x)=\bot]\le\tfrac12,\qquad
\mathcal L(S^*(x)\mid S^*(x)\ne\bot)=\mathcal L(\operatorname{View}_{P,V^*}(x))
\]
for every \(x\in Y\). Here \(\mathcal L\) denotes the probability distribution, and equality requires equality of each record's probability. Nonfailure has positive probability, so conditioning is defined.

Every simulator has a strict polynomial bound on every input and random tape, rather than an expected-time bound. Its polynomial and description may depend on the fixed verifier \(V^*\), but not on \(x\). It receives \(x\) alone, with no witness, prover interaction, nonuniform advice or separate auxiliary input. It may use the fixed verifier's description internally; no black-box simulation requirement is imposed. There is no common random string, oracle, computational assumption or multiprover resource. This retains the saved input-only convention; an auxiliary-input or expected-time variant is not substituted.

Class equality quantifies over all promise problems and permits the perfect proof system to differ completely from the statistical one. PZK is contained in SZK under these conventions: repeat a perfect simulator independently polynomially many times, retain the first nonfailure output and use any fixed record if all runs fail. The latter event can be made negligible while preserving a strict polynomial bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that every promise problem in the stated SZK class also belongs to the stated PZK class, or exhibit a promise problem in SZK and prove that it admits no PZK proof in this model. The positive direction need not be a uniform compiler from protocol descriptions. An oracle separation, a failure of one proposed compiler, a perfect-zero-knowledge PCP or multiprover protocol, or an honest-verifier-only result without a matching transformation does not resolve the unrelativized equality.

context_blocks.text: Zero knowledge formalizes the idea that a verifier can reproduce what it sees without receiving help from the prover. Statistical simulation permits a negligible discrepancy between distributions. Perfect simulation requires exact agreement after the allowed failure event. Goldreich’s textbook asks whether this difference changes which statements can be proved.

The failure convention is part of the model. A strict polynomial-time perfect simulator that never fails is a different requirement, often called super-perfect zero knowledge. Allowing an expected polynomial runtime is also a separate definitional issue discussed in the source. Neither convention is silently substituted here.

PZK is contained in SZK: repeat the bounded-failure perfect simulator polynomially many times until it succeeds, and use an arbitrary output if every attempt fails. The remaining probability of failure is negligible, while successful outputs retain the exact distribution. The open direction asks whether negligible simulation error can always be eliminated by some proof system.

Bouland, Chen, Holden, Thaler and Vasudevan construct an oracle relative to which SZK is not contained in PZK. This supplies evidence against equality and rules out a proof that relativizes in the corresponding way. It does not separate the classes in the ordinary model specified here.

Gur, O’Connor and Spooner explicitly retain PZK versus SZK as open in their 2024 paper. Their perfect-zero-knowledge construction is for probabilistically checkable proofs, where a verifier queries a proof oracle. That achievement concerns a different access model from ordinary interactive proofs and leaves this equality unresolved.

The target asks for a class equality, not a quantitative improvement in a particular cryptographic protocol. Its resolution would determine whether exact distributional privacy has an intrinsic expressive cost. TCS-1929 instead concerns zero knowledge for streaming interactive proofs with a memory restriction.

cards.title: Identity-based encryption from arbitrary public-key encryption
cards.formal: Does the existence of IND-CPA-secure public-key bit encryption imply an adaptively IND-ID-CPA-secure identity-based bit-encryption scheme for identity space \(\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\) with polynomial-size public parameters, under the classical standard-model conventions below?
cards.definitions:
All algorithms are uniform probabilistic Turing machines with worst-case polynomial bit running time in their explicit input lengths; decryption is deterministic. The security parameter \(\lambda\) is supplied in unary. An adversary is a nonuniform family of randomized Boolean circuits of size polynomial in \(\lambda\), including its advice and random-input nodes. All random bits are independent and fair. A function \(
u:\mathbb{N}	o [0,1]\) is negligible when for every positive integer a there exists \(\lambda _{0}\) such that \(
u (\lambda )\le \lambda ^{- a}\) for all \(\lambda \ge \lambda _{0}\). Security is quantified separately over every such adversary family, with a negligible bound allowed to depend on the family. A public-key bit-encryption scheme consists of \(Gen(1^{\lambda})=(pk,sk), Enc(pk,b)=c\) for \(b\in \{0,1\}\), and \(Dec(sk,c)\in \{0,1,\perp\}\). There is one negligible \(
u\) such that for every \(\lambda\) and b, \(\Pr[\operatorname{Dec}(sk,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,b))
e b]\le
u(\lambda)\), over key generation and encryption. In the IND-CPA experiment Gen is run, the adversary receives pk and selects bits \(b_{0},b_{1}\) and a state, an independent uniform \( eta \in \{0,1\}\) is chosen, \(c=Enc(pk,b_{ eta})\) is returned, and the adversary outputs \( eta '\). Require \(|\Pr[ eta\prime= eta]-1/2|\) to be negligible. The adversary may perform any polynomial number of public encryptions on its own before and after the challenge. There is no decryption oracle. Bit encryption suffices; longer messages are represented by bit lists. An identity-based scheme has \(Setup(1^{\lambda})\)=(mpk,msk), Extract(msk,id)=\(sk_{id}\) for every \(id\in \{0,1\}^{\lambda}\), EncID(mpk,id,b)=c, and \(DecID(sk_{id},c)\in \{0,1,\perp\}\). Public parameters include the scheme description, and mpk,msk,\(sk_{id}\) and ciphertexts have length bounded by fixed polynomials in \(\lambda\). For all \(\lambda ,id,b\) require \(\Pr[\operatorname{DecID}(\operatorname{Extract}(msk,id),\operatorname{EncID}(mpk,id,b))
e b]\le
u(\lambda)\) for one negligible \(
u\), including setup, extraction and encryption coins. In the adaptive security experiment the adversary first receives mpk. It may request keys for identities of its choice, each query answered by a fresh run of Extract. It then selects a challenge identity id* not previously queried, two message bits \(b_{0},b_{1}\) and retained state. The challenger samples an independent uniform bit \( eta\) and returns EncID(mpk,\(id*,b_{ eta}\)). Further adaptively chosen extraction queries are allowed for every identity except id*. Finally the adversary guesses \( eta\). Its absolute advantage over \(1/2\) must be negligible. The number and total length of queries are bounded by the adversary’s polynomial size. Illegal challenge or extraction queries abort the game with an independent fair guess, contributing zero advantage. There are no decryption queries; all public encryption calls can be performed by the adversary itself. The existence implication permits non-black-box constructions and provides no random oracle, extra setup or assumption beyond the stated PKE existence. The key generator is part of the IBE functionality, not an external assumption.

cards.title: Dual pseudorandom functions from arbitrary one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of arbitrary one-way functions imply a uniformly efficiently computable dual pseudorandom function family F_lambda:{0,1}^lambda × {0,1}^lambda to {0,1}^lambda with adaptive oracle security in each orientation?
cards.definitions:
The security parameter is lambda, supplied in unary. Efficient algorithms are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time Turing machines; security is against nonuniform probabilistic polynomial-size circuit families with polynomially many oracle queries. A function is negligible if it is eventually smaller than lambda^{-c} for every constant c>0. All message, instance and witness lengths in a security experiment are polynomial in lambda. No random oracle, trusted hardware or additional computational assumption is available.

One-way functions means that a uniformly polynomial-time computable family f_lambda:{0,1}^lambda to {0,1}^{ell(lambda)}, for some polynomially bounded output length ell, exists such that every adversary given f_lambda(U_lambda) finds any x-prime with f_lambda(x-prime)=f_lambda(U_lambda) with only negligible probability. Inverters know lambda and must output a lambda-bit preimage. The function need not be injective or a permutation.

F is deterministic and publicly evaluable in polynomial time. In the first experiment choose a uniform secret K and provide an adaptive adversary with oracle x maps to F(K,x); compare its output distribution to an oracle chosen uniformly from all functions from lambda-bit strings to lambda-bit strings. In the second experiment instead supply x maps to F(x,K), with the same random-function comparison. For each experiment separately and each adversary, the difference in acceptance probabilities must be negligible. Repeated random-function queries return the same value. The adversary may evaluate the public F on any explicit pair without restriction.

No experiment provides both secret-key orientations simultaneously, and symmetry F(x,y)=F(y,x) is not required. Key and input domains are the same full bit-string space, with independent uniform key sampling in either game. The construction may use the description of the assumed one-way function and non-black-box techniques; one-way permutations or collision-resistant hashing are not assumed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked construction and reductions proving both adaptive PRF games from arbitrary one-way functions, or refute the unrestricted implication. A standard PRF secure only in the first orientation does not suffice, and a black-box-only separation does not rule out other constructions.

cards.title: Compact general-circuit homomorphic secret sharing from DDH
cards.formal: Editorial independent-client variant: does DDH imply two-server, one-private additive homomorphic secret sharing for arbitrary polynomial-size Boolean circuits, with independently shared input bits and output shares of size independent of the evaluated circuit?
cards.definitions:
The security parameter is lambda, supplied in unary. Efficient algorithms are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time Turing machines; security is against nonuniform probabilistic polynomial-size circuit families with polynomially many oracle queries. A function is negligible if it is eventually smaller than lambda^{-c} for every constant c>0. All message, instance and witness lengths in a security experiment are polynomial in lambda. No random oracle, trusted hardware or additional computational assumption is available.

Assume an efficient generator of cyclic groups G of prime order q with generator g, unique polynomial-length encodings and efficient operations, where log q is polynomial in lambda and q≥2^lambda. DDH asserts that (G,q,g,g^a,g^b,g^{ab}) and (G,q,g,g^a,g^b,g^c), for independent uniform a,b,c in Z_q, are computationally indistinguishable. Public group parameters are sampled honestly; no pairing, trapdoor or stronger group assumption is supplied.

For every polynomially bounded n, client i with bit x_i runs Share(pp,1^n,i,x_i) with fresh independent randomness to give strings s_i1,s_i2 to the two servers. Sharing does not know the circuit or other inputs. Server j locally runs Eval(pp,j,C,s_1j,…,s_nj) on any Boolean circuit C:{0,1}^n to {0,1} of polynomial size, without communicating with the other server. It outputs y_j in Z_q. The decoder is addition modulo q; correctness requires y_1+y_2=C(x) modulo q except with negligible error for every polynomial-size input/circuit family.

Privacy means that for either fixed server j and any two n-bit vectors x,x-prime, the distributions of pp together with all its shares (s_1j,…,s_nj) are computationally indistinguishable. The same parameters can be used in polynomially many fresh sharing batches, with security required for adaptive chosen equal-length input pairs in a left-or-right sharing oracle for one fixed server. Neither server ever sees the other’s shares. No robustness against incorrect evaluations or hiding of the public circuit is demanded.

Share runs in polynomial time in lambda+n, independently of C; Eval runs in polynomial time in lambda+n+|C|. Each output share is exactly a Z_q element and thus has size depending only on lambda, not circuit size or depth. This specifies an independent-input additive variant; setup contains only the public group parameters, with no circuit-specific preprocessing.

HSS limited to branching programs, output strings growing with circuit size, or a decoder that performs the full circuit computation does not meet the target.

cards.title: Constant-round concurrent zero knowledge from LWE alone
cards.formal: Does the specified ordinary LWE assumption imply a constant-round plain-model concurrent zero-knowledge argument for every NP relation, with no a priori bound on polynomially many interleaved sessions and with expected-polynomial-time simulation?
cards.definitions:
The security parameter is lambda, supplied in unary. Efficient algorithms are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time Turing machines; security is against nonuniform probabilistic polynomial-size circuit families with polynomially many oracle queries. A function is negligible if it is eventually smaller than lambda^{-c} for every constant c>0. All message, instance and witness lengths in a security experiment are polynomial in lambda. No random oracle, trusted hardware or additional computational assumption is available.

The selected plain-LWE assumption is decisional LWE in dimension lambda, with q the least prime at least lambda^3 and integer error distribution assigning probability proportional to exp(-pi e^2/lambda^2) to each e in Z, reduced modulo q. For every polynomial m(lambda), a uniform matrix A in Z_q^{m by lambda}, a uniform secret s in Z_q^lambda and independent errors e give (A,As+e) computationally indistinguishable from (A,u) with uniform independent u in Z_q^m. Hardness is against the circuit adversaries above with negligible distinguishing advantage. This explicitly fixes polynomial modulus and inverse-polynomial relative noise; it does not assume evasive LWE, subexponential security or leakage resilience. It is an editorial parameter choice, not a claim that every formulation called LWE is equivalent.

For each polynomial-time relation R(x,w), the protocol has a uniform polynomial-time honest prover given (x,w) and verifier given x. There is an absolute constant r for this protocol, independent of lambda, x and concurrency, bounding the number of messages per session. Completeness is 1 minus negligible for valid witnesses. Argument soundness means every polynomial-size cheating prover makes an honest verifier accept a false polynomial-size instance only with negligible probability. No knowledge-extraction requirement is imposed.

For zero knowledge, consider any efficient malicious verifier controlling polynomially many sessions, with arbitrary polynomial auxiliary input and an arbitrary fixed polynomial-size list of valid statements and witnesses for honest provers. It can initiate sessions from this list adaptively, interleave their messages arbitrarily, and abort sessions. Honest prover instances use fresh randomness. For every such verifier there must be a simulator, given the statements and verifier auxiliary input but no witnesses, whose expected running time is polynomial in the security parameter and total instance length and whose output is computationally indistinguishable from the verifier’s joint view, including its random tape, received messages and output. The simulator can use the verifier’s program non-black-box. Its polynomial may depend on that verifier.

The protocol is fixed before the adversary’s concurrency polynomial is known. There are no registered player identities, trusted setup, timing guarantees, random oracle or bound on the number of distinct verifier identities. This explicitly selects the standard fixed-list statement formulation and expected polynomial simulation; it does not require online straight-line simulation or adaptive choice of previously unspecified statements.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked constant-round protocol with completeness, argument soundness and concurrent simulation from the specified LWE assumption, or prove this implication impossible. Bounded-player, bounded-concurrency, superpolynomial-simulation and black-box-only results must be distinguished from the target.
cards.why: The target combines minimal assumptions, concurrency and a constant interaction cost.

cards.title: Doubly efficient PIR with quasilinear server preprocessing
cards.formal: Under the specified Ring-LWE assumption, is there unkeyed single-server PIR on every N-bit database with deterministic server-only preprocessing time and storage N times poly(lambda,log N), and worst-case online client/server time, communication and client workspace poly(lambda,log N)?
cards.definitions:
Use security parameter lambda and negligible error as a function of lambda. The selected Ring-LWE family has power-of-two dimension d, ring R_d=Z_q[X]/(X^d+1), q=2^{ceil(sqrt(d))}, and independent integer error coefficients with probability proportional to exp(-pi e^2/d^2), reduced modulo q. For any polynomial number of samples, (a_i,a_i s+e_i), with common uniform s and independent uniform a_i in R_d, must be indistinguishable from independent uniform pairs to nonuniform polynomial-size classical adversaries as d grows. This explicit subexponential-modulus family is an editorial parameter choice. It imposes no circular-security or evasive assumption. Algorithms may choose d polynomial in lambda+log N.

The database D is any N-bit string. Prep(1^lambda,D) deterministically creates a static server data structure without communicating with a client or generating secret client keys. A fresh client given only lambda,N and index i generates a query and short temporary state. The server answers using random access to its data structure, and the client recovers D_i from the answer and its state. There is no database-dependent advice, offline download or pre-established shared secret at the client. Correctness is at least one minus negligible for every D and i.

Privacy requires indistinguishability of the server’s entire view for any two adaptively chosen index sequences of equal polynomial length, with fresh client randomness for each query. The server may know D and the complete preprocessed structure; its memory-access pattern and random coins are part of its view. Security is against polynomial-size adversaries for every N polynomially bounded in lambda, while the efficiency formulas are required for all lambda,N. The client need not hide the number of queries, and database confidentiality and malicious-server answer correctness are not required.

Costs use a bit-cost random-access machine: a memory access to an O(log(N+lambda+2))-bit word costs that many bit operations; arithmetic is charged for its actual bit complexity. Every stored bit and transmitted bit counts. There must be one polynomial p with preprocessing time and stored bits at most N p(lambda,log(N+2)), and worst-case time, communication and workspace per query at most p(lambda,log(N+2)). Preprocessing is independent of the eventual client and query sequence; no amortized online bound is substituted.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked construction and proofs of the specified preprocessing, online costs, correctness and privacy from the stated Ring-LWE assumption, or refute this precise variant. An N^{1+epsilon} bound for every fixed epsilon is not a quasilinear bound, and client-specific preprocessing does not qualify.
cards.why: The question asks whether privacy-preserving database access can have almost optimal preparation as well as fast queries.

cards.title: Polynomial-time computationally sound verification of \(\#\mathrm{SAT}\)
cards.formal: Do there exist deterministic uniform algorithms \(P,V\), integers \(C>c\ge1\), and a constant \(K\ge2\) giving the following plain-model argument system for exact \(\#\mathrm{SAT}\), without unproved hardness assumptions? On a Boolean formula \(\Phi\) encoded in \(N\) bits, \(P\) produces a proof of length at most \((N+1)^C\) in time \(T_P(N)=2^{K(N+1)^c}\). The verifier runs in time \(K(N+1)^C\) and outputs either the exact number of satisfying assignments or the rejection symbol \(\bot\). Completeness requires \(V(\Phi,P(\Phi))=\#\mathrm{SAT}(\Phi)\) on every valid formula. Soundness requires that every uniform randomized adversary running in any fixed polynomial in \(T_P(N)\) has only negligible probability, as a function of \(T_P(N)\), of generating a length-\(N\) formula and a proof on which \(V\) outputs an incorrect number. This card fixes the unconditional version of the source question; conditional constructions are recorded below.
cards.why: Exact counting requires certifying that no satisfying assignments were missed, as well as that counted assignments exist. This question tests whether computational soundness can give deterministic short verification of such global information while retaining an honest prover with a specified running time. It connects the power of proof systems with derandomization and the distinction between uniform computational attacks and arbitrary false witnesses.
cards.status_note: Open Problem 4.5 of the 2023 source was checked together with the 3 April 2025 revision of Chen–Rothblum–Tell on 2026-09-14. The latter gives conditional polynomial-time verification under strong hardness assumptions; this card explicitly selects unconditional existence with its honest-prover/adversary convention. A bounded later-work search found no unconditional resolution.

sentences: The task is to check the exact number of satisfying assignments to a Boolean formula in polynomial time.
An exponential-time honest prover supplies a short proof to a fully deterministic verifier.
Even adversaries running in any polynomial in the honest prover’s time must almost never find a false counting claim that the verifier accepts.
A 2025 theorem gives such verification for polynomial-space claims under strong hardness assumptions.
This card asks whether the specified counting-verification system exists without those unproved assumptions.

cards.definitions:
Fix a polynomial-time parsable binary encoding of formulas over AND, OR and NOT. An instance lists its \(n\) variables explicitly, so \(n\le N\), and its formula is a finite tree with leaves among those variables and Boolean constants. The value \(\#\mathrm{SAT}(\Phi)\) is the number of assignments in \(\{0,1\}^n\) on which the formula evaluates to one, including choices of any listed unused variables. The answer is written in binary and has at most \(n+1\) bits. Measuring resources in the full encoding length fixes the meaning of polynomial-size formulas and includes the cost of reading their descriptions.

The prover and verifier are deterministic multitape Turing machines with finite descriptions independent of input length. The proof is one finite binary string; there is no interaction, oracle, common reference string, advice, secret setup or verifier randomness. The verifier rejects malformed instances and overlong proofs. It halts within its stated bound on every input, reading at most one symbol beyond the permitted proof length to detect excess input. Increasing the fixed constant \(K\) absorbs encoding and rejection overhead. The honest prover must construct its proof in the stated exponential time; mere existence of a proof with no bound on its production is insufficient.

More explicitly, for every uniform probabilistic Turing machine \(A\) whose worst-case runtime on \(1^N\) is at most \(T_P(N)^a\) for some fixed \(a\ge1\), and for every integer \(d\ge1\), there is \(N_{A,d}\) such that, for every \(N\ge N_{A,d}\),
\[\Pr_{(\Phi,\pi)\leftarrow A(1^N)}\bigl[\Phi\text{ is valid},\ |\Phi|=N,\ V(\Phi,\pi)\notin\{\#\mathrm{SAT}(\Phi),\bot\}\bigr]\le T_P(N)^{-d}.\]
Probability is over independent fair random bits used by \(A\). Any output that is not a valid formula/proof pair is a failed attack. The adversary chooses both the formula and its proof, knows \(P,V\), and has no nonuniform advice or auxiliary input. The polynomial exponent \(a\) may be arbitrarily large and is not fixed by the protocol. Negligibility is measured in the honest prover's time, rather than merely inverse polynomial in the formula length. The constants \(c,C,K\) and the two machines must be fixed before quantifying over adversaries and accuracy exponents.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such a system exists, including all completeness, uniformity, running-time and soundness requirements, or prove that no such system exists. A positive answer must be unconditional. A construction assuming a conjectured hard function is progress but does not settle this selected version. Randomized verification, interaction, a setup string, soundness only against polynomial-in-input-length adversaries, or an unbounded honest prover changes the question.

context_blocks.text: Computational soundness permits incorrect proofs to exist, provided no adversary with the specified resources can generate a false instance together with an accepted proof. Ordinary NP soundness forbids every false proof. Allowing nonuniform advice would let an adversary hardwire a false pair at each input length, removing this distinction.

The honest prover is allowed exponential time, and the adversary is allowed every polynomial in that time. Requiring a polynomial-time honest prover would instead give a polynomial-time exact counting algorithm by composing prover and verifier. Allowing an arbitrarily stronger honest prover than the attacker would also distort the model; the later paper explains why.

The 2023 source gives, under strong assumptions, verification in time \(2^{\varepsilon n}\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), with an honest prover and adversaries using \(2^{O(n)}\) time. Its next question asks for a polynomial-time verifier.

The 2025 paper proves \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\subseteq\mathrm{cs}\text{-}\mathrm{NP}\) under strong assumptions about functions that remain hard for small-space computation on efficiently samplable inputs. Its Definition 1.1 explicitly allows a polynomial-time verifier with an exponential-time honest prover. Applying its polynomial-space verification result to exact-count claims gives conditional progress on this card, since exact counting can be performed in polynomial space. The paper does not prove the required hardness assumptions.

cards.title: Exponentially hard weak versus strong one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of an exponentially hard weak one-way function imply the existence of an exponentially hard strong one-way function, in the following nonuniform-adversary, negligible-success formulation? The premise is that there exist a uniform polynomial-time computable length-preserving function \(f\), a real \(a>0\), an integer \(k\ge1\), and \(n_0\), such that \[\operatorname{Inv}_f(C,n)\le1-n^{-k}\] for every \(n\ge n_0\) and every circuit \(C\) with \(n\) inputs, \(n\) outputs and at most \(2^{an}\) gates. The desired conclusion is that there exist another uniform polynomial-time computable length-preserving function \(g\) and a real \(b>0\) such that, for every integer \(d\ge1\), there is \(n_d\) with \[\operatorname{Inv}_g(C,n)\le n^{-d}\] for every \(n\ge n_d\) and every such circuit with at most \(2^{bn}\) gates. cards.definitions:
A length-preserving function is a single map \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) with \(|f(x)|=|x|\), computed by one deterministic multitape Turing machine in at most \(A(n+1)^r\) steps on every input of length \(n\), for some fixed constants \(A,r\). The same convention applies to \(g\). There is no oracle or advice in forward evaluation.

For a circuit \(C:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^n\), define its inversion success by \[\operatorname{Inv}_f(C,n)=\Pr_{x\leftarrow U_n}\bigl[f(C(f(x)))=f(x)\bigr],\] where \(U_n\) is uniform on all length-\(n\) bit strings. Finding any length-\(n\) preimage counts as success; the output need not equal the originally sampled \(x\). The challenge is sampled by applying \(f\) to a uniform input, not by choosing a uniform element of its image.

Circuits are finite directed acyclic graphs of fan-in-two AND and OR gates, fan-in-one NOT gates and constants, with named inputs and outputs. Size counts noninput gates, including constants; no restriction is placed on fan-out. Real size limits mean their integer floors. Every circuit is allowed independently at each input length, including circuits with information built into their wiring and constants. No uniform procedure for generating the attack circuits is required. Deterministic circuits suffice for the displayed average-success bound: a randomized attack is a distribution over such circuits, and averaging cannot exceed their common bound.

Weakness means a fixed inverse-polynomial fraction of the sampled challenges defeats every allowed attacker. Strongness here means that the maximum success of any allowed attacker is negligible: smaller than every fixed inverse power for sufficiently large lengths. The exponent \(b\) is fixed before \(d\). This explicitly uses negligible success against exponential-size circuits; it does not add a separate exponentially small success requirement. Security is measured against the input length of each function itself, on all sufficiently large lengths. Both functions are length-preserving, following the source's stated convention; arbitrary padding is not assumed to preserve exponential hardness.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of this implication, or a proof of its negation. A positive answer may use an arbitrary construction or existence argument and need not preserve the original security exponent. It must produce a single polynomial-time function with a positive linear exponential attack-size exponent and negligible inversion success. A negative answer must refute the existence implication itself; a barrier for black-box transformations or for a restricted amplification method is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: The reverse implication is immediate: negligible inversion success also leaves an inverse-polynomial fraction of inputs hard. The substantive question is the weak-to-strong direction. It does not ask to prove that one-way functions exist without assumptions.

The usual direct-product amplification evaluates the weak function on many independent blocks. Its enlarged input length can turn exponential security in a block length into only stretched-exponential security in the new length. The 2025 revision explicitly identifies this loss as the unresolved issue.

Security-preserving amplification is known under regularity assumptions: at a fixed input length, every value in the image of a regular function has the same number of preimages. The present premise includes arbitrary functions with unequal fiber sizes, so that special case does not establish the general implication.

The question is about existence of a suitable strong function. It does not demand a black-box reduction, restrict forward computation to constant depth, or require the new function to use the same input length as a single invocation of the old one. Its exponential guarantee is nevertheless measured in its own full input length.

cards.title: Linear-seed pseudorandom generators from one-way functions
cards.formal:
Can every efficiently evaluable length-preserving one-way function be converted into a fully explicit pseudorandom generator with seed length linear in the function's input length, while retaining the following quantitative security?

Precisely, for every integer \(b\ge1\), do there exist integers \(A,K,q,r\ge1\), \(\ell_0\ge4\), and one deterministic compiler \(\mathcal B_b\) such that the following holds? Its input is a Boolean circuit \(F:\{0,1\}^{\ell}\to\{0,1\}^{\ell}\) of size at most \(\ell^b\), integers \(\ell\ge\ell_0\), \(1\le s\le2^{2\ell}\), \(m>A\ell\), and \(1\le e\le2\ell\). Write
\[
 \varepsilon=2^{-e},\qquad
 t=\left\lfloor\frac{s}{K(m2^e)^q}\right\rfloor,
\]
and require \(t\ge1\). Suppose every inversion circuit \(I\) of size at most \(s\) satisfies
\[
 \Pr_{x\leftarrow U_{\ell}}[F(I(F(x)))=F(x)]\le\frac12.
\]
The compiler must produce a circuit \(G:\{0,1\}^{d}\to\{0,1\}^{m}\), with \(1\le d\le A\ell<m\), in at most \(K(m+1)^r\) bit operations, such that every Boolean distinguishing circuit \(T\) of size at most \(t\) satisfies
\[
 \left|\Pr[T(G(U_d))=1]-\Pr[T(U_m)=1]\right|\le\varepsilon.
\]
The construction may depend on \(s\) and \(\varepsilon\): a separate generator is permitted for each requested pair of these parameters.
cards.why: The amount of true randomness needed by a cryptographic generator can determine whether a hardness assumption yields an efficient deterministic simulation. The question asks whether arbitrary one-way functions support the same linear seed scale available in more structured cases without discarding the quantitative hardness guarantee.

cards.definitions:
The uniform distribution \(U_j\) assigns equal probability to all binary strings of length \(j\). All random variables in the probability expressions are fresh uniform strings of their indicated lengths. The generator itself is deterministic once its seed is fixed.

Circuits are finite directed acyclic Boolean circuits with fan-in-two AND and OR gates, constants, and negations on wires. Size counts AND and OR gates; inputs, constants, fan-out and negations are free, following the source's nonuniform-time convention. A circuit is encoded by a topologically ordered gate list with binary wire indices and polarity bits, followed by the output wires. Negation chains are reduced to a polarity bit. This fixes a polynomial-length representation of a size-\(\ell^b\) function circuit. An inverter has \(\ell\) input and \(\ell\) output bits; a distinguisher has \(m\) input bits and one output bit. Their descriptions may depend arbitrarily on \(F,\ell,s,m,e\). They are not required to be generated by a uniform algorithm. Allowing additional independent random coins does not strengthen either hypothesis or conclusion, since averaging over the coins reduces the relevant bound to deterministic circuits.

Inversion succeeds on any preimage of \(F(x)\), not necessarily the particular sampled \(x\). There is no injectivity, regularity or preimage-size promise on \(F\). The hardness hypothesis is a finite-parameter implication: the compiler is not required to decide whether the supplied circuit really is hard to invert. It must halt with a well-formed generator and the stated seed and time bounds on every input satisfying the syntactic parameter conditions; pseudorandomness is required when the inversion hypothesis holds.

The exponent \(b\) fixes the polynomial evaluation bound of the underlying function. The constants and compiler may depend on \(b\), but not on the particular \(F,\ell,s,m,e\). The integers are supplied in binary and the circuit is explicitly listed. The resource bound is time on a classical multitape Turing machine, including reading the inputs and writing the entire generator circuit. Circuit evaluation consequently also takes polynomial time in \(m\). A uniformly polynomial-time family of functions supplies circuits with some fixed polynomial exponent, so this formulation gives the source's polynomial-output-time explicitness. It does not allow exponential preprocessing hidden in the generator description or polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\) when that quantity is superpolynomial in \(m\).

The chosen parameter range states the nontrivial quantitative regime. At sufficiently large \(\ell\), every function on \(\ell\)-bit inputs has an inverse-selection lookup circuit smaller than \(2^{2\ell}\); greater claimed hardness would therefore have a false premise. With that upper bound on \(s\), errors smaller than \(2^{-2\ell}\) give a displayed time bound below one. Those cases are not additional positive-time security targets. Restricting error to dyadic values loses at most a constant factor when rounding any desired error downward, which can be absorbed in \(K\). The condition \(m>A\ell\) specifies output lengths beyond the allowed linear seed threshold and ensures genuine stretch. The target is asymptotic in \(\ell\), hence the fixed initial cutoff \(\ell_0\).

Both \(s\) and \(e\) are construction inputs, not only quantities used afterwards to assess a single generator. In particular, the question does not require one generator for a fixed \(F,m\) to satisfy all security-error pairs simultaneously. The compiler may inspect and use the full description of \(F\); no restriction to black-box oracle calls is imposed. The exponent \(q\) in the security loss is fixed before the varying parameters and cannot grow with them. Thus the bound is exactly of the form \(s(\varepsilon/m)^{O(1)}\), up to a fixed multiplicative factor and integer rounding.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked construction of the compilers and their constants, together with the uniform polynomial bit-time bound, linear seed bound and stated security implication for every admissible input; or give a complete Lean-checked refutation of this existence statement.

A construction only for permutations, regular functions or another proper subclass is insufficient. Mere existence of some cryptographic generator from a one-way function does not meet the seed-length and quantitative-security requirements. A lower bound restricted to black-box constructions does not refute this unrestricted target. A larger-than-linear seed bound, a security-loss exponent that grows with the input, or unbounded preprocessing is insufficient. The yes-or-no proposition and asymptotic bounds have no numerical approximation tolerance.

cards.title: Optimal private sample complexity for nonsmooth nonconvex optimization
cards.formal: Editorial zero-order variant: determine the sample complexity of uniformly polynomial-time central \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-private algorithms returning \(X\in\mathbb R^d\) with \[\mathbb E\,\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial_\alpha F(X))\le\beta\] for all population objectives in the normalized class below. Determine matching upper and lower bounds up to factors polynomial in \(\log(2+d+1/\alpha+1/\beta+1/\varepsilon+1/\delta)\). Expectation includes the independent dataset and algorithm randomness.
cards.definitions:
The decision variable is \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), with Euclidean norm. Each component obeys \(|f(x;\xi)-f(y;\xi)|\le L\|x-y\|_2\) for all x,y. Assume the expectation defining F is finite and an initial point \(x_0\) is given with \(F(x_0)-\inf_x F(x)\le\Phi\). No convexity or differentiability is assumed. The dataset consists of N independent samples from P; the empirical loss is their average, a different objective from F.

For a locally Lipschitz function h, its Clarke subdifferential \(\partial h(x)\) is the closed convex hull of limits of gradients at differentiability points approaching x. For \(\alpha>0\), define the Goldstein subdifferential \(\partial_\alpha h(x)=\operatorname{conv}\bigcup_{\|y-x\|_2\le\alpha}\partial h(y)\). A point is \((\alpha,\beta)\)-Goldstein stationary when \(\inf_{g\in\partial_\alpha h(x)}\|g\|_2\le\beta\). The radius alpha and residual beta are separate parameters. This does not assert local or global minimality.

Datasets are adjacent when one sample is replaced. Approximate central privacy means that for every adjacent D,D' and measurable output event E, \(\Pr[A(D)\in E]\le e^\varepsilon\Pr[A(D')\in E]+\delta\). Privacy must hold on all datasets, while utility is measured on independent samples from the population. The private output is the returned point; raw sample-dependent oracle evaluations are internal. The source analyzes function-value oracles and also discusses gradient access, and distinguishes single-pass from multiple-pass methods.

For this selected variant set \(L=\Phi=1\), \(x_0=0\), \(d\ge1\), \(0<\alpha,\beta,\varepsilon\le1/2\), and \(0<\delta\le\varepsilon/100\). Components are jointly measurable in the sample and location, globally 1-Lipschitz, with finite population expectations. The input consists of N independently sampled component-function oracles. A zero-order call supplies a sample index i and a real vector x and returns the exact value f(x;xi); gradients and subgradients are not available. Calls may be adaptive and samples may be reused. Each call costs one operation, in addition to the cost of constructing its d-dimensional argument. Use an exact-real RAM with arithmetic +, −, ×, ÷, square roots and comparisons, and independent uniform real draws in [0,1], each charged one operation. All sampled and returned quantities must be measurable. There is no uncharged optimization or integration oracle. One uniform algorithm family must have expected total operation count bounded by one fixed polynomial in N, d, 1/alpha, 1/beta, 1/epsilon, and log(1/delta), on every dataset in the component class. It must terminate almost surely. Privacy holds on every pair of adjacent datasets in that class, not only typical samples. The utility requirement is expected population Goldstein residual, not a per-sample or empirical condition. These access, cost, normalization, parameter and utility choices are editorial specifications of the source’s broader question.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a sample bound \(U(d,\alpha,\beta,\varepsilon,\delta)\), a single uniform algorithm attaining it under the stated cost bound, and a lower bound \(L\) against every algorithm obeying the same model, with \(U/L\) bounded by a fixed polynomial in the displayed logarithm throughout the parameter domain. Prove privacy, expected population utility, sample and time bounds in Lean. Lower bounds for a larger algorithm class are admissible; bounds restricted to a smaller oracle class are not. State any computational assumption explicitly; conditional lower bounds yield only a conditional characterization. An algorithm for component-wise relaxed stationarity does not meet this target.
cards.why: The tradeoff connects privacy, statistical sample size and a general notion of stationarity beyond smooth optimization.

cards.title: Efficient split-state non-malleable codes approaching capacity
cards.formal: Do uniform polynomial-time two-share nonmalleable codes exist with k message bits, equal share length ell(k), negligible statistical error in k, and rate k/(2 ell(k)) tending to 1/2 as k tends to infinity, against all independent tampering functions on the two shares?
cards.definitions:
For each positive integer k, Enc_k is a randomized algorithm mapping {0,1}^k to pairs (L,R) in {0,1}^{ell(k)} squared. Dec_k is deterministic on every such pair and returns a k-bit message or a failure symbol bottom. The length ell(k) is computable in polynomial time and polynomially bounded. Both algorithms are uniform and run in polynomial time in k on every input and random tape; honest decoding equals the message with probability one. No shared setup secret or computational hardness is assumed.

For every pair of arbitrary deterministic maps f,g:{0,1}^{ell(k)} to {0,1}^{ell(k)}, there must exist a probability distribution D_{f,g} on {0,1}^k union {bottom,same} independent of the encoded message. For every message m, the total variation distance between Dec_k(f(L),g(R)), where (L,R) is sampled by Enc_k(m), and the following simulated variable is at most eta(k): sample d from D_{f,g}, output m if d=same, and otherwise output d. One and the same D_{f,g} must work for all m. The error eta is bounded by one negligible function uniformly over all f,g,m: for every c>0, eta(k)<k^{-c} eventually. The simulator need not be efficient.

Tampering maps may be computationally unbounded and know the public code but are fixed independently of the message and encoding randomness. Each sees only its own share; correlated choices of maps are covered by mixtures of deterministic pairs. The target is single-shot nonmalleability, not adaptive repeated tampering or leakage resilience. Rate counts both shares, and convergence to 1/2 is a single uniform family with ell(k)=k+o(k), not a claim about an unbounded-time existential code.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked uniform code family with perfect correctness, the statistical simulation property and the limiting rate, or prove that no such efficient family exists. Computational nonmalleability, bitwise tampering or more than two shares does not answer this information-theoretic two-share question.
cards.why: This asks whether efficient split-state coding can reach its information-theoretic capacity.

cards.title: Subpolynomial-key perfectly secure three-server DPFs
cards.formal: Does there exist a fixed finite Abelian group \(G\), with \(|G|\ge2\), and a uniform three-server distributed point function with perfect correctness, perfect privacy against any one server, and worst-case key length \(\ell(N)=N^{o(1)}\)? For every integer \(N\ge2\), location \(\alpha\in[N]\), and value \(\beta\in G\), key generation must produce three binary keys \((k_0,k_1,k_2)\) such that \[\sum_{i=0}^{2}\operatorname{Eval}_i(k_i,x)=\begin{cases}\beta&x=\alpha,\\0_G&x\ne\alpha\end{cases}\qquad\text{for every }x\in[N]\] with probability one. For each individual \(i\), the distribution of \(k_i\) must be identical for all pairs \((\alpha,\beta)\) with the same \(N\). Every generated key must have at most \(\ell(N)\) bits. The fixed output group may be chosen as part of a positive answer; requiring all output groups is the source's separate question.
cards.why: Distributed point functions compress secret shares of a sparse vector while letting each holder evaluate its share locally. Resolving the three-server question would locate a basic boundary for information-theoretic compression and privacy, with consequences for private retrieval and secure computation that use additive reconstruction.

sentences: A distributed point function gives three servers compact shares of a vector supported at one secret location.
Each server can evaluate its own share, and the three outputs must add to the requested point function.
A single key must reveal exactly no information about either the location or the stored value.
The target is a key length smaller than every positive power of the domain size over some fixed nontrivial finite Abelian group.
Known subpolynomial constructions achieve perfect privacy with four servers or statistical privacy with three, a distinction retained in a 2026 survey.

cards.definitions:
Write \([N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}\). A finite Abelian group is a finite set with an associative and commutative addition, identity \(0_G\), and additive inverses. Its elements have fixed binary names, and its addition table is fixed with the scheme. The point function is zero away from one specified input and takes the specified value there. The case \(\beta=0_G\) is included.

A scheme consists of one randomized Turing machine \(\operatorname{Gen}\) and three deterministic Turing machines \(\operatorname{Eval}_i\), all fixed independently of \(N,\alpha,\beta\). The generator receives the binary encodings of \(N,\alpha,\beta\) and produces three finite bit strings. It may use independent fair bits and must halt with probability one. This convention permits exact sampling from a fixed group of odd order by rejection sampling. Each evaluation machine halts on every valid key and domain input and returns one element of \(G\). The key determines \(N\); its encoding, all public corrections, and any parameter descriptions used in evaluation count toward key length. The machines and the fixed group table are public. There is no additional shared random tape, hidden setup, or uncounted data depending on the particular point function.

This card asks for the information-theoretic key-length bound: it imposes no running-time bound beyond these algorithmic termination conditions. Perfect correctness means that the displayed identities hold simultaneously for all domain inputs with probability one over key generation. Perfect privacy means equality of each single key's entire probability distribution, including its length. Consequently even unlimited computation and arbitrarily many evaluations of that key cannot reveal the location or value. Privacy against a coalition of two servers is not required.

The bound is uniform over locations, values, server indices, and all keys having positive probability. Subpolynomial length means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\), some \(N_\varepsilon\) satisfies \(\ell(N)\le N^{\varepsilon}\) for all integers \(N\ge N_\varepsilon\). The same fixed group and algorithms must work for all \(N\). A security parameter is unnecessary because the privacy error is exactly zero.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such a scheme exists, or a proof that no such scheme exists. A positive answer must specify the algorithms and prove correctness, equality of all required key distributions, termination, and the asymptotic key-length bound. A negative answer must cover every fixed nontrivial finite Abelian output group. Statistical privacy with arbitrarily small positive error, or a construction using four servers, does not meet this target.

context_blocks.text: The source obtains subpolynomial keys with three servers when privacy has a small statistical error, and with four servers when privacy is perfect for suitable fixed output groups. This question asks whether three servers can also achieve exact privacy.

The requirement hides both the special location and its output value. Ordinary private information retrieval permits a client to reconstruct replies using additional private information; such a protocol is not automatically a distributed point function whose server outputs add directly to the desired value.

The card makes the output-group scope explicit: existence for some fixed nontrivial group. It does not require a bound uniform over growing groups. The later paper extends the groups supported by efficient information-theoretic constructions, but the checked statements use different server counts or permit statistical security.

The 2026 survey continues to distinguish the known four-party perfectly secure construction from the three-party statistically secure one. Its stated literature snapshot is February 2026, even though the arXiv version was submitted in July.

cards.definitions:
The common input is the full truth table \(x\) of a function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), with \(n\geq1\) and \(N=2^n\). Let \(C(f)\) be its minimum Boolean circuit size. Fix the standard basis of binary AND and OR and unary NOT, with constant inputs available, arbitrary fan-out, one output, and size equal to the number of gates. Circuits are acyclic and compute every truth-table entry correctly.

A yes-instance satisfies \(C(f)\leq N^\varepsilon\). A no-instance satisfies \(C(f)>N^{1-\varepsilon}\). Inputs between these thresholds have no required decision outcome. The strict no-threshold follows the formal definition in the later source; the thresholds need not be integers. The constant \(\varepsilon\) is chosen once, not supplied per instance. The task has both low-complexity and high-complexity promised inputs at arbitrarily large lengths.

An interactive proof has an honest prover \(P\) and a randomized verifier \(V\). Total communication, rounds and verifier computation are polynomial in \(N\), the explicit truth-table length. No computational bound is imposed on the prover. On every yes-instance, the honest interaction accepts with probability at least \(2/3\). On every no-instance, every cheating prover, including an unbounded one, causes acceptance with probability at most \(1/3\). This is a proof system; soundness only against efficient provers would be an argument system.

Computational zero knowledge requires that for every randomized polynomial-time verifier \(V^*\), including one given arbitrary polynomial-length auxiliary information \(z\), there is a randomized polynomial-time simulator \(S_{V^*}\). Given only \(x,z\), it produces a distribution computationally indistinguishable from the entire view of \(V^*\) in the honest-prover interaction on \(x\). That view includes the common input, auxiliary information, verifier randomness, messages and final output. The simulator is not given a small circuit or other witness.

Indistinguishability is required on all yes-instances: every polynomial-size distinguishing circuit has only negligible advantage in \(N\), uniformly over these instances and polynomial-length auxiliary strings. Negligible means smaller than \(N^{-c}\) for every fixed positive \(c\) at sufficiently large \(N\). The simulator and verifier use the ordinary polynomial-time convention of the later source. No setup, random oracle, trusted third party or hardness assumption is supplied.

The chosen circuit basis fixes a concrete representation. The existential constant-gap formulation tolerates constant-factor changes of standard finite bases by choosing a slightly wider gap and handling finitely many small lengths separately. It does not identify circuits with a shortest program: MINKT instead bounds the program length needed to print a string within a supplied time budget, and its gap parameters constitute a separate choice.

The target asks for one protocol meeting worst-case completeness, soundness and zero knowledge at every input length. A protocol that succeeds on most inputs from a particular distribution or only at infinitely many lengths is a weaker result.
cards.answer_criterion: Give some fixed admissible gap constant and a protocol with proofs of polynomial verifier and simulator cost, completeness, soundness against all provers, and computational zero knowledge against arbitrary efficient auxiliary-input verifiers, without assuming one-way functions or another hardness premise. A negative answer must rule out the specified protocols for every constant in this selected gap family. Failure for that family would not by itself refute all alternatives in the original broader question.

cards.title: Sublinear communication for perfectly secure two-party computation
cards.formal: Is there a uniform two-party protocol in the trusted correlated-randomness model that perfectly computes every Boolean circuit \(C:\{0,1\}^n\times\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) with polynomial setup and computation, and online communication \(O(n+g(s))\) for some function \(g(s)=o(s)\), where \(s\) is the circuit's supplied size? More precisely, seek fixed algorithms, constants \(K,q\ge1\), and \(g:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb R_{\ge1}\) with \(\lim_{s\to\infty}g(s)/s=0\), such that every circuit and every pair of inputs satisfy the correctness and privacy conditions below; dealer computation, total setup length and both parties' computation are at most \(K(n+s+1)^q\), while at most \(K(n+g(s))\) bits are exchanged online. The circuit is arbitrary, without a layering or depth restriction. The additive input-length term fixes the source's sublinearity question in a form that also covers circuits of linear size.

sentences: Two parties want to compute a Boolean circuit while keeping each input perfectly private.
A trusted dealer can distribute correlated randomness before either input is supplied.
The question asks whether polynomial setup and computation can give online communication sublinear in the circuit size, apart from the input-length cost.
Such savings are known for layered circuits, while completely optimal communication can require exponential setup.
The unresolved target covers arbitrary circuits with perfect passive privacy and shared outputs.

cards.definitions:
A circuit is an explicitly given finite directed acyclic graph with \(2n\) input vertices, Boolean constants, fan-in-two AND/OR gates, NOT gates, and one designated output. Fan-out is unrestricted. Let \(s\) count all vertices, including inputs and constants; in particular \(s\ge2n\). Gates and predecessors are encoded in topological order with binary indices. Both parties and the dealer know this public description. The inputs \(x_0,x_1\in\{0,1\}^n\) are private to their respective parties. The size in the bound is that of the supplied circuit; the protocol may optimize its computation, but cannot charge an artificially padded circuit to increase its communication allowance.

Before the parties receive their inputs, a trusted randomized dealer, given only \(C\), samples finite correlated strings \((r_0,r_1)\) and privately sends \(r_b\) to party \(b\). These strings may depend on \(C\) but not on either input. The dealer then takes no further part. Dealer randomness consists of independent fair bits; its computation and output length obey the polynomial bound on every run. Independent local random tapes can be included in these strings. After this phase the parties are deterministic machines on their input, setup string and message history. Their descriptions are fixed across all circuits and lengths, and their complete online runtimes obey the same polynomial bound. There is no other setup, oracle or computational hardness assumption.

The parties exchange binary messages and output private bits \(y_0,y_1\). Perfect correctness means
\[\Pr[y_0\mathbin\oplus y_1=C(x_0,x_1)]=1\]
for every input pair, where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. The task uses the source's shared-output convention: neither party is required to learn the reconstructed answer. Perfect privacy against one passive corruption means that, for each \(b\) and each fixed \(C,x_b\), the distribution of party \(b\)'s entire view is identical for every choice of the other party's input. Its view includes \(r_b\), all sent and received messages and its output. A passive adversary follows the protocol and may inspect that entire view with unlimited computation; the parties do not collude. Privacy and correctness have zero error.

Online cost is the worst-case number of bits sent in both directions, over inputs and all dealer outcomes of positive probability. Message boundaries, control information and input-dependent stopping must be encoded in this communication; timing and silence are not free channels. There is no separate round bound beyond polynomial runtime. The dealer's private deliveries are excluded from online communication but included in the setup-length bound. For every family whose circuit size is polynomial in \(n\), the stated \(\operatorname{poly}(n+s)\) resource bound is polynomial in the input length, as required by the source. A single choice of algorithms, \(K,q,g\) must work for all such families, not only a fixed function or depth.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence, including perfect privacy, correctness, polynomial setup/computation and a uniform sublinear \(g\), or prove that no such protocol and resource bounds exist. A protocol for layered circuits only, a computationally secure construction, or a truth-table protocol using setup exponential in \(n\) does not settle this target. A negative answer must rule out all sublinear savings allowed above, rather than only exactly optimal or one-round online communication.

context_blocks.text: The input-independent setup is a resource, not a free truth table of the function. Beaver-style evaluation uses linear-size correlated randomness and linear online communication. A one-time truth table can make communication linear in the input length, but its exponential setup falls outside this question.

Couteau gives perfect passive-security protocols for layered circuits with communication \(O(n+s/\log\log s)\) for a fixed number of parties and a constant-size output, using polynomial storage. In a layered circuit every edge joins consecutive layers. Transforming a general circuit into this form can increase its size and therefore does not automatically give sublinear cost relative to the original circuit.

The 2023 source proves exponential setup lower bounds when each party sends exactly as much information as its input, including a stronger bound for a single online round. Its functions have a two-bit shared output and input domain size \(N\); the lower bounds are in \(N\), which is exponential in input bit length. These endpoint results do not rule out \(O(n+g(s))\) communication with additional interaction.

Computationally secure protocols may replace large correlations by short pseudorandom descriptions under hardness assumptions. Perfect privacy here requires exact equality of view distributions even for an unbounded observer, so those constructions answer a different question.

cards.title: Polynomial-length constant-query locally decodable codes
cards.formal:
Do there exist an integer \(q\ge1\), real constants \(C\ge1\), \(d\ge1\) and \(0<\delta<1/2\), such that for every integer message length \(k\ge1\) there are an integer \(n\) with \(k\le n\le Ck^d\), an injective encoding
\[
 E_k:\{0,1\}^k\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^n,
\]
and randomized local decoders \(D_{k,i}\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\), satisfying
\[
 \Pr[D_{k,i}^{\,z}=x_i]\ge\frac23
\]
for every message \(x\in\{0,1\}^k\) and every received word \(z\in\{0,1\}^n\) differing from \(E_k(x)\) in fewer than \(\delta n\) coordinates, while each decoder reads at most \(q\) bits of \(z\) on every execution?
cards.why: Determine whether a constant number of bit probes can recover any requested message bit despite a constant fraction of adversarial corruptions using only polynomial storage. This is a central locality-versus-redundancy question with connections to private information retrieval and complexity theory.
cards.status_note: Bounded primary-source checks through 17 September 2026 found no verified resolution of polynomial-length constant-query binary local decoding in the unrestricted model. General fixed-query lower bounds remain polynomial, the August matching-vector bounds restrict the construction class, and the September constant-rate result permits amortized relaxed decoding. This is not an independent full audit of those results.

sentences: A binary locally decodable code lets a decoder recover any requested message bit from a few bits of a corrupted codeword.
The target is a fixed constant number of probes with a fixed positive fraction of arbitrary errors.
The stored length may be any fixed polynomial in the message length, and nonlinear encodings are allowed.
The question concerns existence, without an extra demand for an efficient uniform construction.
A complete Lean-checked answer must establish this family or rule out all such constant-query polynomial-length families.

cards.definitions:
Here \(k\) counts message bits and \(n\) counts stored codeword bits. The Hamming distance between two length-\(n\) words is the number of coordinates where they differ. The allowed corruptions are precisely the words at Hamming distance strictly less than \(\delta n\), as in the source definition. In particular the uncorrupted codeword is included. The constants \(q,C,d,\delta\) are fixed before \(k\); they do not depend on the message, requested coordinate, corruption or code length. The blocklength \(n=n(k)\), encoding and decoder descriptions may depend on \(k\). Polynomial blocklength does not require constant rate or a polynomial of any prescribed degree.

This is an existence question in the classical randomized bit-query model. For fixed \(k,n,i,E_k\), a deterministic query procedure is a finite binary decision tree of depth at most \(q\). Each internal node is labelled by a coordinate \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\); the oracle returns the single bit \(z_j\), and this chooses the next child. Each leaf is labelled by the output bit zero or one. A randomized decoder is a probability distribution over such trees, fixed independently of \(x\) and \(z\). This describes adaptive queries: later coordinates may depend on earlier answers. Repeated queries count toward the same bound, and early stopping is allowed. The tree distribution may depend on the requested index and the code, but the only information it learns about the actual received word is through the queried bits.

The probability in the statement is solely over that decoder's private randomness. The guarantee holds separately for every triple \((x,z,i)\); a single random choice need not decode all message coordinates at once. Corruptions may depend on the full encoding and message and are computationally unrestricted, but \(z\) is fixed before the decoder draws its randomness. There is no secret key or randomness shared with the channel. The output is one bit: an erasure symbol, a candidate list or success only averaged over requested indices does not meet the definition.

Encoding linearity, systematic form and local correction of every codeword coordinate are not required. There is no bound on encoding time, decoder computation between queries or description length, and no additional requirement that one efficient uniform program construct the family. The finite decision-tree formulation makes the query resource explicit without granting access to any unqueried received bits. Codes must be available for every message length under one set of constants; a finite catalogue or a query bound growing with \(k\) does not suffice.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of this existence statement, specifying or proving the existence of the encodings and decoders and verifying the common constants, polynomial blocklength, worst-case query bound and all corruption/success quantifiers; or give a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation.

An efficient explicit construction is sufficient but is not required. A negative proof must rule out every fixed query count and every polynomial degree, including nonlinear codes and the unrestricted decoder model. A lower bound only for two or three queries, only for matching-vector constructions, or only for locally correctable codes does not establish that negation. Relaxed, approximate, list or amortized decoding and growing-alphabet symbol queries require a proved conversion meeting the exact binary single-bit requirements. No approximation tolerance applies to the yes/no target.

source_formulation.text: Are there binary locally decodable codes with a constant number of queries, a fixed positive decoding distance and blocklength polynomial in the message length?
source_formulation.caption: Paraphrase of Vadhan, Open Problem 7.53, printed p. 252 / PDF page 255; the per-coordinate success probability comes from Definition 7.35, printed p. 241.

context_blocks.text: Local decoding retrieves one chosen message bit without scanning the stored codeword. The positive constant corruption fraction prevents a direct read of a systematically stored bit from meeting the requirement.

The textbook gives polynomial-length binary codes with polylogarithmic query complexity and asks whether the query count can be constant. Its cited constant-query constructions instead have superpolynomial blocklength.

The general odd-query lower bounds apply even to nonlinear binary codes. For each fixed query count their blocklength bounds are polynomial, so they leave open a sufficiently large polynomial exponent in this existence question.

The August 2026 matching-vector bound yields superpolynomial length within a particular three-query construction framework at fixed modulus. The target permits other encodings and any fixed query count.
The subsequent August preprint also bounds three-restricted matching-vector families, without claiming a lower bound for every binary locally decodable code.

Relaxed decoders may report failure on some corrupted inputs. Their shorter codes and theorems comparing relaxed and full decoding do not automatically give the required success on every requested message bit.

The September 2026 construction combines relaxed outputs with amortizing queries over a consecutive block of message symbols. Constant queries per recovered symbol in that model are different from a constant total number of probes to recover any one requested bit.
